achievements.label: Professor of Industrial Engineering, University of Ibadan (2002)
Fellow, Nigerian Institution of Production Engineers

api::profile.profile.bio:
Ayodeji Emmanuel Oluleye was born on 18 September 1956 in Efon Alaaye, Ekiti. His father, General Oluleye, was a high-ranking officer in the Nigerian Army whose postings took him and his family all over the country. Ayodeji therefore attended 5 primary schools across Nigeria before gaining admission into GCI in 1969. He was famous in Grier House for representing the House in the Interhouse Shuttlecock Relay Competition every year he was in school.  He was a bright student who attained a Grade 1 in his School Cert exam in 1973. After his A Levels, he gained admission to the University of Ibadan, where he was recognized as a national scholar and was the recipient of the Ondo State Merit Award. He graduated in 1979 with a B.Sc. in Agricultural Engineering. He then proceeded to the UK for postgraduate studies at the Cranfield Institute of Technology. There,  he obtained an M.Sc. in Agricultural Machinery Engineering in 1981. Not forsaking his athletic prowess, he was the 100m, 200m, long jump and triple jump champion. He later obtained his Ph.D. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Ibadan  in 1989.

On his return to Nigeria in 1981 Oluleye joined the academic staff at his alma mater, the University of Ibadan, where he rose through the ranks to become a Professor of Industrial Engineering in 2002. In the process, he published over 100 scientific papers as well as chapters in books and peer reviewed journals. He supervised scores of PhD candidates and trained hundreds of engineers. As Professor and Head department, he strengthened postgraduate monitoring systems, and established industry linkages that ensured a steady supply chain of graduates for specialised industrial roles. He also served on the university’s Implementation Task Force on Classroom and Laboratory Refurbishment and was a member of the Faculty of Technology Board of Studies.

Oluleye also  headed several Committees including the ICT, Internationalisation Strategic Plan and the STEPB PostBasic Science Education project funded by the World Bank, UI Vision and Mission Committee, and the MacArthur Grant Implementation Committee which administered millions of dollars in grants. As Dean of Industrial Engineering, he guided his faculty to first prize at the UI 60th Anniversary Exhibition, formulated collaborative agreements with various industrial and international institutions, developed a Space Management System for accreditation, and established new academic benchmarks and standards for Industrial, Production and Systems Engineering.

Outside the university, Oluleye was a member of the Ondo State Board of Commerce and Industry. He contributed to the establishment of a fundmatching scheme for smallscale industries. He also served on the Industrial Masterplan Study Team under the Federal Ministry of Industries.  Over the years, Oluleye became a major contributor to postgraduate education across Nigeria at various institutions including Obafemi Awolowo University; Nigerian Defence Academy, a; University of Benin; University of Nigeria Nsukka; Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka; Nigerian Defence College, Abuja; Bells University of Technology; and Federal University of Technology, Akure. He was also a Visiting Scientist to the University of KwaZuluNatal, South Africa. Oluleye served as a member of the Board of the Nigeria ICT Forum of Partnership Institutions, where he contributed to ICT training, bandwidth cost reduction, and grant-making under the Partnership for Higher Education in Africa.  He also cochaired the Strategy, Policy, and Management Track of the Nigeria Network Operators Group.

Professor Oluleye is a COREN registered engineer, Member, Nigerian Society of Engineers, Fellow, Nigerian Institution of Production Engineers, Fellow, Institute of Management Consultants, and he is a Chartered Management Consultant.

In conclusion, this high-achieving scholar and Grierson has blended high academic attainment with superior technical expertise in his chosen field to serve his university, his country and the African continent with distinction, thus bringing pride to GCI and Grier House.

achievements.label: Federal Minister of Natural Resources and Social Services
Leader of Opposition, Western House of Assembly

api::profile.profile.bio:
Gbadamosi Adegoke Adelabu was born in Ibadan on 3 September 1915, the son of Sanusi Ashinyanbi and Awujola Adelabu. From 1925, he attended St David's C.M.S. School, Kudeti, Ibadan, later transferring to the C.M.S. Central School, Mapo. Being a very bright student, he had no difficulty gaining admission into Government College, Ibadan, the recently founded elite secondary school for boys, which he attended from 1931 to 1936.

He was a Grierson, having been assigned to that House the very next year after it was founded. His last name at that time, based on his father’s first name, was Sanusi. He was described by his tutors and peers as a brilliant student. Some would say later that he was overconfident and abrasive. By the time he was in 6th Form in 1936, he was the Head of School. This was a vaunted position of responsibility that prepared him admirably for his future career in business and politics. A colorful personality even in his youth, Adelabu’s antics became the stuff of legend decades after he left GCI and Grier House.

On leaving GCI in 1936, Adelabu passed the entrance examination into Yaba Higher College. He performed so well that he was given an academic scholarship by UAC to study Commerce since it was his ambition to go into business. However, after only 6 months, Adelabu left the school, having been offered employment by UAC as an assistant to the district manager in Ibadan.  But he soon left UAC in 1937 to become a merchant in agricultural produce. And in 1939, he became an agricultural inspector and later supervisor of a cooperative society headed by the legendary Akinpelu Obisesan. He stayed with the cooperative until 1945, when he accepted a second job offer with UAC. Having gained enough experience, after a few years, he went into the textile trading business.

It was at this time that Adelabu began to show a lively interest in local politics. He secured the position of Administrative Secretary to the Ibadan Native Authority. And for the local government elections of 1951, Adelabu and others, including Augustus Akinloye, formed the Ibadan People's Party, which over the years stood in opposition to the Action Group led by Obafemi Awolowo. Adelabu then led his small party into an alliance with the NCNC of Nnamidi Azikiwe. Adelabu became active in the organization of the NCNC in Ibadan, and as his profile began to rise, he became recognized as the de facto head of the Ibadan chapter of the NCNC.

In 1952, Adelabu published his first book, “Africa in Ebullition,” detailing his political vision.

For the 1954 elections, Adelabu formed a new organization, the Ibadan Taxpayers Association. At the same time, he was forging strategic alliances with many local political groups including the Mabolaje Grand Alliance. During the local elections in 1954, this alliance won the majority of seats into the Ibadan District Council, paving the way for Adelabu to become chairman. In the federal elections in 1954, Adelabu won a seat to the Federal House of Representatives. He now became the First National Vice President of the NCNC, and was appointed Federal Minister of Natural Resources and Social Services, a post he held concurrently with his position as chairman of the Ibadan District Council, from January 1955 to January 1956.

In 1955, Adelabu's administration was a subject of an inquiry into allegations of corruption in the district council. He was forced to resign his two positions at the local and federal levels after the report of the inquiry was critical of his conduct. In 1956, as leader of the NCNC in the Western region, his party lost decisively to the Action Group. Adelabu then became the leader of opposition in the Western House of Assembly. After this loss, Adelabu, to restore his political ascendancy, sought to carve out a Yoruba Central State from the Western Region. However, this proposal was rejected in 1958 by the majority of legislators in the regional house of representatives.

At the height of his fame as an astute but uncompromising politician, Adelabu died on March 25, 1958 in a motor vehicle accident on the Lagos–Ibadan road. Suspecting foul play, his supporters rioted in the streets of Ibadan for several days, turning his nickname “Penkelemesi” into a violent slogan of frustrated political ambition. Thus it was that controversy followed this famous Grierson throughout his life and at his death.

achievements.label: National Triple Jump Record, Grier Cup (1964)
Captain of Athletics, Grier House and Western Region

api::profile.profile.bio:
Oluyomi Adeyemi-Wilson was born in Lagos on January 4, 1945. After his primary school education at St. Peters Primary School, Faji on Lagos Island, he spent 5 years at Igbobi College from 1958 to 1962. He then came to GCI for his 2-year Higher School Certificate course from January 1963 to December 1964. He had always been good in athletics and had worn his school colors with pride at Igbobi College, but it was when he came to GCI and was assigned to Grier House that he became a star.

Adeyemi-Wilson’s specialties were the long jump, triple jump and high jump. He was so good in all three that on a single day on the GCI Main Field he broke the school record in all 3 events. More athletic glories followed. He captained the Athletic teams for Grier House, GCI and the Western Region for the Hussey Shield interregional athletics competition. At the Grier Cup competition in 1964, he set a national record with a distance of 49 feet, 2 ½ inches in the triple jump. As the best athlete in GCI, he won the Victor Ludorum Trophy that same year, forever enshrining his name in the Grier House rolls of honor. His leadership qualities while he was a student in GCI led to his being selected as a school prefect and receiving the Headmaster’s Award given by Mr. D. J. Bullock in his last year in school.

After leaving GCI, Adeyemi-Wilson received a full scholarship to study Mechanical Engineering at Washington University, St. Louis, Missouri in the Unted States. There, he continued to shine in athletics and academics. He was a letterman in athletics at the university, and he also made the Dean’s List for exceptional academic performance. But then, his hopes for furthering his brilliant athletic career was cut short by an hamstring injury in 1967. After obtaining his BSc  in Mechanical Engineering from Washington University, he proceeded to another famed university in the United States, the Ohio State University, where he obtained his MSc in Mechanical Engineering in 1970.

On returning to Nigeria, Adeyemi-Wilson served professionally with various reputable companies most notably Mobil Producing Nigeria for 32 years, from where he retired as General Manager, External Production. A highly celebrated individual throughout his life, Adeyemi-Wilson is the recipient of various awards and honors: President, Athletic Federation of Nigeria, Fellow, Nigerian Society of Engineers. Member Society of Petroleum Engineers and Nigerian Institute of Management, and Life Member, Nigerian Conservation Foundation, He is a lifelong member of 2 Engineering Honors Societies in the United Stares - Pi Tau Beta and Pi Tau Sigma.

As a notable Grierson, Adeyemi-Wilson shares with Hardin Ekperigin and Victor Ojutalayo the honor of being the most recognized names and best loved athletes in the annals of Grier House.

achievements.label: Lay Reader, St James Cathedral, Ibadan

api::profile.profile.bio:
Samuel Victor Ayodele Ajomale was born in Ede on May 14, 1918. He had his primary education at St. Andrew’s College Demonstration School, Oyo and Government Middle School, Iyaganku. For his secondary education, he initially spent a year at Ibadan Grammar School before he passed the competitive examination for admission to Government College Ibadan .

Entering GCI in 1936, he was assigned to Grier House where over the next 6 years he performed brilliantly in the classroom and on the sports field. He earned his house colors in multiple sports including athletics, where he specialized in the 100 yards dash, football, cricket, swimming and lawn tennis. On the Grier House football team, he played the center forward position when the House won the interhouse football trophy in 1940, just before World War II caused a relocation of GCI students to Lagos. A natural leader, he was Captain of Athletics for the school and was Head of House of Grier House in his last year in school.

After leaving GCI, Ajomale undertook further studies at the School of Agriculture, Moor Plantation, Ibadan, University College Ibadan and the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. As an expert in tropical agriculture, he served meritoriously in various institutions all over the country as an agriculturist, entomologist and civil servant. He worked at the Federal Department of Agricultural Research and the National Cereals Research Institute, both at Moor Plantation. He also worked as a Director at the Nigerian Horticultural Research Institute, Idi Ishin, Ibadan. A man of deep faith as well as science, he was a Lay Reader at the St James Cathedral, Oke Bola, Ibadan. Despite his active life as an agriculturist and civil servant, Ajomale was very active in efforts to maintain GCI and Grier House on a good footing. He was the recipient of the GCIOBA National Merit Award in 1986.

On retirement, he led a peaceful life, surrounded by his family in his residence in Ibadan where he  died on November 17, 2014, aged 96 years.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Gabriel Akinola Deko was born on October 30, 1913 in Lagos. His father was Emmanuel Deko, a carpenter from Idanre who was living temporarily in Lagos at that time. His mother was Siyanbolu from Igbotun, Okitipupa. Gabriel was born a year before Nigeria became a country as a colony and protectorate of Britain in 1914. A very bright child from childhood, Gabriel was educated at home by his father and then at St Peter’s School, Ita Faji on Lagos Island. He gained admission to the CMS Grammar School Lagos. But after a few months, he won a scholarship to attend the new Government College in Ibadan which was established that same year, 1930. In GCI, he was assigned to Grier House, the newly founded second House in the school.

In his new environment in Grier House, Akin Deko soon established himself as perhaps the smartest student not just in his class, but in the whole school. A master of all subjects, he placed first in almost every subject he took. What was surprising, because physically he possessed a small frame, was that he was also good in sports, particularly in athletics. He is credited to have been one of the first students in GCI to use the new “Western Roll” technique in clearing the bar in the high jump, setting a school record in the process. He also shined in practical hands-on subjects like metal work and woodwork.

Akin Deko came under the special attention of the Grier House Master, V.B.V. Powell, under whose guidance, he thrived. As a student, Gabriel always seemed to be on the go. He was also very likable. He made friends with everyone, especially the schoolmasters who were mainly Englishmen in the service of the colonial administration. It did not surprise anyone when, after only 4 years in GCI, Gabriel passed the Cambridge school certificate exam with flying colors. He did so well in fact that he was offered a scholarship to pursue his post-secondary education from 1934 to 1937 at the Yaba Higher College, then the only tertiary institution of learning in Nigeria.

After obtaining his Diploma, he returned to his alma mater, GCI as a tutor in Science and Agriculture. He rose to the post of Assistant Housemaster and then Housemaster of his old house, Grier House. Then from 1947 to 1950, after being awarded a government scholarship, he studied Building Technology at Brixton School of Building, London, England. His career after he returned to Nigeria was in teaching, agriculture and civil construction. But he also devoted a great part of his life to political leadership, public service and sports administration, being a foundation member of the Action Group in Owo, and serving as a Minister in the Western Region government of Obafemi Awolowo. Through all this, Akin Deko was very committed to the welfare of GCI and Grier House. He was a long-serving Chairman and later Life Patron of the GCI Old Boys Association.

Akin Deko died after a short illness on November 6, 1987. He is remembered today as perhaps the foremost son and cherished old boy of GCI and Grier House. His illustrious name is enshrined among the brightest and best of the 1930 set - the very first to be called Griersons.

achievements.label: Parade Commander, National Youth Service Corps (1983)
Special Assistant to the Attorney General of the Federation

api::profile.profile.bio:
James Akingbola Akinola was born on April 9, 1961 in Ilesa. His father, Venerable Festus Akinyele Akinola, was a clergyman and educationist, while his mother, Beatrice Modupe, was a schoolteacher. He started his primary education at Government School, Owo, which he continued at UMC Demonstration School, Oke Ado, Ibadan.

In 1972, Akingbola Akinola was admitted into GCI and assigned to Grier House. His defining activity in GCI was his membership of the school’s Cadet Unit, which he joined in 1973. He took part in army drills at the Nigerian Army cantonment in Mokola and in time he was the leader and trainer of fellow students who he led in numerous march-past parades both in and outside GCI grounds. We are indeed proud to say that under his leadership, the GCI Cadet marching team regularly excelled at the annual Children's Day and Independence Day celebrations at the Liberty Stadium. Akinola also embraced the full range of sporting activities that GCI offered in his time. He was an outstanding member of the Grier House and GCI basketball teams. He also found expression in music, being the vocalist for the Sound Incorporated Band (SI 3) and  a singer in the School Choir, which at that time was a joint ensemble with Queen's School, Ibadan.

After completing his A Levels, he left GCI in June 1979 for the University of Ibadan where he read Political Science. On graduating in 1982, he served with the National Youth Service Corps in Lagos. Utilizing his training with the GCI cadet unit, he proved his worth and was appointed the overall Parade Commander for the NYSC passing-out ceremony at the Tafawa Balewa Square, Lagos in June 1983. This was a very colorful parade that was reviewed by President Shehu Shagari. He then embarked on the study of law. He enrolled at the University of Lagos, where he earned his LL.B in 1986. He proceeded to the Nigerian Law School and was called to the Nigerian Bar in 1987.

Akinola began his law practice at the Civil Litigation Department of the Federal Ministry of Justice, Lagos in November 1987. A year later, he moved into private practice, where he has remained for four decades. In the middle of this however, he had a spell of public service as a Special Assistant to the Attorney General and Federal Minister of Justice, Chief Bola Ige. He held this position until December 2001, when Bola Ige was tragically assassinated.

In January 2002, Akinola returned to private practice at the Law Union in Lagos. His professional standing grew steadily, culminating in his elevation to the Inner Bar as a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) in 2021. In 2024, he was admitted as a member of the Body of Benchers, the apex legal body charged with regulating the legal profession in Nigeria and for admitting practitioners of the highest distinction.

Akinola also built a distinguished career in arbitration, becoming a recognized authority in commercial and maritime dispute resolution within Nigeria and internationally. He is a Fellow and Chartered Arbitrator of the Chartered Institute of Arbitration of the United Kingdom, and served as Chairman of the Institute's Nigerian branch. He was also a past President of the Maritime Arbitrators Association of Nigeria and a member of the London Maritime Arbitrators Association (LMAA). His international standing in the field is reflected in his membership of the Board of the African Arbitration Association (AfAA), the Lagos Chamber of Commerce International Arbitration Centre (LACIAC), and the Council of the International Federation of Commercial Arbitration Institutions (IFCAI).

Today, Akinola is being honored as a Grierson who has embodied, to the fullest degree, the ethos of GCI and Grier House of discipline, excellence in whatever one does, and a firm commitment to the public good.

Founding General Manager, Western Nigeria Water Corporation (1967)

api::profile.profile.bio:
Jibril Adebayo Andu was born on 27 October 1925 in Odosenlu-Alaro in Ijebuland. His father’s name was Andu Odupitan. When he was asked in school what his father’s name was, he gave ‘Andu’ as his answer, and this became his surname.  He had his primary education at  United School, Odosenlu-Alaro and Emmanuel School, Isonyin.  In 1940, he gained admission to GCI where he distinguished himself academically. He graduated in 1945 with a Grade One Distinction in the Cambridge School Certificate Examination.

After this, he proceeded to Yaba Higher College, where he obtained the Intermediate Bachelor of Science degree in 1948. In the same year, he gained admission into the newly established University College Ibadan, but his passion for engineering led him in 1949 to travel to the U.K. on a Nigerian Government and Commonwealth scholarship to pursue his ambition to become a Civil Engineer. He graduated from the University of London in 1952 with a Bachelor of Science Degree in Civil Engineering. With a desire for specialization in water resources engineering, he completed advanced professional training in this field. In 1955, he obtained recognition as a Chartered Engineer, thus becoming Nigeria's first Water and Hydrology Engineer. He also obtained an additional engineering diploma from the Imperial College London in 1959.

Andu started his professional career at the  Ministry of Works and Transport in 1955 as an Engineer Grade II from where he rose rapidly to the position of Chief Water Engineer. In 1967, he was appointed the founding General Manager of the Western Nigeria Water Corporation. In this position, he spearheaded one of the most ambitious water infrastructure development programs in Nigeria' history.  His notable achievements include the establishment of the first hydrological unit for systematic water resources data collection, monitoring and analysis in Western Nigeria, establishing the monumental Asejire Waterworks Project in Ibadan, which at that time was the largest in West Africa, and expansion of  urban and rural water supply schemes throughout the Western Region. In 1976, he founded Andu Engineering Services Limited, a private concern dedicated to water resources and environmental engineering.

Andu’s many professional awards and honors include:  Fellow, Nigerian Society of Engineers (FNSE),  Fellow, Institution of Civil Engineers, Great Britain and Fellow, Institution of Water and Environmental Management, London. He was Chairman of the West African Advisory Committee of the Institution of Civil Engineers, Great Britain. He also served as a Consultant to the World Health Organization (WHO) on public water supply projects in developing countries

Later in life, he went back to his hometown as a traditional ruler, where he reigned as Ako-Bada II, Olu of Odosenlu-Alaro. He died  on 16 April 1999 aged 71.

Today, Oba Jibril Adebayo Andu is remembered not just as a forward-looking monarch but as a pioneering engineer, mentor and role model. His contributions to water engineering, a first in this country, transformed communities, improved public health, and laid the foundations for modern water infrastructure development in Nigeria.

achievements.label: Arubayi Block named in his honour

api::profile.profile.bio:
Eduweye Arubayi was born in 1910 in Effurun, now in the Uvwie local government area of Delta State. His father was Chief Gboruwa Arubayi who served as a magistrate of the customary court in Effurun then in the Western Region of Nigeria. Arubayi attended primary school in Effurun before proceeding to Ibadan for his secondary education. He was one of the select students from all over the Western Region who were admitted in 1929 to the new teacher training institution in Apata Ganga, Ibadan. This was the institution which the following year, 1930, became Government College Ibadan. Arubayi was one of the bright students found academically fit to qualify for the stringent standards to be a foundation member of that new secondary school.

Arubayi was immediately chosen by V. B. V. Powell, the newly appointed  Grier Housemaster, to be one of the first school and house prefects. He and a few others were also allowed to complete their education in just 3 years, not the regular 6 years, Thus, Arubayi was able to pass out of GCI in 1931. In Grier House, he stood out for his leadership qualities and top performance in sports. So much was this so that after leaving Grier House, one of the dormitory buildings in the House was named after him as the ARUBAYI BLOCK. The only other Grierson so honored was his classmate and fellow pioneer prefect, Odiase.

After leaving GCI, Arubayi pursued his post-secondary education at the Survey school in Oyo. After this, he became a Licensed Surveyor and joined the Federal Ministry of Lands and Surveys in this capacity.  His surveying job took him all over the country. After almost a decade, he went into private practice as a surveyor. It is on record that most of the land in the area of the former Midwest Region, which is now Edo and Delta States, were surveyed by him. Apart from his devotion to his profession and his family, Arubayi was very much committed to the traditional culture of this people. In his later years, like his father before him, he was made a traditional chief of the Uvwie kingdom of Delta State.

Arubayi died in September 1987 at his home in Effurum, aged 77yrs. He will always be remembered as the former student and Grierson who bestowed his name on a dormitory block in Grier House.

achievements.label: Professor of Neurology, University of Ibadan

api::profile.profile.bio:
Olajide Feyisara Bademosi was born in Abeokuta on February 25, I941. His father was Olajide Bademosi, and his mother, Mariam Ajisola nee Wilhelm, was the granddaughter of a former Alake of Egbaland. A precocious talent in academics and sports, Jide, as he was known from childhood, had a brilliant stint in primary school, first at the Holy Trinity Anglican School in Kano (1943-49) and then at St. Andrew Anglican School in Ondo (1950-52). After this, he was admitted to GCI at age 12 in 1953. He was assigned to Grier House.

Jide was said by his contemporaries to have been rather playful in his junior years in Grier House. Still, his academic precocity shone bright. And he was always at the top of his class. He also became a very good chess player. It was in the field of sports however that he would establish his lasting fame in Grier House and GCI. He quickly mastered several sports - football, hockey, swimming, table tennis and lawn tennis - and he represented his House and the school in several of them. But it was in cricket that Jide would be forever remembered. Right from his first year in Grier House, it was obvious to all observers that he was destined to be one of the great cricketers for which the school was already becoming famous. His skills in cricket, both as a tenacious opening batsman and a tricky bowler, earned him the nickname ‘Bad Moses.’ This was a play on his last name, Bademosi. He led his Grier House teams to capture the inter-house trophy in both hockey and football as a Junior in 1956 and a Senior in 1959.

His cricket-playing prowess as a prodigious batsman and efficient bowler earned him a reputation that quickly spread beyond the walls of GCI to many schools that GCI played against. These were the select group of elite schools in southern Nigeria that played cricket in those days - Kings College, Igbobi College, St Gregory’s College, Edo College, Benin, as well as the other government colleges - Umuahia, Ughelli, Owerri and Afikpo. Jide was of course the captain of his junior and senior cricket teams for both Grier House and GCI. And in his final year in GCI in 1960, he captained the Western Region team to victory over all opponents at the Morocco-Clarke Cup inter-regional cricket competition. His dominance as a batsman in that series became the talk for decades in Nigerian cricket circles.

In 1961, by virtue of his sterling academic record in GCI and high grades in the Higher School Certificate exam, Jide was admitted to the University of Ibadan to study Medicine. But true to his grit and character, he did not allow the rigors of medical school to deter him. He continued to play cricket at the University of Ibadan. He played for his university’s team, and what is more, took his skills to the international level. Thus, he started playing for the Nigerian national cricket team from 1962 in an uninterrupted run that continued until he retired in 1981 due to health reasons. He was the revered captain of the Nigerian cricket team from 1975. And throughout his cricket-playing career, he distinguished himself as an allrounder, playing the skill roles of a first-class batsman and a very effective and deadly medium fast, in-swing and off-cutter bowler.

While he was carving out a niche for himself on the cricket field, Jide went on to become an outstanding medical researcher, clinician and professor. He earned a well-established reputation as one of the outstanding Nigerian neurologists and academicians of his time. At a relatively young age, Jide Bademosi became a Professor of Neurology at the College of Medicine of the University of Ibadan.

For his personal skills and mentorship of others, Jide Bademosi came to be known and respected as one of the ‘fathers” of the sport of cricket in Nigeria. He is affectionately called ‘Skipper” by all his ‘boys’ to whom he imparted many useful life lessons not only in cricket but in being successful in various fields and professions. Owing him this debt of gratitude are many well respected cricketers some of whom went on to teach younger players the skills they learned from their “skipper.” Among these are former GCI students who went on to play for the Nigerian national team. These include Kolade Mosuro (Carr House), Bayo Ayodele (Field), Deji Otegbeye (Grier), Seye Fadahunsi (Swanston), Sola Olopade (Swanston) and Ladipo Idowu (Swanston). Non-GCI cricket players who also benefited from Jide’s tutelage include Jake Onyechi, Okon Ukpong, Kome Agodo, Uche Ntinu, and Vincent Olise – outstanding individuals who in their own rights, became household names in Nigeria cricket.

Jide Bademosi’s notable leadership positions on behalf of Nigerian cricket include the following: Captain, Nigerian national cricket team: 1975-1981; Chairman, Oyo State Cricket Association: 1986-1989; and Vice Chairman, Nigerian Cricket Association: 1987-1989.

Today, we honor Jide Bademosi, a remarkable Grierson and GCI old boy, for his intellect and achievement as a physician and his dominance in international cricket. We also revere him for his personal skills as a warm-hearted teacher, team captain and medical professor who has made the world better by enriching the lives of his contemporaries and juniors in various fields of human endeavor.

achievements.label: Master of Arts in History, Edinburgh University

api::profile.profile.bio:
Joseph Morakinyo Beckley was born in Lagos on June 6,  1914. His Egba family who were originally from Abeokuta, had settled in an area of extensive rich farmland in a place known as  Ojokoro near Agege. He attended primary school at the African Church Primary School, Ojokoro, from where he passed the entrance exam to be admitted to GCI in 1930. He was in that historic first set of students assigned to Grier House.

He did well in the classroom and in sports. Under the direction and training of V. B. V. Powell, his Grier House Master, he shone in athletics, becoming a champion long-distance runner for the house and the school. In the Grier Cup competition in 1933, he came first place in the mile race. After leaving GCI, he undertook further studies to achieve his ambition of being an educationist, by attending the Yaba Higher College and accumulating experience in teaching and administration. After this, he entered the service of the Northern Region Department of Education. He was one of the first indigenous Nigerian tutors at Government College Zaria, which at that time was known as Kaduna College before it moved to Zaria; later still, it was  renamed Barewa College. This is a school that is now famous for having produced many  national leaders including Nigeria’s first Prime Minister, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa and the military heads of state, Yakubu Gowon, Murtala Mohammed and Umaru Musa Yar’Adua.

Like many of his exceptional classmates from the 1930 set, Beckley did not stay in one place for long. He had caught the bug for high academic achievement from his years in GCI and Grier House. We are therefore not surprised that he soon left to go overseas for postgraduate studies. This was at Edinburgh University in Scotland where he bagged a Master of Arts degree in History. He came back to serve with the Western Region with whom he enjoyed a fruitful and distinguished decades-long career in the civil service.

Among the many honors and awards bestowed on him for meritorious service to his country were the Order of the Niger (OON) and the Award of Recognition from the Ogun State Public Service . On retirement, he led a peaceful family-oriented life in his residence at Bodija Estate, Ibadan. He  died in Ibadan on August 14, 1975 after a short illness.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Sabiru Oladeni Bisiriyu (who later changed his surname to Biobaku after leaving GCI) was born on June 16, 1918 in Igbore, Abeokuta. His father, Sanni Oloyede Biobaku, a Moslem, was a prominent Egba chief and wealthy transporter, who was determined to give his brilliant son a superior education. For his primary education, Biobaku attended Ogbe Methodist Primary School, Abeokuta, from where he gained admission to Government College Ibadan in 1932. He was assigned to Grier House, where he distinguished himself as a bright scholar who shined in History and English Literature. While in school, his last name was Bisiriyu, the name of his maternal grandfather; this was changed later in life to his father’s name. In Grier House, he achieved fame as one of those who contributed to the early fame of the house magazine, the ‘Mustard Seed,’ and for winning many prizes for his English essays and compositions. One later peculiarity of his life was that he cherished his school number (121) so much that he always included this number in many items he possessed, including the registration number of all his personal motor vehicles.

Like many of his peers of that early generation, on finishing from GCI in 1937, Biobaku had his first taste of higher education at the pioneer Yaba Higher College from 1938 to 1940.  After his sojourn in Yaba, armed with a diploma in Education and determined on a teaching career, he went back to Ibadan as a tutor at his alma mater, Government College, Ibadan. In the following years, he taught at other prominent schools all over the nation, most notably Government College, Umuahia. After this, he travelled to England to study at Trinity College, Cambridge University from 1945 to 1947. He obtained a first-class bachelor’s degree with double majors in History and English from Cambridge in 1947.

A few years later in 1950, he would again travel to England for further studies. This time, it was at the University of London's Institute of Historical Research for his MA and PhD in History. On his return to Nigeria, he briefly entered the political arena. He became the Secretary to Obafemi Awolowo, the first Premier of the Western Region.  Incidentally, Biobaku was a student of Awolowo when the latter taught in his primary school in Abeokuta prior to launching his spectacular political career.

After this, Biobaku went back to academia. He lectured, wrote dissertations and learned books, and became a rising star in academic circles. As one of Nigeria’s foremost pioneering historians, Biobaku was the author of countless publications on the history of Nigeria and the Yoruba people. The most well-known of his books are The Egba and their Neighbours 1842–1872, Origin of the Yorubas, Sources of Yoruba History and The Living Culture of Nigeria. Apart from this, he also headed the editorial board of Encyclopedia Africana, and he was the first African Registrar of the University of Ibadan.

In 1965, Biobaku was appointed to the post of Vice-Chancellor of the University of Zambia. But at the same time, he was pressured by Nigeria's Prime Minister, Alhaji Abubakar Tafawa-Balewa, to accept the vacant post of Vice Chancellor of the University of Lagos. There was controversy with this appointment because of some political and ethnic undertones. In 1966, a year after he accepted this appointment, Biobaku was stabbed, during a public event, by a student at the university, Kayode Adams, who incidentally had also attended Government College Ibadan. To this day, the motives for this dastardly attempt on Biobaku’s life are not very clear. But Biobaku survived this attack to continue serving in his position as the second indigenous Vice Chancellor of the University  of Lagos until 1971.

Biobaku’s career in academics and public service was distinguished, varied and exemplary. His many areas of interest and contributions to learned discourse include his detailed proposals to reform Nigeria’s governing structure. He recommended increasing the power of local governments to a greater extent than was hitherto advocated or practiced.  In his speeches and writings, he was also a powerful champion of Pan-Africanism. On the administrative side, he was at various times the chairman of the Nigerian National Antiques Commission and the Nigerian Textile Mills.

Biobaku was the recipient of many honored posts and decorations in his lifetime. He was made Pro-Chancellor, Obafemi Awolowo University. And among his many awards, he received the C.M.G. from the British Queen and the Commander of the Niger (C.O.N.) from the President of Nigeria. He died on February 8, 2001, aged 83.

He is remembered today as a great Grierson and one of Nigeria’s most famous academicians and historians, one of the first to illuminate the history of an African people, the Egbas, with authenticity and local verisimilitude.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Harding Ekperigin was born on April 20, 1913 to an Itsekiri family in Warri. He seemed to have carried with him from his mother’s womb the quickness of limb and unmatched eye-hand coordination that are the hallmarks of a great athlete. He was already a champion runner in his primary school, Government School Warri, when he  won a scholarship to attend GCI in 1932. He did not disappoint the hopes placed on him, for he shone like the star he was right from the start.

As a Grierson in his first year in Form I, he regularly beat boys who were in Junior A on the athletic field – in sprints, hurdles, relay, pole vault, high jump and long jump - even though he was supposed to be in Junior B. During his six years in Grier House from 1932 to 1937, he held a record in every school athletic event he participated in. These included 100 yards, 220 yards, 440 yards, long jump and triple jump. In addition, he captained Grier House in football, cricket, badminton and swimming. Thus, by the time he left Grier House he had won the epithet ‘captain of all games’ - an honor never since equaled in the history of the House.

During the Grier Cup competition in 1937, Ekperigin broke the Nigerian schoolboy records in multiple events including the 120 yards hurdles and the long jump. His 22ft, 2 1/2in record in the latter event stood as a Grier Cup record for a decade until 1947. He also attended Loughborough College in the United Kingdom  where he graduated in 1952 with a Higher National Diploma in Physical Education. Like his mentor, the legendary Grier House Master, V. B. V. Powell, Ekperigin became a noted innovator and pillar of sports in Nigeria. He was one of the founders of the Lagos Athletic Club and the Amateur Athletic Association of Nigeria.

Although a knee injury later cut short his active participation as a competing athlete, he became one of Nigeria’s most notable athletic coaches and sports administrators. He led the Nigerian athletic team to the Commonwealth Games in Vancouver in 1954; and he coached the team for several Olympic Games (Rome 1960, Tokyo 1964 and Mexico 1968). He wrote many books on sports and physical education. And he singlehandedly designed the Physical Education curriculum for all secondary schools in the Western Region in the 1950s and then for the Midwest Region in the early 1960s after this new region was created in 1963. He later retired from the Ministry of Education to join the Bendel State Sports Council.

Acclaimed as the first Grier House sports superstar, Ekperigin was not just a great athlete, he was one of that rare breed – an all-rounder. As a Grierson and legendary sportsman, he set the tone for the dominance of Grier House in sports in the early years after the House was established in 1930. He died in Benin City on January 18, 1981.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Gilbert Nixon Imafidon Enobakhare was born in September 1918 in the village of Oko, near Benin City. His father, Enobakhare Aghedo, a farmer, was a descendant of Chief Aghedo, the Odionwere of Ogbelaka and high priest of Aruosa.

Enobakhare had his primary education at the Baptist School, Benin City, from 1926 to 1932. In 1932, he passed the highly competitive entrance examination for acceptance into Government College, Ibadan. His taking up this offer was initially delayed due to his family’s poor financial straits. But he was able to further his education with the financial support of the Benin Native Administration and Oba Akenzua II of Benin.

Once he enrolled at Government College Ibadan in January 1933, Enobakhare  proved his mettle. While sports participation was not his ‘forte,’ Enobakhare’s performance in the classroom was exceptional, resulting in his being given a double promotion to Form 3 at the end of his first year in the school. He gained the respect of his teachers and fellow students through his diligence, discipline, and superior intellectual performance.

At this end of his school career in GCI, in 1938, Enobakhare received a scholarship to attend Yaba Higher College in Lagos. At that time, this was the only institution for tertiary education in Nigeria. He studied Mathematics, Physics, and Education, and graduated from Yaba in 1941 with the Nigerian Diploma in Education.

He continued his education at the University of London by external study and in 1946, he became one of the first Nigerians to obtain the Bachelor of Science degree in Special Mathematics from this university, followed in 1948 with a Master of Science degree in Mathematics from the same university, specializing in Dynamics and Differential Equations.

After this, Enobakhare devoted most of his professional life to education, starting his teaching career as a master at King’s College, Lagos. After stints at various schools and colleges in the then Western Region, Enobakhare returned to his alma mater to teach Mathematics and Physics at Government College, Ibadan, from 1941 to 1954, during which time he was also the House Master at Grier House. His GCI teaching career was interrupted by a brief period when he helped set up the newly established Edo College, Benin City, of which he was made Principal in 1958. In the same year, he returned to GCI as the first Nigerian principal of his alma mater..

During his life, Enobakhare derived his greatest joy from the many lives he touched from teaching. Many of his students would later rise to national prominence. Among them were Prince Solomon Akenzua, who became the 38th Oba of Benin, Dr. Abel Guobadia, Ambassador and later Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Professor T. M. Yesufu, a fellow GCI old boy who became the first indigenous Vice Chancellor of the University of Benin, and many others who Enobakhare mentored and steered to distinguished careers in education, business, engineering and public service.

In the midst of his work as a teacher, Enobakhare was able to obtain a study leave to go to England for further studies at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he obtained a Master of Arts degree. Promotions and accolades came fast to the diligent and accomplished Enobakhare. From 1959 to 1963, he was the Staff Inspector of Education in Western Nigeria. Thereafter, he entered the civil service of the Mid-West Region which became Bendel State. He served with distinction as Permanent Secretary in several ministries, including Education, Finance, Health, and Works.

After he retired from the civil service, Enobakhare did not remain idle. He became the founder and first Chairman of the Institute of Continuing Education, Benin City. He also served as the pioneer Dean of the Faculty of Education at the University of Benin between September 1974 and June 1975. A man of many parts, Enobakhare was also deeply committed to the preservation of the Edo language. He authored numerous books and manuscripts on Edo language, history and culture, reflecting his determination to preserve important aspects of his Edo heritage for coming generations. And throughout his involvement in these various fields - education, public service and cultural promotion - Enobakhare’s personal ethos lay in diligence, incorruptibility, and an unwavering dedication to serving others.

Enobakhare was known for his extensive friendships, sound judgment, and genuine concern for others.  In his leisure hours, he enjoyed books, music, singing, and playing the violin. He was an active and committed member of the Anglican Church. At St. Matthew's Cathedral, Benin City, he served in several leadership capacities, including Adviser on Educational Matters to the Diocese, Acting Chairman of the Standing Committee, Patron of the Anglican Youth Fellowship, and member of the committee that helped establish St. Michael's College of Theology in Benin City.

In Grier House, G. N. I. Enobakhare is remembered as one of our most notable and influential Griersons - student, tutor, House Master and Principal. He used his tenure in his various positions to enhance the school’s long-established reputation for moral discipline and excellence in many fields of endeavour.

achievements.label: First African Secretary General of OPEC (1975–1976)

api::profile.profile.bio:
Meshach Otokiti Feyide was born on March 31, 1926 in Ipele, in the Western Region of colonial Nigeria, He attended Government College Ibadan from 1940 to 1945, living in Grier House, After a brilliant academic career in GCI especially in Mathematics and Science, Feyide left the shores of his native country for the United Kingdom where he studied at 2 reputable institutions of higher learning:  Cambourne School of Mines and Imperial College, University of London.

On his return to Nigeria after qualifying as a Petroleum Engineer, Feyide enjoyed a distinguished career in his chosen profession spanning several decades. He served mainly in the federal civil service, notably in the Federal Ministry of Mines and Power. Rising rapidly through the ranks, he became Nigeria’s first Chief Petroleum Engineer in 1964, and Director of Petroleum Resources in 1970. He became the Chairman of Nigeria’s only refinery in the 1970s while also serving as Director of several key oil companies in the Niger Delta area in that era of the “oil boom.” And when, on the recommendation of his government, he became the Secretary General of OPEC from January 1, 1975 to December 31, 1976, he was the first African to hold that powerful position.

Under his careful stewardship, Nigeria’s oil production significantly increased, catapulting Nigeria to 8th place in global oil capacity. This was a prodigious achievement for Feyide, conducted with the honesty, excellence and respect for order and due process that would become rare in the subsequent chequered history of the petroleum industry in Nigeria.

Otokiti Feyide is a distinguished Grierson who will be remembered as the first Nigerian to qualify as a Petroleum Engineer. He was part of that special breed of the hardy and disciplined ‘pioneer’ sets who gave Grier House its tradition of excellence in the epochal first decade of its existence.

achievements.label: Head of the Army Cadet Unit
Master's in International Law and Diplomacy, University of Lagos

api::profile.profile.bio:
Olugbenga Jegede was born on June 23, 1964 in Ibadan, His dad, Emmanuel Jegede, was a Radiographer at the University College Hospital (UCH) before he retired to attend law school. His mother, Theresa, was a staff at the UCH Family Planning Clinic.  Jegede grew up in the UCH compound in the company of childhood friends such as Segun Cole, Jide Ogunro, and Bola Akioye who also later attended GCI.

After attending Alafia Nursery and Primary School, Mokola from 1967 to 1975, Jegede was admitted to GCI and assigned to Grier House in 1975. He credits his teur Yinka Gbotosho ’75 with easing his transition from primary school to the tough boarding secondary school environment. Because of his love for parades and march-pasts, he joined the GCI Army Cadet Unit when he was in Form 2. His team won the First Prize in the March Past during several of the Children’s Day and Independence Day celebrations held annually at Liberty Stadium, Ibadan. He was also a member of Sounds Incorporated (SI), the school band for which he played keyboards. In his last year during the 1981-82 session, he became Head of the Army Cadet Unit. He was also co-Prefect for Hockey and Head of School.

After leaving GCI, Jegede studied at the University of Lagos from 1982 to 1985, obtaining a BSc in Economics. This was followed by a NYSC posting in the same institution, and a master’s degree in international law and diplomacy, also from the University of Lagos, in 1987.

His first job after graduation was with the Department of State Services (DSS) from November 1987 to May 1993. After this, he joined the Shell Petroleum Development Company, where he worked in various areas of operation for 28 years until he retired in 2021.

Olugbenga Jegede is an outstanding leader and example of his generation, who despite many challenges, kept the flag of excellence and achievement flying for Grier House and GCI.

Chairman, Western State Public Service Commission
Past President, Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria

api::profile.profile.bio:
Michael Adebayo Ifaturoti was born in Ilesha on October 10, 1925. His parents were Adegbola Ifaturoti of the Odundun ruling house of Ijeshaland, and Ajayi Ifaturoti nee Onigbogi, who was descended from a lineage of Ijesha chieftains dating back to the mid nineteenth century.

For his primary education from 1933 to 1939, Ifaturoti started school in Ilesha, his hometown. But he finished at Aremo Anglican School, Ibadan. By dint of superior academic prowess, he was offered a full six-year scholarship when in January 1940, he gained admission into the now famous Government College Ibadan. He was assigned to Grier House where he took part in all activities including sports. In particular, he learned to play lawn tennis very well -  a pastime that would give him much pleasure throughout his life.

Ifaturoti would say later in his life that the most important lessons he ever learnt were those imparted to him in Grier House. He performed very well in various subjects, especially English and Mathematics. And he became an avid reader – so much so that he made a reptation for himself as being the second student by that time in the history of GCI, after the renowned Adegoke Adelabu also a Grierson, to have read every book in the school library. He wrote as well as he read, and he contributed articles regularly to the ‘Mustard Seed,’ the House magazine. Ifaturoti was a house prefect in his final year in Grier House. And to cap an excellent academic record in school, he was one of the distinguished students in GCI who passed the Cambridge School Certificate Examination in Grade 1 in December 1945.

On leaving school and needing a job, Ifaturoti applied to, and was immediately employed by the Department of Mines. His superiors there offered him a scholarship to study Mining Engineering in England. However, Ifaturoti elected to pursue an academic degree at the university. What appealed to him was the opportunity and distinction of attending primary school, secondary school and university all in the same town of Ibadan. He would be one of the first Nigerians to attend university in their own country. This was how he became one of the first students admitted into the newly established University College Ibadan. He graduated from UCI in 1954, obtaining a Bachelor of Science degree with a rare combined honours in Mathematics and Physics.

Not resting on his laurels, Ifaturoti went om to pursue post graduate courses in England - first at the University of Leicester from 1955 to 1956, and then at the prestigious London School of Economics from 1961 to 1962. From these two institutions, he bagged postgraduate diplomas in Education and Personnel Management. He would later add a final feather to his academic cap with a Master of Arts degree in History in 1981from his original alma mater, which had now been renamed the University of Ibadan.

Armed with a superior education from these distinguished institutions of learning, Ifaturoti spent the remainder of his life serving with honour and dedication in the public and private sectors in Nigeria. He was a pioneer indigenous senior management staff at the United Africa Company (UAC) between 1960 and 1974. During this time, he was the Principal of the UAC Training College in Lagos. He also held the positions of Personnel Manager at the Nigerian Breweries, Lagos and Niger Motors, Ibadan. His public service included tenures as the Western State Commissioner of Economic Development and Planning (1974-75) and Commissioner of Education (1975). He was also Chairman of the Western State Public Service Commission (1976-78) and Chairman of WEMABOD, later renamed O'dua Investments Company. Ifaturoti was the founder and principal partner of one of Nigeria’s first indigenous management consultancy firms, MAIC Ltd. And from 1981 to 1986, he was the Group Personnel Controller of SCOA at its headquarters in Lagos.

During his long and distinguished professional career, Ifaturoti was an active member of various professional associations and bodies. He was a foundation member of the Institute of Management Consultants of Nigeria (IMCN), Fellow and past President of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPMN), as well as Fellow and Vice Chairman of the Nigerian Institute of Management, (NIM) in addition to being a member of the British Institute of Personnel Management (BIPM). He also had a stint at academics, lecturing at the graduate school of the University of Ife’s Faculty of Business Administration in the 1970s and 1980s.

In 1957 at age 32, Ifaturoti married his sweetheart who he had met as a fellow undergraduate at the University College Ibadan. She was Olusolape Folasade Akinkugbe, first daughter of Chief D. A. Akinkugbe (1898-1980), the Odofin of Ondo. Their union was blessed with five children who all made a success in various professional callings in and outside Nigeria.

Ifaturoti never forgot his roots. As a member of the traditional council in his native Ijeshaland, he was conferred, for his dedication to the affairs of his people, with the traditional title, ‘Loja Wasare Ijana’. A man of deep commitment to the well-being of his fellow men Ifaturoti was the sponsor and patron of various civic, philanthropic and religious causes in his hometown of Ilesha and other parts of Nigeria. At the age of 81, on February 21, 2007, Ifaturoti passed away peacefully at his home ‘Ule Ayo’ located in the Okeopo district of the ancient city of Ilesha.

Ifaturoti was a man who lived and died according to the high arching principles he had learned as a Grierson.

Professor of Applied Mathematics, Federal University of Technology, Akure
Chairman, Ondo State Universal Primary Education Board

api::profile.profile.bio:
Kayode Ogunmoyela was born in Ifon, in present day Ondo State on December 1, 1950. He attended St. Barnabas (later renamed St. Paul’s) Primary School in Ifon, He then briefly enrolled in the District Council School. Idi-Ope, Oyo, before gaining admission into Government College, Ibadan.

During his time in Grier House from January 1963 to December 1969, Ogunmoyela made his mark. He was bright academically. And he shone in sports at a very high level. While in Form 4 in 1966, he won a tightly contested school table tennis championship against the previously undefeated Adewale Thomas ’62 of Carr House. He played multiple other sports, including football, hockey and cricket for the house and school. He was captain of the house table tennis team which won several interhouse trophies on behalf of Grier House. He was a member of the GCI Football and Table Tennis teams. A confident leader who combined strictness with a loving disposition towards his mates and juniors, he was made Head of House in his final year in Sixth Form in 1969.

After leaving GCI, Ogunmoyela read Mathematics at the University of Ife. In 1973, while serving in his national youth service year in the former East Central State of Nigeria, he won the maiden Head of State Award which was given to the 12 most outstanding NYSC members from each of the twelve states of the Federation. After this, Ogunmoyela proceeded to Exeter University, UK where he obtained his PhD in 1980. After a stellar academic career teaching at the University of Ife and later at the Polytechnic, Ibadan, he settled at the Federal University of Technology, Akure where he became a Professor of Applied Mathematics. He also had time for public service. He was a well-known figure in Ondo State politics. One of Ogunmoyela’s lasting contributions was in his position as the Chairman of Ondo State Universal Primary Education Board between 1994 and 1999. For his leadership and service to his community, Ogunmoyela was the recipient of several chieftaincy titles including those of Gbobaniyi of Uso and Ajiroba of Ifon, Ondo State.

Ogunmoyela was serving his people in these various academic and public service roles when he was involved in a ghastly motor vehicle accident that eventually led to his death in 2015. Today, he is remembered as a worthy Grierson and Head of House whose leadership qualities and sterling performance in multiple areas, including sports, made him one of the most celebrated Griersons of his generation of the mid to late 1960s.

achievements.label: National Senior Record, 880 Yards and Mile (1958–1962)

api::profile.profile.bio:
Victor Olusegun Ojutalayo was born on August 10, 1940. His father, Gabriel Elusoji Ojutalayo, a GCI old boy of the 1931 set who was in Swanston House, had earned fame during his time in the school as a notable long-distance athlete nicknamed “Sukuru Boy”.

After a distinguished primary school education at N.A. Primary School Ibadan, St. John’s Primary School, Owo and St. Stephens Primary School, Modakeke, where he outshone his schoolmates in academics and athletics, Ojutalayo commenced his studies at Government College Ibadan in September 1955. His admission was remarkable because two of his brothers had also gained admission to GCI in the same year: Kole, assigned to Carr House and Johnson, assigned to Swanston House.

In Grier House, Ojutalayo soon made his mark as a generational talent on the athletic field. Like his dad, he was a star. He won many laurels for Grier House and GCI including the Victor Ludorum trophy in 1962.  Outside the athletic field, in the classroom and on the House grounds, Ojutalayo came to the notice of everyone who met him as a born leader who was disciplined, focused, and committed to excellence in everything he pursued.

Ojutalayo’s fame in athletics came from his dominance in long-distance events. Between 1958 and 1962, he held the national senior record and the Commonwealth secondary school record in 880 yards and the mile. And on a memorable day in 1957, he broke the GCI record in the mile previously held two decades earlier by his father, Gabriel. While still in school, Ojutalayo made a name for himself as an international athlete. He competed for the Nigerian national team, and his exploits were recorded by the national newspapers and sports journals of the day.

After leaving GCI, Ojutalayo was encouraged to study Agricultural Economics by Gabriel Akin-Deko, a Grierson of the 1930 set who served as Minister of Agriculture during the golden era of the Western Region in the late 1950s and had a distinguished international career with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Ojutalayo began his university studies at the University of Nigeria Nsukka. But when the Nigerian Civil War broke out in 1967, Victor transferred from Nsukka to the University of Ibadan, where he completed his degree.

After graduation, Ojutalayo embarked on a career in agricultural research, development and planning. He had stints in the private sector and the World Bank where he contributed to that organization’s agricultural development plans for African countries.  After this, Ojutalayo took his experience into the civil service in Nigeria at the national and state level. This allowed him to rise to the position of Commissioner for Agriculture and Natural Resources in Oyo State, which incidentally was a position held two decades earlier by his mentor, Gabriel Akin-Deko.

As he became very active in corporate leadership and public service, Ojutalayo continued to shape sports development policy in Nigeria. At various times, he was Chairman of the Nigerian Hockey Federation, member of the Nigerian Athletics Federation, and leader of the Nigerian delegation to various international sports competitions, including the Seoul Olympic Games.  For his services to his country, state and school, Ojutalayo was honored with the “Heroes of Yesteryears” award.

A proud son of Ile-Ife, Ojutalayo was conferred with the traditional title of Woye Lakogba. He used this position to work with Ooni Sijuwade in developing an enduring blueprint for many development projects in Ile-Ife. He was deeply committed to the preservation of Yoruba culture and traditional communal life. His home was a place of hospitality, advice, and  support for family, friends and strangers. Thus, he was a life-long guide and mentor for family members and other young people he met in the course of his profession and government service. Among these were Professor Oye Ibidapo-Obe, one time Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos, Dr Wale Babalakin, GCIOBA National President, Mr. Tayo Babalakin, Dr. Omitowoju and many others. He was a longtime Chairman of the Lagos branch of GCIOBA.

Victor Ojutalayo passed away in November 1999 in his house at Ogudu GRA Lagos at the age of 59 years.

Today, he is remembered as one of the most outstanding schoolboy athletes of his generation. His sports prowess has placed him on a pedestal with legendary Nigerian athletes of that era such as A. K. Amu, Immanuel Ifeajuna and Violet Odogwu.  By personifying the spirit of Grier House and GCI in his character, leadership qualities and sports performance, Victor Ojutalayo remains a model for every Grierson.

First Class, Mathematics, University College Ibadan (1955)
Ph.D. in Applied Mathematics, St Andrews University (1960)

api::profile.profile.bio:
Victor Omololu Sowemimo Olunloyo was born in Ibadan on April 14, 1935 to a Christian father, Horatio Olunloyo and a Moslem mother, Bintu Tejumola Abebi Olunloyo. His family is reputed to be one of the first to embrace Western education in the city of Ibadan after Christian schools were established in Ibadan by the English missionaries, David and Anna Hinderer in the nineteenth century. An early female member of the family, Yejide Olunloyo, was, according to tradition, one of these pioneer pupils of these missionaries. Reputedly, she was the one after whom Yejide Girls Grammar School, Ibadan was named.

From an early age, Olunloyo astounded his parents, teachers and peers with his academic brilliance and aptitude for various subjects. This was especially true in Mathematics, which he embraced from his primary school days at Holy Trinity Primary School, Ebute-Ero, and later at Olowogbowo Methodist Primary School, Lagos Island. His family’s frequent relocations then took him to St Peter’s Primary School, Aremo, Ibadan. After this, he attended St Paul’s Anglican Primary School, Gbongan, where he concluded his primary education in 1947.

In 1948, when Olunloyo sat for the entrance examination to Government College, Ibadan, he ranked 10th out of 2,000 applicants, securing a full scholarship that paid for his education in GCI. Despite the untimely death of his father during his first year in GCI, he quickly rose to the top of his class. He excelled in academics and sports. In cricket, he earned accolades as the opening bowler for the school team. When he sat for his Higher School Certificate (HSC) exams, he was the top performing student in the entire Ibadan Province.

After leaving GCI in 1953, he enrolled at the University College Ibadan, after first studying privately for his A-levels, which he completed in 1954. A recipient of a scholarship to study Mathematics, Olunloyo completed his bachelor’s degree in record time, graduating first class in 1955. He spent less than a year obtaining his degree since he had already scaled his A-levels and Inter-BSc by self-study which enabled him to pass the requisite exams and be given advanced placement.

PhD (Applied Mathematics) St. Andrews University, Scotland. 1960. Thesis: Numerical Determination of the Solutions of Eigenvalue Problems of the Sturm–Liouville Type.

Author of many learned articles in the areas of Numbers Theory and Applied Mathematics.

Youngest person, at age 27, to serve as a Minister in the Western Region of Nigeria.

State Commissioner in multiple Ministries: Economic Development, Education, Special Duties, Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs.

Chairman of the Western Nigeria Development Corporation.

Governor, Oyo State, 1983

In midlife, Olunloyo left academics to become immersed in politics and public affairs.  He vied for and won the highly contested post of Governor of Oyo State. In time, he became one of the most recognizable names in the public eye not just in Yorubaland but throughout Nigeria. This notable Grierson became an idolized public figure who was honored during and after his life for the brilliance, original thinking and overarching achievement with which he blessed our world, and for the warmth of his friendship with friends and opponents alike.

Olunloyo died in his hometown of Ibadan on 6 April 2025 at the age of 89 years. He was mourned by monarchs, commoners and heads of state. Since then, many public institutions have been named after him. These include the Ibadan Polytechnic and the Omololu Olunloyo Recreational Park in Ibadan. A sometimes controversial figure, Olunloyo remains one of the most well known Griersons of any generation.

Abimbola Onajin was born in Ibadan. His father, Samuel Olaniyi Onajin, hailed from Ondo but settled in Ibadan after securing employment with the Western Region Agriculture Department in Moor Plantation where he became Station Manager. Thus, as a boy, Onajin lived next door to GCI. The primary school he attended was the N.A. Practicing School which abutted the GCI Main Field. There was never any doubt which secondary school he was going to attend - especially since 2 of his older brothers attended GCI and were Griersons.

Onajin was admitted to GCI in January 1958.  Living in the dormitory in Grier House for the next seven years, he became known as a cheerful and intelligent student, who lived the life of a super talented Grierson. A leader in the classroom, the house grounds and on the sports field, he was very good in several sports especially football, athletics and cricket. As a recognized generational talent, he became captain of cricket not only for Grier House but GCI. He was active in many students’ clubs including being the president of the Science Society. In his final year in Sixth form, he was made a school prefect and Head of House. But Onajin transferred to Swanston House in the middle of his tenure as Head of Grier House because of a controversial fallout he had with his Housemaster over the discipline of erring junior boys.

After leaving GCI, Onajin won an academic scholarship to study Electrical Engineering at the G Chalmers University, Guttenberg in Sweden. On his return to Nigeria, he worked in various companies including SCOA to spearhead many landmark innovations in motor vehicle manufacturing and  assembly.

Today, Onajin is remembered as a sports icon and leader - the prototypical Grierson and GCI old boy who would stoutly defend truth and honor in the face of pressure to do what he knows to be wrong.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Tunji Otegbeye was born in Ilaro on July 14, 1926. For his primary education, he attended Christ Church Primary School in Ilaro. before entering Government College Ibadan, where he was assigned to Grier House, in 1942. His time in Grier House, which spanned the years of World War 2, when GCI was temporarily relocated to the St Theresa’s convent compound in Oke Ado, helped shape the intellectual curiosity, independent thinking and fearless spirit that would characterize the rest of his life. By the time he left Grier House in 1947, he was fully developed with a caring nature, social ideology and the firm goal of devoting his life to helping his fellow human beings and alleviating human suffering.

In 1948, the year after leaving GCI, Otegbeye was one of the pioneer students at the newly established University College, Ibadan, where he was admitted to study Medicine. After completing his preclinical studies in Ibadan, he proceeded to the UK where he completed his clinic rotations at the Middlesex Hospital Medical School, London, graduating in 1956. While in Britain, Otegbeye became deeply involved in left-wing politics with the Nigerian Union and the West African Students' Union. He served in various leadership positions in these 2 organizations, and campaigned actively for Nigerian independence. An eloquent public speaker, he was a familiar presence at London's Hyde Park Speakers' Corner, where he used his gifts for oratory to argue for self-determination for colonized African nations and social justice in all parts of the world.

Returning home in 1957, he worked at the University College Hospital, Ibadan, and then the Lagos Town Council. He then left government service to go into private medical practice, establishing Ireti Hospital in Lagos in 1960. Under his stewardship, this hospital grew into a well-known and respected private hospital group. His medical practice reflected his personal philosophy of serving humanity without emphasis on financial considerations. Thus, he made sure that patients who were unable to pay received treatment.

A humanist with a deep belief in social justice and political activism, Otegbeye became one of Nigeria's foremost voices for youth participation in the political life of the nation. He believed firmly in social democracy and Pan-Africanism. He played a leading role in the establishment of the Nigerian Youth Congress (N.Y.C.) in 1960, and later served as its President. The N.Y.C. mobilized students, workers, and young professionals against the pervasive influence of colonial mentality, ethnic division, and political injustice which plagued Nigeria after its independence from Great Britain. Under his leadership, the organization became one of the most influential progressive youth movements during Nigeria's First Republic. Then in 1963, he founded the Socialist Workers and Farmers Party of Nigeria (SWAFP), with a political platform that promoted socio-economic equality, workers' rights  and national unity. His radical ‘socialist’ views placed him in conflict with successive governments in Nigeria. At various times, he suffered arrests, prolonged detention, and political persecution. Despite this, at great risk to his own life and health, he remained steadfast in defending freedom and promoting democratic ideals for the nation.

Otegbeye was a patriot who cooperated with the government when the occasion demanded. During the Nigerian Civil War (1967-70) he acted as a liaison between his country and the Soviet Union. In his adult life, he mentored young people, supported educational initiatives, and contributed generously to the development of his Ilaro hometown and district in the Yewa area of Ogun State. When Otegbeye passed away on 9 October 2009 at the age of 84 years, he left behind an unforgettable legacy defined by courage, principled living and a firm adherence to a progressive political ideology including the provision of affordable health care to all people.

A man of singular passion and commitment, Otegbeye believed that the outstanding education he received in GCI bestowed on him an obligation to serve. His life story as a Grierson reminds us that our ambition should not merely aim for financial success, but that we should aim to use our gifts to improve society.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Born in 1923 as the first son of Oba Akenzua II and heir to the ancient Benin Empire, Prince Solomon Aiseokhuoba Igbinoghodua Akenzua attended primary school at Government School, Benin. He was a brilliant student, full of wisdom beyond his years. These traits prepared him to pass the tough entrance examination and interview to be admitted into Government College Ibadan in 1940.

A story is still told that Prince Akenzua turned up in the school compound in GCI accompanied by a dozen palace servants carrying his personal belongings. The indignant GCI Principal was said to have ordered these porters to take all the baggage back to the school gate from where the young prince was made to carry, with his own hands, just one portmanteau and the few belongings he would actually need in school. The story, though popular and pleasing to the romantic ear, appears to be apocryphal.

The young Prince Akenzua was assigned to Grier House, where he set out to distinguish himself in his studies and in several house and school-sponsored sports activities like any commoner. He quickly found his niche in the playing fields and classrooms of his famous school. At the end of six years, he sat for and passed with flying colors, the tough University of London Matriculation Examination, which qualified him to gain admission into Yaba College, Lagos in 1945.

At the end of his course at Yaba, Prince Solomon proceeded to King’s College, Cambridge University where he studied Law and Administration. He bachelor’s degree in Law in record time and was called to the Bar. He then returned to Nigeria to join the Eastern Nigeria Civil Service as a District Officer in 1957. He later transferred to the Federal Civil Service where he rose to the highest position of Permanent Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Health. In 1973, he left this position to become the regional representative of Gulf Oil Company, now Chevron. After this stint in the corporate world, he was appointed Commissioner for Finance for the Bendel State of Nigeria during the military administration of Major-General Agbazika Innih in 1975.

Prince Akenzua knew he had to prepare for the challenges that would face him in the performance of his duties as the next Oba. He therefore retired finally from public service and went back to the palace in Benin. He began to learn under the tutelage of his father, Oba Akenzua II. This period of training proved to be timely and important for the monarch-in-waiting. For on Saturday, March 23, 1979, Prince Solomon Akenzua became the 38th Oba of Benin on the death of his father. He assumed this ancient throne with the resplendent title of Omo N’Oba N’Edo, Uku Akpolokpolo, Erediauwa, CFR, Oba of Benin.

As heir apparent to the seat of the ancient line of monarchs of the Benin Empire, the prince had been christened Solomon at the time of his birth. This was due to the influence of his father who was a devout Christian. For it was predicted that the young prince would grow up to be as wise as King Solomon. His second name Igbinoghodua, “The Lord will be your strength” in the Bini language, and his third name, Aiseokhuoba “No one would dare invite your wrath” were all given on him by his royal grandfather, Oba Eweka II. Those birth names, and the royal title he assumed on becoming the monarch – Erediauwa, “The one who has come to put the house in order” - proved portentous during his reign as the Oba of Benin. As one of the most revered traditional rulers in Nigeria, Oba Erediauwa skillfully steered the ship of state to usher in an unprecedented time of peace and tranquility in his kingdom. The Oba supervised a monumental transformation of Benin City. This ancient capital of the Bini people was rapidly transformed from an old village of mud-walled houses to a modern city of wide boulevards, tree-lined university campuses and gleaming high-rise office buildings.

Despite his power and status, the former Prince Solomon continued to remember his days in Grier House and GCI. He communicated frequently with his former classmates and entertained delegations of GCI old boys when they called on him in his palace in Benin City. Full of wisdom and years, Oba Erediauwa died on March 16, 2015. He was succeeded by his son, Ewuare II. From a simple life as a lowly Grierson to monarch of an ancient empire, the story of Prince Solomon Akenzua continues to intrigue and inspire generations of Griersons.
