api::profile.profile.bio:
Ayotunde Rosiji was born on February 24, 1917 in Abeokuta. His father was a policeman. After his primary school education at Christ Church School, Abeokuta, he first attended Ibadan Grammar School for a year before being successful in the entrance examination to GCI where he was a student between 1933 and 1938. In Grier House, he impressed everyone with his affinity for Science, Math and Physics and his dedication at the school Workshop where he helped to design and operate various types of mechanical devices, Everyone knew he wanted to be an engineer.

Like many of his classmates of that brilliant pioneer generation, after leaving GCI, Rosji was one of the earliest students admitted to the Yaba Higher College where he studied Engineering. After this, he worked as an engineer with Shell. But after a few years, he became restless and proceeded to the United Kingdom where he turned to the study of Law, receiving a Bachelor’s degree from the University of London.

Rosiji would later become one of the most notable and controversial politicians of the Nigerian First Republic. He was one of the founders of Obafemi Awolowo’s Action Group, the dominant political party in the Western Region throughout the 1950s. He was the first Secretary-General of this party. Later, he switched sides to the N.C.N.C. and became the first Federal Minister of Health from 1957 to 1959. He later switched to the N. N. D. P. under S. L. Akintola who had split from Awo’s Action Group. In this new dispensation, he was made Federal Minister without Portfolio in 1964 and Minister of Information from 1965 to 1966 under the Balewa government. His political posts ended when the government was overthrown in Nigeria’s first military coup. After leaving politics, Rosiji made a name for himself as an industrialist. He owned and operated a series of factories and industrial concerns in Lagos and the southwest of Nigeria. Despite a busy life in engineering, industry, law, politics and public service, Rosiji was a philanthropist and avid patron of art, music and wildlife conservation. He was a founder and life-long patron of the Musical Society of Nigeria (MUSON). Rosiji died on July 31, 2000 in Lagos, aged 83 years.

Like T. M. Aluko, G.N.I. Enobakhare and many of his classmates in the ’33 set, this engineer turned lawyer, statesman and industrialist is an icon. The name of Ayo Rosiji, though controversial in some political quarters, symbolizes Grier House as the birthplace of excellence and multi-talented accomplishment.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Andrew Esanjumi Sagay was born in a small village outside Sapele on February 22, 1912. This was before Nigeria became a nation as a British colony and protectorate in 1914. His parents were of Itsekiri and Bini stock. He had 10 siblings. His eldest sister was the mother of 2 distinguished GCI old boys, Banwo Smith ’59 and Zai Smith ’63, both of Field House. Sagay had his primary education at Government School, Sapele. He did very well and passed the entrance examination and interview for admission into Government College Ibadan in 1930.

Once he arrived in GCI, he was assigned to the newly created Grier House where he shared a dormitory with Akin Deko, who became his life-long best friend. He came under the wings of the charismatic House Master, V. B. V. Powell, who would become his life-long mentor and friend. In sports, Sagay was said to have been a long-distance runner. But his skills were mainly exercised in the classroom where he was a much-acknowledged master of many subjects.

After 4 years in GCI, Sagay was one of the lucky few to be admitted to the newly established Yaba Higher College, on the basis of a highly competitive exam in which he placed first among all candidates. He was selected for the elite pre-medical course. But Sagay discovered he could not stand seeing dead bodies being dissected in the Anatomy class. He therefore switched to Botany. On graduation from Yaba Higher College in 1935, Sagay returned to his alma mater GCI as a tutor in Science and Agriculture. His responsibilities included managing the school farm. He was very popular with the mostly white staff and was admired by his students who were happy to have a Nigerian tutor.  He also earned a deserved reputation as a disciplinarian. The story is told of how Sagay as a tutor once administered 54 strokes of the cane to an erring T. M. Aluko when the latter was a student. Despite this, he was fair, and he set a good example to his students. Like his mentor, V. B. V. Powell, he later became House Master of Grier House for a very short period after Akin-Deko left the position to travel to England for further studies.

Eager to advance his career, Sagay travelled to England in 1948, His flat mate in his London digs was a fellow Grierson, S. B. Biobaku ‘32. With the encouragement of V. B. V. Powell, he was admitted to Oxford University on a scholarship and obtained his bachelor’s degree in 1951.

On returning to Nigeria, he worked as a botanist at the Federal Ministry of Agriculture,  based in Ikeja. He then transferred to the Ministry of Education of the Western Region and was posted to Government College Ughelli as a Science Master. He also served as an Inspector of Education for the Ministry, and in 1958, was Principal, Government Teachers Training College, Ibadan.  After this, he went on a sabbatical leave to the U.S.A. working for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). He also earned a Master’s degree in Education Psychology from Ohio University. When the Midwest Region was created in 1963, Sagay moved to the Midwest civil service as Principal, Edo College Benin until 1968. Between 1969 and 1972, he was the Assistant Director, Adeyemi College of Education, Ondo, a position that afforded him a rewarding academic affiliation with the University of Ife.

Like many other Griersons of the earliest generation, Sagay took pleasure in public service. He was Chairman, Board of Trustees, College of Education, Abraka, and Chairmanship of the Bendel State Public Service Commission. He resigned these appointments after the military overthrow of the civilian government of the Second Republic headed by Shehu Shagari on December 31, 1983. Sagay then went into private business in the agronomic sector. He managed his family farm on a land that had belonged to the Bini maternal side of his family as a gift from an Oba of Benin in the 19th century. On retirement, Sagay lived the rest of his life peacefully in his home in his maternal hometown of Benin-City, where he passed away at the age of 86 in July 1998.

Today, Sagay is remembered as a unique Grierson, like Deko ’30 and Enobakhare ’33, who was a student, tutor and Housemaster in Grier House. He is also famous as the first Head of School of GCI.

api::profile.profile.bio:
Timothy Mofolorunso Aluko was born on June 14, 1918 in Ilesha. He had his primary education at the Holy Trinity School, Amofe, then at the St. John’s School from 1926 to 1931. He gained admission to Government College Ibadan which he attended from 1933 to 1938. He was assigned to Grier House. His student days were marked by his penchant for storytelling and essay writing. He won several school prizes in Literature despite his undoubted mastery of the Sciences especially Mathematics and Physics. He was also active in sports. He played lawn tennis for Grier House and the school.

Like many of his classmates of that era, after leaving GCI, he was one of the earliest students admitted to the Yaba Higher College where he studied Civil Engineering between 1939 and 1942. After this, not resting on his laurels, he proceeded to the United Kingdom to pursue further studies in Civil Engineering and Town Planning at the University of London.

On returning to Nigeria, he joined the colonial Civil Service. Over the years, he rose to high leadership positions as a civil engineer and administrator working for various government agencies. At various times, he was the Federal Director of Public Works and Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Works and Housing before he served as a  Minister of Finance of the Western Region. He later left the civil service to go into academics. At the same time, he went back to school to earn a PhD in Municipal Engineering from Newcastle University in the United Kingdom in 1976.

Despite a busy life in public service, T. M. Aluko found time to follow his passion as a writer, developing the creative skills that he had honed in his student days in Grier House. His novels, all of whom were acclaimed bestsellers, include: One Man, One Wife, 1959, One Man, One Matchet, 1964, Kinsman and Foreman, 1966, Chief, the Honorable Minister, 1970, His Worshipful Majesty, 1973, and Our Born Again President, 2009. Apart from fiction, he published 2 autobiographies: My Years of Service and The Story of My Life, 2007. He also wrote and edited a book about GCI: Built on the Rock – the first 25 years, published in 1979. Among his many awards are the O. B. E. (Order of the British Empire) in1963, and the O. O. N. (Order of the Niger) in 1964. T. M. Aluko died on May 1, 2010 in Lagos, aged 91 years.

We remember T. M. Aluko today as an iconic name from the first generation of exceptional Griersons who created a reputation for intellectual brilliance and multi-talented accomplishments for GCI old boys, especially in public service and literary accomplishment.

Akinwande Oluwole Babatunde Soyinka was born on 13 July 1934 in Aké, Abeokuta. He attended primary school at St Peter’s School in his hometown. A child prodigy and avid reader, his parents encouraged his literary pursuits. By 1945 aged only 11, he gained admission into Abeokuta Grammar School, the second oldest secondary school of the CMS in Nigeria founded in 1908. However, his ever-inquisitive spirit led him to change school within one year to the more prestigious Government College Ibadan in 1946.

During his years in GCI, Soyinka did well in his studies, but he was rebellious and difficult to deal with. For this reason, he spent time in all 4 Houses – Swanston, Field, Carr and lastly Grier.  After 5 years in GCI, he enrolled in 1952 at the University of Ibadan, then known as the University College Ibadan. Ever a rebel and iconoclast, he founded, while an undergraduate, the famous students’ club, the Pyrates Confraternity. The impetus for this, according to Soyinka, was to ‘bring back the age of chivalry and fight for social justice.’ It was not his intention to establish a cult of young law breakers.

After briefly working for the government in the Forestry Department after leaving the university, Soyinka left Nigeria in 1954 for England to study at the University of Leeds, where he became the editor of the university's magazine, The Eagle. It was at this time that his literary creativity blossomed. He began to write poems and short stories including audio recordings for the BBC Lecture series. On his return to Nigeria in 1959, he was already a full-fledged author though he also worked as a lecturer in the Drama Dept at various times between 1962 and 1967 at the Universities of Ife, Lagos and Ibadan.

After Independence in 1960, Soyinka became alarmed at the political direction Nigeria was taking. He opposed, first the “illegal” government of Chief S. L. Akintola, the Premier of the Western Region, who was said to have rigged an election, and then General Yakubu Gowon for his conduct of the Nigerian Civil War and what Soyinka perceived as the ill-treatment of the Ibo ethnic group whose leader, Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu, seceded from Nigeria in 1967 to form the rebel enclave of Biafra, thus precipitating the Nigerian Civil War (1967-70). For his conscience-driven opposition to the Civil War and his social activism, Soyinka was jailed for 22 months, from August 1967 to October 1969. An account of his prison experience is told in his famous book, “The Man Died,” which was later banned by the Nigerian government.

After his release from prison, Wole Soyinka returned to his regular profession of university lecturer, writer and playwright. He wrote many plays which were performed on radio and in theatres in Nigeria and the UK. He translated works by other authors including D.F. Fagunwa’s famous “Ogboju Ode ninu igbo Irunmole.” He also wrote many academic and non-academic articles and essays, and became a regular feature of influential national and international magazines and newspapers, as well as numerous radio and TV shows. His literary works include three novels, ten collections of short stories, seven poetry collections, twenty-five plays and five memoirs which GCI students are encouraged to read as literary classics. The third in this series of memoirs, titled “Ibadan – the Penkelemesi years,” covers Soyinka’s time at GCI.

In 1986, Soyinka was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first black African to be so honored. The citation referred to Soyinka’s "wide cultural perspective and poetic overtones fashioning the drama of existence.” And in July 2024, President Bola Tinubu named the National Arts Theatre after him to commemorate his 90th birthday.

Throughout his life, Soyinka fought against oppression wherever he saw it. He became Nigeria’s most famous prodigal son and a global icon for social activists fighting for human rights the world over. Today, we celebrate Soyinka as the most famous writer and poet that Nigeria has ever produced. Although he lived in all four Houses in existence when he was in GCI, Grier House was the last house Wole Soyinka called home - thus qualifying him to be classified as a proud Grierson.

Rotimi Ayodele Kayode Jaiyesimi was born in Ibadan on 6 June 1954 to Alfred Koku Jaiyesimi (an old Grierson of the 1936 set) and Regina Ayoola Jaiyesimi. He started his primary school education at the famous Mrs Funmilayo Kuti’s school, Abeokuta and finished in Ibadan at the United Missionary College (UMC) Primary School. He was admitted to GCI in January 1966. His accomplishments as a Grierson include being School Prefect and Head of Grier House in his final year and President, Philatelic Society. In sports, he was a cross-country runner.

After leaving GCI, Jaiyesimi attended the University of Ibadan where he qualified as a physician with a Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree in 1978. This was followed by specialization in the field of Obstetrics and Gynaecology with training at the University College Hospital (UCH) Ibadan and the United Kingdom. He is a Fellow of the West African College of Surgeons (FWACS), Obstetrics & Gynaecology Faculty, 1986 and Member, Royal College of Obstetricians & Gynaecologists, (MRCOG), 1988. He was eventually made a Fellow of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (FRCOG) in 2001. Jaiyesimi’s academic forays extend beyond Medicine. He obtained a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree from the University of Newcastle, 2000 and a master’s degree in medical law (LLM) from Northumbria University, Newcastle in 2007. He became a Senior Member, Faculty of Medical Leadership and Management (SMFMLM), Associate Medical Director for Patient Safety, Consultant Obstetrician and Gynaecologist and Adjunct Professor of Law

Mindful of his roots and formative years in Grier House and GCI, Jaiyesimi was a founding member of the GCIOBA Europe Branch (First Vice chairman, 1993 to 1998; Second Chairman, 1998 to 2001). Among his many achievements and honours are: Government College Ibadan National Merit Award, 2019, University of Ibadan Lifetime Achievement Award, 2018, Excellence Award Recipient, Celebrating excellent contribution to the UK National Health Service at 70 years, Nigerian National Health Care Professionals (UK), 2019, Lifetime Achievement Award, National B.A.M.E Health & Care Awards, 2023, Pioneer Nigerian National Diaspora Merit Award in Medicine and Healthcare, 2023, Lifetime Achievement, Artistes Managers Association in Nigeria (AMAN), 2025. Hospital Services Journal (HSJ) National Award for Innovation, and The Value and Improvement in Patient Information Management Award for the development of online, real-time mortality review tool (MARS), 2014

A man of energy, intellect and integrity, Rotimi Jaiyesimi is honoured as a former Grier Head of House who became an internationally renowned professor - a role model for current and future Griersons.

api::article.article.title: Grier House: A Brief History
api::article.article.excerpt: Grier House was founded in January 1930. This was the year in which the school of which it was a part, Government College Ibadan, was formally established as a secondary school. For a year before that, this school was a…
api::article.article.body:
Grier House was founded in January 1930. This was the year in which the school of which it was a part, Government College Ibadan, was formally established as a secondary school. For a year before that, this school was a teacher training school. In 1930, students who had already spent a year in the teacher training school were merged with a fresh new intake into Class 1 of the new school.

The House derived its name from Selwyn Macgregor Grier, a British colonial officer who was the Director of Education for southern Nigeria when the decision was taken to establish Government College Ibadan. His deputy Director of Education was another Englishman, E. R. Swanston after whom Swanston House was named. Swanston House was the first House because it had been a dormitory since 1929 when the teacher training school was in place.

The first Grier Housemaster was V. B. V. Powell. It was he who gave the House many of its traditions including the House Crest, Color, Motto, House Prayer, House Supper and emphasis on sports excellence. In his honor, house prefects in Grier House are called Powellites. Powell House is also named after him.

In 1930, Grier House was located close to the GCI main gate. In 1952, it moved to a new site near Field House which was established in 1948. In 1982, all students were vacated from the House due to a policy of the Oyo State Government to abolish boarding houses. After this, the building became dilapidated. The new building we have today was built in 2024 through the kind donation of an old boy, Wale Babalakin ’71. The first group of boys moved into it in 2025.

api::article.article.title: Selwyn Macgregor Grier
api::article.article.excerpt: Selwyn Macgregor Grier is the patron of Grier House. He is the person after whom the House is named. He was born in England on April 1, 1878. He was educated at a famous public school, Marlborough College, and then…
api::article.article.body:
Selwyn Macgregor Grier is the patron of Grier House. He is the person after whom the House is named. He was born in England on April 1, 1878. He was educated at a famous public school, Marlborough College, and then Cambridge University. After teaching for a few years in various public schools in England, he decided to come to the British colony of Nigeria in 1906 as an educationist. He was initially based in Bauchi in Northern Nigeria. Later, he was promoted to Director of Education for the Southern Provinces. It was in this position that he made the decision to establish a teacher training school in Ibadan in 1929. A year later in 1930, this school became a secondary school for boys and was called Government College Ibadan.

Grier left Nigeria in 1929 even before Grier House was established in 1930. He was posted to the West Indies as the Colonial Secretary of Trinidad and Tobago. Over the next few years, he gained further promotions. In 1935, he became Governor in Chief of the Windward Islands of the West Indies. The day on which this news reached Grier House is celebrated as the ‘Red Letter Day.’ A year later in 1936, he was knighted by the King of England with the K.C.M.G. (Knight Commander of St Michael and St George) title. This is why we now refer to him as Sir Selwyn Macgregor Grier.

Unfortunately, his health deteriorated due to an eye ailment which rendered him functionally blind. Soon, he could no longer perform his duties as Governor. In 1937, Grier returned to England, where he died on November 8. 1946.

api::article.article.title: Villiers Barcham Vaughan (V. B. V.) Powell
api::article.article.excerpt: V. B. V. Powell was the first Housemaster of Grier House in 1930. He was born in 1904 in New Zealand. He attended 2 public schools: Christ’s College, Christchurch, New Zealand; then Clifton College, England. After this,…
api::article.article.body:
V. B. V. Powell was the first Housemaster of Grier House in 1930. He was born in 1904 in New Zealand. He attended 2 public schools: Christ’s College, Christchurch, New Zealand; then Clifton College, England. After this, he gained admission to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge University where he represented his university (as a ‘Cambridge blue’) and England in athletics.

After graduating from Cambridge, he joined the Colonial Service and was posted to Nigeria in 1927. Aged only 23, he was appointed Superintendent of Education in Western Nigeria. From there, he was posted to the new teacher training school in Ibadan in 1929  to teach Mathematics and History. In 1930, when this school became GCI and a new dormitory was added, he was named the Housemaster. It was V. B. V. who named the house after S. M. Grier.

From his youth, his three given names were difficult to pronounce. So, he went by his initials – V. B. V. The boys in Grier House had a nickname for him ‘Very Bad Very Poor’ based on his initials and last name. He was also called ‘Pip’ by some of his close friends. V. B. V. created most of the traditions of Grier House. These include the House Crest, House Color, House Motto, House Prayer, House Supper and the Cup of Unity. He also established the emphasis of Griersons for performance and excellence in sports.

Beyond Grier House and GCI, V.B.V. was important in the development of sports in Nigeria. He played cricket for Nigeria in 1935. He started the Grier Cup athletic competition for secondary schools in 1933, as well as the Hussey Shield for the various regions in the 1950s. He  became Acting Principal of GCI in 1941 and full Principal in 1944. He left GCI in 1947 to become Principal of Government College, Ughelli. Powell House was named after him. And Grier house prefects are known as Powellites in his honor.

api::article.article.title: Who are Griersons?
api::article.article.excerpt: Gabriel Akin Deko, agriculturist and government minister. T. M. Aluko, engineer, turned novelist and social commentator. Wole Soyinka, human rights activist and Nobel Prize winner. Omololu Olunloyo, brilliant…
api::article.article.body:
Gabriel Akin Deko, agriculturist and government minister. T. M. Aluko, engineer, turned novelist and social commentator. Wole Soyinka, human rights activist and Nobel Prize winner. Omololu Olunloyo, brilliant mathematician and maverick politician. Harding Ekperigin, sports icon and multi-sport record holder. Sabiru Biobaku, ground-breaking historian and university Vice-Chancellor. G. N. I. Enobakhare, GCI student, tutor, housemaster and principal who became an educationist who had the ears of kings and heads of state. Oba Erediauwa, revered monarch of the ancient Benin empire. Leslie and Hope Harriman, brothers who became diplomats and deal makers. Jide Bademosi, world-renowned neurologist and captain of the Nigerian cricket team. Victor Ojutalayo, Head of school and winner of the Victor Ludorum trophy. Rotimi Jaiyesimi, Head of House and professor of Obstetrics and Gynecology. Akingbola Akinola, cadet unit leader turned acclaimed lawyer and international mediator. The list goes on and on.

What do all these persons have in common? They started off as boys who lived their teenage years in Grier House. They slept in its dormitory beds, studied in its prep room and competed on its playing fields. Like all new boys, they studied for the House Test and learnt from their ‘teurs.’  They sometimes broke rules and were punished like other Grier boys through the generations. But they went forth from this very place to conquer the world. What they took from here were the age-old Grier House traditions of excellence, achievement and humility with which they changed their own lives and illuminated the world around them.

They dared to learn. For well has it been said: What starts in Grier House changes the world!

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Government College Ibadan is Founded
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: Government College Ibadan is founded, beginning as a teacher training school established by Selwyn Macgregor Grier, Director of Education for the Southern Provinces. V. B. V. Powell is posted there to teach Mathematics and History.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Grier House is Founded
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: In January 1930 Government College Ibadan becomes a secondary school and Grier House is founded as its second House, after Swanston House, with V. B. V. Powell as its first Housemaster. He names the House after Selwyn Macgregor Grier and gives it its Crest, Colour, Motto, House Prayer and House Supper.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: The Grier Cup is Started
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: V. B. V. Powell starts the Grier Cup athletic competition for secondary schools. Around the same year, the tradition of moonlight stories begins in Grier House.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Red Letter Day
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: News reaches Grier House that Selwyn Macgregor Grier has been made Governor of the Windward Islands. The day is marked on the calendar with a red circle.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Wartime Exile
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: During the Second World War, Griersons leave their dormitory and live in exile in Lagos and at St Theresa's Convent, Oke-Ado, until 1945.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: The Cairn
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: A rock is placed in front of the old Grier House to mark the end of the Second World War and the return of Griersons to their dormitory.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Grier House Moves to a New Site
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: Grier House moves from its first site close to the main gate to a new site near Field House.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: First Nigerian Principal
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: Gilbert Nixon Imafidon Enobakhare, a Grierson of the 1933 set and former Housemaster, becomes the first Nigerian Principal of Government College Ibadan.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Boarding is Abolished
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: All students are moved out of Grier House following an Oyo State Government policy abolishing boarding houses. The building falls into disrepair.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: Wole Soyinka Wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: Wole Soyinka, for whom Grier House was the last House he called home, becomes the first Black African awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: A New Grier House
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: A new Grier House building is built through the donation of Wale Babalakin, a Grierson of the 1971 set. The first group of boys moves in during 2025.

api::timeline-event.timeline-event.title: The Grier Museum and Library Opens
api::timeline-event.timeline-event.body: The Grier Museum and Library is established in October 2026 as a legacy project of the Grier History and Traditions Committee.

api::tradition.tradition.title: The House Song
api::tradition.tradition.description: O Grier House, let us for thy dear honour yearn. Let us from experience past this lesson learn,
api::tradition.tradition.body:
O Grier House, let us for thy dear honour yearn.
Let us from experience past this lesson learn,
That discipline leads but to our one true goal,
Devotion true must be our unfailing role.
We dare to learn both from victory and defeat.
If once our best is done, then we all can meet
To sing loud in praise of Thy untarnished fame,
That both past and present cherish just the same.
United in spirit, we uphold Thy Grace
Of unbroken justice taught in every race.
Griersons, thy true greatness must strive sure to shield
We dare to learn always and we’ll never yield.

audio.alt: Members of the Grier House Marching Band with an impromptu rendering of the House Song, October 12, 2026
