api::tradition.tradition.title: The House Pledge
api::tradition.tradition.description: I pledge with all my heart, That wherever I am,
api::tradition.tradition.body:
I pledge with all my heart,
That wherever I am,
And whatever I do,
In duty bound,
I will be a worthy and honourable member
of Grier House in particular
and Government College in general.
May God be my guide!

api::tradition.tradition.title: The House Prayer
api::tradition.tradition.description: O God, who, despite the many imperfections Of all human creeds and religions,
api::tradition.tradition.body:
O God, who, despite the many imperfections
Of all human creeds and religions,
Doth reveal unto this House the Excellency of Thy grace.
We dedicate our young lives to Thy service,
So, rule our hearts, and direct our aspirations
That we may see in every aspect of our daily duties,
The real attributes of Thy true Religion and Virtues,
And in our humble endeavour,
To be the best that we can be.
May so discipline our lives
To fit ourselves for the services of our brethren
And the furtherance of Thy kingdom,
here on earth.
Hear our prayers, O Heavenly Father.
Amen

api::tradition.tradition.title: The House Test
api::tradition.tradition.description: All new students entering Grier House, irrespective of class, are expected to be taught the history and traditions of Grier House and to be tested on this knowledge. This is the House test which is taken at the beginning of each school year. The student is prepared for this test by his teacher or ‘teur.’

api::tradition.tradition.title: Banjo’s Prize
api::tradition.tradition.description: The first-year student with the highest score in the House Test is given a prize which is known traditionally as Banjo’s Prize which may have a monetary value.

api::tradition.tradition.title: The House Supper
api::tradition.tradition.description: Towards the end of the school year, a special supper is held for all students, the House officials including the Housemaster and House Governor, old Griersons and other invited guests. At this special meal, students sit next to old boys and learn from their stories and experiences. During this House Supper, toasts are made by the oldest old boy, Head of House, the youngest student and the Housemaster.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Cup of Unity
api::tradition.tradition.description: The special cup used for the toasts at the House Supper is called the Cup of Unity. The toasts made from this cup as follows: 1) Oldest old boy: “I drink to the past.” 2) Youngest boy: “I drink to the future.” 3) Head of House: “I drink to the present.” and 4) Housemaster: “I drink to the past, present and future.”

api::tradition.tradition.title: Honors Board
api::tradition.tradition.description: A carved wooden board with names of House officials, prefects and Griersons who have won achievements and honors for Grier House during that year.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Saturday Night Socials
api::tradition.tradition.description: An occasion for students to come together for a fun-filled evening in the prep room with debates, recitations, drama sketches, song competitions and even physical sports like boxing with gloves and pillow fights. The highlight of the evening is always music (played in the old days on the gramophone) and dancing.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Pillow Fights
api::tradition.tradition.description: Two boys face each other armed with pillows filled with soft cotton wool. The fight ends when one of them has had enough. It is usually part of the Saturday evening socials, but these impromptu fights can take place on other occasions.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Treasure Hunt
api::tradition.tradition.description: The whole House is divided into teams, each with a leader who is a senior boy. The teams are presented with the same clues for which they have to seek answers. These are usually written on pieces of paper and hidden somewhere on the House or school grounds. The first team to get all the clues right wins.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Moonlight stories
api::tradition.tradition.description: This tradition started as a spontaneous event around 1933 when some boys in Grier House under the influence of the moonlight, remembered their villages in the Niger Delta and started telling each other folktales from their different cultures. This tradition appears to have gone out of practice.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Saturday Morning Inspection
api::tradition.tradition.description: Boys stand next to their bed and locker while the Housemaster, accompanied by the Head of House and other prefects, inspects each boy’s personal space as well as the whole House grounds for tidiness and compliance with house rules.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Red Letter Day
api::tradition.tradition.description: This was the day marked on the calendar by a red circle on which the telegram was received in Grier House of the elevation of Sir Selwyn Macgregor Grier to the position of Governor-General of the Windward Islands in the West Indies in 1935.

api::tradition.tradition.title: The Cairn
api::tradition.tradition.description: This is a piece of rock that was placed in front of the old Grier House in 1945 by the Housemaster to mark the end of the Second World War and the return of Griersons to their old dormitory after they had been in exile in Lagos and St. Theresa’s Covent, Oke-Ado between 1940 and 1945.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Powellites
api::tradition.tradition.description: This is the name given to house prefects in Grier House in honor of the first Housemaster, Mr. V. B. V. Powell.

api::tradition.tradition.title: House Punishments
api::tradition.tradition.description: Traditionally, a variety of punishments are meted out to erring junior students in Grier House by senior boys and prefects. The most notable are:
api::tradition.tradition.body:
- Standing on the locker or table.
- Cutting grass or other activities of environmental cleaning.
- Cleaning the toilet.
- Performing chores for a senior boy.

api::tradition.tradition.title: Other traditions
api::tradition.tradition.description: Further customs passed down through the generations of Griersons.
api::tradition.tradition.body:
- The teacher-boy mentoring system. Teachers are also known as ‘teurs.’
- Confiscation of clothes and other possessions left lying around.
- Auction sales of confiscated items.
- Conferment of house colors on students who represent Grier House in sports

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: A Visitor to Grier House in 1983
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: Late in the harmattan season in early 1983, an old Grierson alighted out of a taxi that deposited him in front of the iroko tree that had stood sentinel in front of the House as far as anyone could remember. This gentleman was visiting GCI…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
Late in the harmattan season in early 1983, an old Grierson alighted out of a taxi that deposited him in front of the iroko tree that had stood sentinel in front of the House as far as anyone could remember. This gentleman was visiting GCI and had come to see his beloved Grier House. He looked forward excitedly to revisiting the scene of many escapades, disappointments and triumphs of his youth. But he was confronted by a sight he never thought would assail his eyes. Where he and other Grier House students once lived, studied, played and slept, he saw a ragged, chattering group of ill-clad boys and girls. They told him in poor English that what he regarded as the hallowed dormitories of his Grier House was their day school – Apata Ganga High School. The visitor was a bibliophile. A true Grierson, he was educated and accomplished and read widely. In particular, he was rather partial to the works of the Romantic poets of the early nineteenth century in Europe. He now remembered some lines by Uhland, the celebrated German poet. And as he stood underneath the ancient iroko tree that still stood like a sentry beside that block of building that used to be the Herrington block of his beloved Grier House, he uttered these words silently to himself.

> I ride through a dark land by night
> Where there is no moon
> And never a star to bless me with light.

Government College Ibadan was now no different from the other neighborhood schools that served the local population of Apata Ganga, Omi Adio and Odo Ona. It pained many Griersons and GCI old boys that their school was now just one of many schools in its shady tree-dotted compound. On further enquiries at the school principal’s office, the visitor was informed that the school no longer offered a tough entrance examination for aspiring students. And of course, gone was the time-honored 3-day residential interview that had been established since 1930 by Rev Squire and V.B.V. Powell. Where now were those special privileges given by successive governments since colonial times to the specially picked students of a special ‘model’ school?

The result showed in a rapid decline in academic standards. At the end of that school year 1983, out of 250 boys who sat for the West African School Certificate Examination, only 20 passed. This 8% pass rate was so shocking when compared to the 100% pass rate that was taken for granted just a decade earlier that many GCI old boys, including our visiting Grierson did not even want to believe it.

Some old boys thought they saw dark forces at play. For surely they conjectured, the decision handed down by the Oyo State government after it came to power in 1979 was not just a travesty. It stemmed from jealousy on the part of some persons high in the ranks of the state  government who wanted to humble a superior institution they had been unable to get into in their time. After all, the governor who had made that decision was the lawyer and politician, Bola Ige. Everyone knew he was an old boy of Ibadan Grammar School. This, after all, was an institution that for decades was looked down upon by GCI boys of every generation as a lowly ‘ayo’ school.  In the eyes of many GCI boys therefore, the action of his government was nothing less than an act of sabotage and betrayal. But those among them who thought more deeply about the matter realized that this government, which was elected on a populist agenda to bring universal free education to the masses despite meager resources in cash and personnel, simply had no choice.

Thus it was that political events outside the control of the school and its students punctured the happy cocoon of that tree-dotted compound in Apata Ganga. For half a century, its unsuspecting students had lived charmed lives. Perhaps some of them, like that old Grierson visiting the school in 1983, now realized that maybe they were mere guinea pigs in a quixotic experiment that became trapped in its own glorious past. They had lived in a gilded cage cut off from the real world. And now, this anomaly of a pristine spot in a corrupt and underdeveloped country was no longer tenable or desirable by the rest of the country. Time, it has been said, waits for nobody. In this case, time was not prepared to wait for any institution either. Not even one as storied as GCI.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: Bisiriyu and the Mustard Seed
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: The first ten years of the existence of Grier House marked the beginning of many of the traditions that would be taken for granted for the next half-century by later generations of Grier House students. For instance, some of the foundation…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
The first ten years of the existence of Grier House marked the beginning of many of the traditions that would be taken for granted for the next half-century by later generations of Grier House students. For instance, some of the foundation students a few years after 1930, began to write articles, stories and gossip about themselves, their friends  and their experiences in Grier House. All these were written laboriously by hand. They dipped their wooden-handled steel-nibbed pen in blue-black ink and scribbled their thoughts and ideas on ruled sheets of white paper. At one point - no one knows when – the students began to refer to their logs as the “Mustard Seed.”  For they surmised that this was an idea that would germinate and grow like the proverbial seed in the Bible.

At first, the Housemaster made himself the Editor of this monthly publication, with a student assigned to him as his Assistant Director. This changed when Bisiriyu ’32 was made the full Editor in 1935 with A. Y. Eke ’33 as his Assistant Editor. To many of his friends in Grier House, Bisiriyu was in a class by himself, a Moslem among so many Christians. And indeed, he had come to Apata Ganga from a strange world indeed. Before coming to GCI, he lived in a large compound in Abeokuta in the company of scores of other children who were his siblings, half siblings and cousins under the watchful eye of numerous adults - parents, step-parents (his dad had six wives), grandparents and various other family members and guardians. In his grandfather’s compound, he had the choice of several pets to play with. These included two exotic birds - a crane and an ostrich!

Bisiryu was brought up as a Moslem. Just a few decades earlier in the late nineteenth century, men in his town had travelled by foot from Egbaland to the Arabian desert on pilgrimage to the holy places of Islam in Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. It took them years to get there, and many never returned. One of those who did return – a man named Ibrahim who later established a famous Quranic school which Bisiryu attended -  had settled in Arabia and fought against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War. After this, he married an Arab wife and came back home to Abeokuta after 40 years with three beautiful olive-skinned daughters.

Throughout his childhood in Igbore and Oke-Ijaiye districts of Abeokuta, Bisiriyu was surrounded by adults and children who he called Alhaji, Alhaja, Qudus, Saudatu, Zubeidat, Giwa, Shittu and Tajudeen. Not Thomas, Samuel, John or Gabriel as his onigbagbo friends would. After the age of 3, he had been sent to a Quranic school, ile keu. There, he had won prizes for his memorization and recitation of suras in their original Arabic from the Holy Quran. But in his primary school, the Ogbe Wesleyan School in Abeokuta, he had studied Bible verses in class and listened to Christian sermons.

Bisiriyu was therefore conversant with the ways of his Christian friends and the white tutors that he had to interact with in Grier House. Besides, his love of spoken and written English had embedded in him a strong respect for England and the British way of life as it was vicariously practiced in GCI. All the same, he always remembered that before he was allowed to come to Ibadan to attend Government College after he had been offered a government scholarship, his grandfather had made him promise not to allow himself to be converted to Christianity in his new environment. This revered maternal grandfather, Bisiriyu Giwa, was an ‘alfa’ who wore a long, embroidered kaftan with a fez on his head when he rode his colt to the Jummat Friday prayers. He was the head of their devoutly Moslem family.  His dad, Sanni Oloyede Biobaku, known to everyone by his initials, S.O.B., had died earlier in the same year 1931 that his son received notice of his admission to GCI.

Bisiriyu had given his maternal grandfather’s name as his surname when he started school. This was the same eminent gentleman mentioned in A. K. Ajisafe’s book ‘History of Abeokuta,’ which was published in the early years of the twentieth century. But later in life, after leaving GCI, Bisiriyu changed this surname to his own father’s last name which was Biobaku. His father, S.O.B., was a colorful character who had a fetish with names. Since his own given name, Sanni, started with an S, he named his children who came in rapid succession, Sariyu, Sidikat, Sikiru, Saburi, Samodu, Saamota and Sikiratu. And when her ran out of names starting with S, he went to R, another letter in the alphabet – Rasaki, Rigaliyu, and on and on. It was a good thing that S.O.B. had many children from his multiple wives. Thus, he had an ample field to work with in this game of name-giving.

For Bisiriyu, it was his love of English language and prose however, not his knowledge of Arabic names that stood out for him as he made his mark in Grier House as a young master of the written word and Editor of the House magazine. But he also distinguished himself in other significant ways in the House and school, while he was there from 1932 to 1937. Although he was diffident about sports when he first arrived in school, by his third year he had become a minor star for Grier House in athletics. He set a Junior A record of 63 inches in the high jump using a modified ‘Western roll’ technique. In Class 5, he was a member of the school’s First Eleven team in football which played King’s College to a draw in a match played on K.C.’s home turf in Lagos. He became a good debater and essay writer. With some of his friends, he started the ‘Philosophical Society,” a students’ club whose members wrote articles and organized debates in GCI and between GCI and other schools. And in his sixth and final year, as the top performing student in his class, he was not just a school prefect, he was the putative ‘head boy’ of the school. At that time, although there were Heads of House for Grier and Swanston, GCI had not started selecting a special boy in his final year as the ‘Head of School.’

After 1935, following Bisiriyu’s precedence, students in Grier House gained full control of the writing, editing and publishing of their monthly newsletter and rag sheet. Subsequently, the ‘Mustard Seed’ became livelier. And sometimes, its content was outrightly pungent. For these student writers and editors were not averse to excoriating their enemies or calling out boys who they perceived had misbehaved or brought the House into repute.  One of these later Editors of the ‘Mustard Seed’ was Abiodun Aloba who came in 1938. Like Bisiriyu, he was a member of the school debate team. And he became a school prefect in his final year. When he was the Assistant Editor of the ‘Mustard Seed,’ Aloba cultivated a biting wit and analytic journalistic approach which served him in good stead when later in life, he enjoyed a celebrated career in journalism.

Not to be outdone of course, boys in Swanston House followed suit. They soon established their own house newsletter called the “Swan Echo.”  But Griersons in general looked askance at this effort. Many of them insisted this was not to be compared to their own ‘Mustard Seed.’

At that time, the ‘Mustard Seed’ - like the House Supper and other ideas that in later years became grand traditions of Grier house - were simple, practical inventions that innovative students and their enterprising housemaster devised to enliven life in a crude and lonely dormitory in the middle of the forest. These innovations created an atmosphere of cohesion and discipline among members of this community of so many students from different backgrounds. It was a slow and unpredictable process. But through it, Grier House became a place of tradition. And it could be said with a fair degree of accuracy that through the wise efforts of V. B. V. Powell and his prefects not getting in the way of innovative students, Grier House brought tradition to the rest of GCI.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: Foundational Sports Heroes of Grier House
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: The acclaimed doyen of sports in Grier House is Harding Ekperigin who came in with the 1932 set. To those who knew him when he was in school, this tall and lanky schoolboy athlete seemed to have been born with the quickness of limb and…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
> ‘If you’ve tried your best
> And summoned all your strength in the effort,
> Then you could always say, Yes,
> I gave to my team all I had in me.’
> Barbara Vance, 2010

The acclaimed doyen of sports in Grier House is Harding Ekperigin who came in with the 1932 set. To those who knew him when he was in school, this tall and lanky schoolboy athlete seemed to have been born with the quickness of limb and unmatched eye-hand coordination that are the hallmarks of a great athlete.  But Ekperigin was not just a great athlete. He belonged to a rare breed. He was a true and complete allrounder. He was born in Warri to parents of the Itsekiri clan.  In his primary school days, he became a champion runner who emerged into the limelight during the Empire Day games held annually all over the Western Region in that colonial period. And when he won a scholarship in 1932 to attend Government College Ibadan, the new secondary school established a couple of years earlier, he did not disappoint the hopes placed on him. From the day he arrived on the compound in Apata Ganga, he shone like a star.

In his first year in Form I in Grier House, Ekperigin regularly beat more senior boys who were in Junior A. Every event in every sport was fair game to him. But it was on the athletic field that he staked his fame - sprints, hurdles, relay, high jump and long jump. During his six years in Grier House, from 1932 to 1937, he held the record in every school athletic event he participated in. These included 100 yards, 220 yards, 440 yards, long jump and triple jump. In addition, he captained Grier House in football, cricket, badminton and swimming. Thus, by the time he left Grier House he had won the epithet ‘captain of all games.’  It was indeed a rare honor which has never since been applied to any other athlete in the history of the House.

During the Grier Cup competition in 1937, Ekperigin broke the Nigerian schoolboy record in multiple events including the 120 yards hurdles and the long jump. His 22ft, 2 1/2in record in the latter event stood as a Grier Cup record for a decade until 1947.  After he left GCI, a knee injury cut short his active participation as a competing athlete. Instead, he became one of Nigeria’s most notable athletic coaches and sports administrators of the colonial era. Like his mentor, the legendary Grier Housemaster, V. B. V. Powell, Ekperigin was a noted innovator and pillar of Nigerian sports when it was in its infancy. He was one of the founders of the Lagos Athletic Club and the Amateur Athletic Association of Nigeria. He led the Nigerian athletic team to the Commonwealth Games in Vancouver in 1956, and to several Olympic Games (Rome 1960, Tokyo 1964 and Mexico 1968). He was the first CEO of the Midwest State Sports Council when it was created in 1963. All in all, Ekperigin set the tone for the dominance of Grier House in sports in the early years after the house was established in 1930.

Other great athletes of that pioneer decade from 1930 to 1939 included boys like J. M. Beckley of the ’30 set. He was the champion in the mile event at the first Grier Cup competition in 1933.

***

During the war years from 1940 to 1945, most sports - athletics, football and cricket - continued for Grier House and GCI students. Swimming however was virtually nonexistent due to the absence of a swimming pool, the students having left their compound in Apata Ganga for exile in Lagos and later, the St. Theresa’s convent in Oke Ado.

Grier House had a dominant football team during those years in exile. Of particular mention is G. E. Egbe of the 1935 set. He captained the Grier House football team that beat Swanston for the  interhouse football trophy in 1940. That year, the Grier House football team fielded seven members of the GCI first eleven, including the flamboyant S. Ajomale ’36 as the high-scoring center forward. The other boys on this famous team included Daniel Igbinogun ’38 in the right back position, O. Oseni ’37 as the center half,  and G. Ibikunle ’38 in the inside right position.

And in that same year 1940, the Grier Cup inter-school athletic competition was held on the main field of GCI in Apata Ganga. With this home field advantage, Ogbe, the aforementioned Grier House football captain, recorded a games record of 41 feet, 10 inches in the shot putt. Incidentally, it was during that same competition that Cyprian Ekwensi ’36 of Swanston House set a Grier Cup record in the 120 yards hurdle. Ekwensi of course went on to become the celebrated author of such novels as ‘Jagua Nana’ ‘Burning Grass’ ‘The Passport of Malam Ilia’ and ‘An African Nights Entertainment.’

***

In the decade following the end of World War II, from 1946 to 1954, sports came back in full force to a Grier House that was eager to reassert its pre-war dominance. This feat however became more difficult after two new Houses were added to GCI – Field House in 1948 and Carr House in 1949. Among the most notable sports-loving Griersons in that post-War era were three whose personalities would catch the public eye after they left school. They were Olunloyo ‘48, Tade ‘51 and Bademosi ‘53. Olunloyo and Bademosi were noted academicians and sportsmen who studied at the University of Ibadan and became eminent scholars after leaving Grier House. Tade made a name for himself in the annals of Nigerian cricket, After his days in GCI were over, he became an inspiration and mentor to many famous names in Nigerian cricket.

Olunloyo’s main contribution to Grier House sports as a student was on the cricket field. In this regard, he brought home a few cricket trophies to the House. As an opening bowler for the school team, he is credited with smashing the hitherto sterling reputation of many opposing batsmen in celebrated matches against Kings College and St Gregory’s College.

Of the  cricket-playing contemporaries of Olunloyo who were prominent in that era, we have to mention the names of two other Griersons. One is Leslie Harriman, who came in 2 years before Olunloyo in 1946. When he was in Grier House, Harriman was said to have astounded his classmates with his knowledge of all things cricket. After he left GCI, he was even better known in Nigerian cricket circles than Olunloyo because of his great moral and financial support for this sport in his later years. The other cricket-playing Grierson is Michael Onajin who came in a year after Olunloyo in 1949. In his time, Onajin, the most senior of 3 brothers who attended GCI, Onajin captained the Grier House and school cricket teams.

As the 1950s rolled in, Harriman  Olunloyo and Onajin were followed in 1951 by two cricket-playing classmates -  Babatunde Akinola and Adebowale Tade. Akinola became so skilled that he was selected captain of cricket for the school as well as Head of House in his last year in Grier House in 1958. But it was the charismatic Tade who was destined to become one of the most well-known cricketers to come out of Grier House and GCI in that post-war era. On entering Grier House in 1951, Tade had little difficulty finding his footing in that sports-obsessed milieu. He took to cricket above all other sports. And by the time he was in Form 3, he had captained the Grier House junior cricket team to an interhouse championship. Two years later, he did the same for the senior team. In his last year in school in 1955, not only did he captain the Grier House and the GCI school teams, he was selected as the first captain for the Western Region team which won the maiden edition of the Morocco-Clarke cricket Cup. This competition had been set up that year to bring together cricket-playing secondary school students from Lagos and the Western Region of Nigeria. Indeed for Tade, cricket was not just a game. It was a life-long passion. After leaving GCI, he continued to play and excel in his favorite sport. He helped to establish several amateur cricket clubs that were prominent in Nigeria in the 50s and 60s. And he was an active member and captain of many of these teams, the best known of which was the Dyaks Cricket Club in Lagos. From this position, Tade became a mentor to a whole generation of Nigerian cricketers.

During that era, we can say that the gods of cricket must have cast their eyes with favor  on Grier House. The first manifestation of this favor was that the unbeatable Tade-Akinola duo was soon joined by a youngster named Jide Bademosi who would become the greatest Nigerian cricketer of his time. Bademosi, who came into Grier House in 1953, took off where Harriman ’46, Olunloyo ‘48, Onajin ‘49, Akinola ’51, Tade ’51 and others left off. In fact, over the next few years, he would vastly outdo his predecessors and mentors. Like Olunloyo, he was very bright intellectually. And like Harriman and Tade, he imbibed the finer points of cricket like a thirsty camel gulping water from an oasis well after crossing a hot desert. He was an innovator and generational talent.

Like Wole Soyinka a decade earlier, Bademosi was one of the youngest and smallest boys in his class. It took him some time to fit in with his older colleagues. His classmates immediately gave him an apt nickname, ‘omode,’ small boy. But Bademosi did not take any offense. He was quiet, smart, funny and even keeled. He laughed with everyone. He kept on the good side of his seniors, did not annoy his classmates, and did not try to get into serious trouble either in the House or in the school. There are no records or anecdotes passed to us that Bademosi ever fought or quarreled with anybody during his years in Grier House

At first, Bademosi came to attention in the House as a very good chess player. But soon, he immersed himself in the great Grier House sports tradition that had been established three decades earlier by V. B. V. Powell. By his second year, he had mastered multiple sports. In fact, he became very good in most sports - football, hockey, swimming, table tennis and lawn tennis. And in the ensuing years, he represented Grier House and the school in most of these. But it was in cricket that Bademosi would come to be remembered as a Grier House legend. From the first day that he was placed in front of a wicket and given a bat to hold and swing around, it was obvious to all observers that he was destined to be one of those earlier-mentioned great cricketers for which Grier House had already become famous. But he was special. His skills in this sport, as a tenacious opening batsman and a tricky bowler, earned him the nickname ‘Bad Moses.’ This was a play on his last name, Bademosi. He led his Grier House teams to the capture of several inter-house trophies, not just in cricket, but in hockey and football as a junior and a senior. Bademosi was the captain of his junior and senior cricket teams for both Grier House and GCI.

Bademosi’s fame spread beyond Grier House. His prowess in cricket earned him an awesome reputation among players from many of the schools that GCI played against in those days. These were the elite cricket-playing institutions such as Kings College, Igbobi College, St Gregory’s College, Edo College, Benin, as well as the other government colleges, Umuahia, Ughelli, Owerri and Afikpo. In his final year in 1960, Bademosi captained the team fielded by the Western Region for the Morocco-Clarke Cup inter-regional cricket competition. And like his hero and mentor, Tade, he led his team to victory. It was around this time that Bademosi acquired another nickname, ‘Ajyde,’ which was the way his name, Jide, was pronounced by those who were not used to the Yoruba language.

We can say that if Ekperigin was the pacesetter who established the standard for the sports dominance of Grier House, Bademosi was the second leg in this baton change. Though not exactly a ‘captain of all games’ like Ekperigin, Bademosi was versatile and dominant. And he moved the race in favor of Grier House, leaving the other Houses behind in that hypothetical inter-generational shuttlecock relay.

In the next 2 decades, many young cricketers in Grier House would claim Bademosi as their mentor. But none would be as close to him as Bimbo Onajin ’58. This Onajin was the third brother by that name. Onajin’s eldest brother Michael has been mentioned in this narrative as captain of cricket for the house and school. He was the mentor who stimulated an interest in the game of cricket in his younger brother when the latter was still in primary school. Michael would impress his younger brother by dropping by at home from the GCI Main Field swinging a bat and still clad in his cricket pads. Their parents lived on the Moore Plantation which was practically next door to GCI. Thus, it was easy for the eldest Onajin brother to come home in the late evening after practicing on the Main Field to catch a bite of this mother’s cooking before dashing back to school. Thus, Bimbo learned to swing a bat and pitch a ball even before he set foot on the GCI compound as a bona fide student.

Bimbo Onajin came into Grier House in January 1958 when Bademosi was in his fifth form. And he rapidly made his mark as a bowler. Onajin later admitted that his skill might have been helped by the fact that he also threw the javelin as a member of the school’s athletic team. According to his reasoning, his athletic training toughened his arm and hand muscles. This helped him to grip the cricket ball tightly and throw it with more velocity. During his early years in Grier House, Onajin was considered a precocious talent in cricket by those who watched him, including the very impressed Bademosi. In fact, the two were as close as brothers. Their two families were related. Years later, Onajin would relate how Jide Bademosi sometimes spent the first few days of his vacation in the Onajin home on the Moore Plantation until transportation could be arranged for him to be taken to Ondo where his own parents lived. By the time Bimbo Onajin was in the fourth Form, he had developed into a teenage cricket sensation. He was so gifted and advanced in his cricket playing acumen that Bademosi, who was then a medical student at the University College Hospital,  Ibadan, would take him out of school to play with cricket teams at the University of Ibadan, the Liberty Stadium, and even out of town at the Race Course, Lagos. It was no wonder that when his time came, Bimbo Onajin became a much-celebrated cricket captain for the House and school like his elder brother Michael.

***

After Harding Ekperigin and Jide Bademosi, the third great once-in-a-generation Grier House sports hero was Victor Ojutalayo. We can say it was he who received the intergeneration sports baton from Bademosi. Ojutalayo met Bademosi in school, having arrived in Grier House in 1955, two years after Bademosi entered.  Victor Ojutalayo’s father, Gabriel Elusoji Ojutalayo, was himself a GCI old boy. He belonged to the 1931 set with school number 94. But he was in Swanston, not Grier House. In those pioneer days, when GCI athletes ran on their bare feet, the elder Ojutalayo earned fame as a notable long-distance runner who was given the nickname “Sukuru Boy” – schoolboy - by older athletes from the Nigerian Army and Police who he competed against.

On entering GCI and being assigned to Grier House, young Ojutalayo was determined to tread in his father’s huge footsteps. And not only that, he set out to improve on his father’s legacy. And in doing so, he was undeterred by the fact that his two brothers who were admitted to GCI the same year as him were in different Houses. One of his brothers, Kole, was in Carr House. The other brother, Johnson, had been assigned to Swanston House. Despite every other attachment of filial love and affection, Victor wanted to prove the superiority of maroon over blue and orange. In the years that followed, as a Grier House stand-out, Ojutalayo emphatically stamped his mark on the athletic field. And in doing so, he brought tears to the eyes of his brothers when he faced their Carr and Swanton teams.

Like his dad before him, the tall and lanky Ojutalayo became a star in mid and long-distance track events. Over the years, he won so many laurels for Grier House and GCI that his friends stopped counting. He capped his stellar school career by winning the Victor Ludorum trophy in 1962, his last year in school. By this time, he was in Upper Six and was a much admired and beloved Head of School under the famous D. J. Bullock, the last expatriate principal of GCI.  By this time, Ojutalayo had already shown that he was marked out for leadership and greatness. In the classroom, on the House grounds, and on the sports field, he came to the notice of everyone who met and interacted with him. The words used to describe him were ‘natural-born leader,’ ‘achiever,’ and ‘best of the best.’ He was admired, by teachers and fellow students alike, for his discipline, focus, and commitment to excellence in everything he put his mind to.

Victor Ojutalayo became a Grier House legend not just because he was a champion who won many trophies during his time. It was because he was a champion who broke records. Thus, between 1958 and 1962, he held the National Senior Record and the Commonwealth Secondary School Record in the 880 yards and the mile. And on one memorable day in 1957, he broke the GCI record in the mile previously held two decades earlier by his father, Gabriel. While still in school, Ojutalayo was already making a name for himself as an international athlete. He competed for the Nigerian national team while still in Grier House. His exploits were faithfully recorded and celebrated by the national newspapers and sports journals of the day.

Many more stories have come to us of Victor Ojutalyo and his high achieving contemporaries, including some who did not attend GCI.  One of these was his dear friend and fellow national athlete. This young man was Sydney Asiodu, who served as Head Boy of Igbobi College in the same year that Ojutalayo was Head of House in GCI. Both were brilliant in the classroom as well as on the sports field and in other arenas of youthful striving and endeavor. They were popular heroes who were admired not just in their respective schools, but all over Nigeria. Those who observed them closely declared they were the bright young hopes of their newly independent country. In fact, Asiodu and Ojutalayo were the first recipients of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Scholarship for Excellence in Sports.

But Asiodu was an Ibo from the eastern part of Nigeria which seceded from the rest of the country at the start of the Nigerian Civil War to form the short-lived, ill-fated enclave of Biafra in 1967. The story that Ojutalayo later told his family was that at the beginning of that national crisis, he pleaded with his friend Asiodu to stay behind in Lagos. But when his friend was unrelenting, saying he had to be with his family who had all gone back to the East, it was Ojutalayo who took Asiodu to the motor park to begin that fateful journey into Biafra. A few months later, Asiodu, one of the most promising sports men and academicians of his generation, was dead – a casualty of the deadly Biafran-Nigerian war. That scene at the motor park which was the last time the two friends would see each other was a farewell that Victor Ojutalayo would never forget.

Our narrative says that Victor Ojutalayo became celebrated as a Grierson because of his vision, brilliance and undisputed talent in and outside the sports arena. His legacy is clear and disputed. He cemented for his generation in the late 50s and early 60s the sports dominance of Grier House that had been established by the 2 generational talents who came before him –  Ekperigin and Bademosi.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: Griersons of the Mid 1970s
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: As our narrative wound its way into the mid and late 1970s, we are happy to note that, despite the changing times, Grier House managed to maintain its most cherished traditions. And the quality of the boys that lived within its walls was…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
As our narrative wound its way into the mid and late 1970s, we are happy to note that, despite the changing times, Grier House managed to maintain its most cherished traditions. And the quality of the boys that lived within its walls was undiminished in terms of intellect, sports achievement, integrity and ambition. These were attributes that had happily been maintained for the four decades since the founding of the House.

This is what Lanre Anibaba, who entered Grier House in September 1973, said years later, ‘When I met an old Grierson who came into Grier House in 1962, which was the year I was born, I was surprised to learn that we used the same slangs like aburi, side agreement and curry, teacher’s pet. Our GCI experience was basically the same.’

It is an axim of human history that each new generation learns from those who came before it. It is in this way that the traditions of a group are passed from one set to the next. The generation of Griersons that came in in the 1970s learned soon enough from the history and age-ole legacy of their House.  In time, they too knew what it meant to be Griersons. And they were not fundamentally different from boys who lived in Grier House in previous decades.

A representative member of the new entrants into Grier House in the early 1970s was Akindele Tewe. He was born in 1962 in Ibadan where his parents had made their home for more than a decade. His father, Chief Cornelius Tewe, was an elected representative in the Western House of Assembly in that historic election of 1953 that brought Awo to power. His mother, Patience, was a civil servant. When Tewe entered Grier House in 1973, the senior boys he met and interacted with on the House grounds filled his ears with stories of the heroic past of their house and school. His deepening sense of the awesome legacy that surrounded him stirred him deeply. He knew he had no choice but to heed this call from the past. He would follow in the grand traditions of this exceptional House that was part of a very special school. He became an active member of various clubs including the Science Society, the Literary and Debating Society and the School Choir. He went through his five years in Grier House between September 1973 and July 1978 determined to play his part in keeping himself and other Griersons on that path of excellence that had been trod for decades by those who came before.

But for Tewe and his set, this heroic past that was talked so much about in Grier House was a difficult act to follow. During their time, outside factors had begun to influence the lives of GCI students. In particular, the reverberations of the military rule of the day could no longer be ignored in a school that tried to tuck itself away in a quiet corner of Apata Ganga. Tewe and his friends lived through the various changes in military leadership in that era, and their outlook on life was affected by these troubling changes. As the baton passed from Gowon to Murtala in 1975, and then to Obasanjo and Yar’Adua in 1976, these boys noticed how inconsistent leadership from the top affected the management of GCI and the quality of the facilities available to them, its students.

For instance, although the central dining room remained open to students from all 5 Houses throughout Tewe’s time in school, the quality of the food provided dropped noticeably compared to the previous decade. Stories now abounded of boys who quarreled with mess boys over their dwindling rations. This was exacerbated in 1978 when a financial crisis at the national level forced the nation’s leaders to institute a regime of budget cuts and hiring freeze at all levels of employment for public servants. Despite these symptoms of a deepening rot in the national edifice, the standard of academics in GCI was reasonably maintained throughout the 1970s. Tewe felt he was taught in the classroom by good tutors who knew their ‘stuff.’ With regard to the academic qualifications of these tutors, the standard had never been higher in the history of the school. Many of the tutors during Tewe’s time had Master’s degrees in their fields. One or two had a PhD. The students even had the services of guidance counsellors for the first time in the history of the school. The traditional GCI penchant for sports was not neglected either. Boys in Grier House and other houses in GCI competed in athletics, football, hockey, cricket and the racket sports. Their jerseys, gloves and boots were top notch. Years later, Tewe remembered that there was a sports equipment outlet in town, ‘Niger Sports,’ which had a contract with the school to supply the boys with sports equipment, jerseys and boots. Interhouse competitions were held in most sports. And the GCI team competed against worthy opponents in Ibadan such as Loyola College, Ibadan Grammar School and the International School.

The highlight of this generation’s stay in Grier House was the FESTAC festival in 1977. There were no TV sets in the Grier House reading room. But one of the younger teachers who lived on the school compound allowed some of the boys to watch the events in his house. They remembered the top acts at the festival with took place at the National Stadium and the newly built National Theater in Lagos. How could the boys ever forget Ipitombi and Osibisa on stage? The Saturday night socials in Grier House were still events that boys looked forward to each weekend. And Griersons of that era, like many of those who came before then, broke bounds to sneak out of the compound for all kinds of reason. Surrounded by the influence of old traditions and new vistas of destabilizing change, a young teenager like Tewe not used to philosophical musings, began to ponder on the hows and whys of human existence and the unpredictable ways of young teenage boys. And somewhere along the way, like Otegbeye ’42 and Soyinka ’46 before him, he became a skeptic.

This generation of Griersons of the mid 1970s were a generally well behaved lot. But outside the school, they recognized that their nation was bedeviled by indiscipline at all levels. This was so bad that the military government declared a ‘war against indiscipline.’ And soon, this state of anomy began to be reflected in the lives of its young people including GCI boys. The social scene enjoyed by GCI students and Griersons became rowdier than it was in the late 1960s. There were parties every weekend to which young females from girls’ schools in Ibadan were invited. Except that now, there was one important change.  Queens School Ibadan had displaced St. Anne’s as the female school of choice for GCI students. The school band, Sounds Incorporated known as S.I., was so much in demand for parties and outside shows that it had two separate bands - a senior and junior ensemble known respectively as S.I. 1 and S.I. 2.

Reggae music reigned supreme during this era. A Grierson who appreciated and fully enjoyed this era for its plethora of music and other social offerings was Damola Ifaturoti ’72. His dad, Michael Adebayo Ifaturoti ’40, was an Editor of the Mustard Seed in 1946. Like many musically-inclined Griersons, the younger Ifaturoti listened on cassette tape players on the House grounds to the music of the revered Jamaican originators of that genre - Jimmy Cliff, Bob Marley and U-Roy. He and his friends also tuned in to the many reggae imitators in Nigeria – Bongos Ikwe, Chris Okosun and others. Some of these boys wanted to be Rasta men. And if the rules in GCI had allowed it, they would have grown their hair into dreadlocks. They still wanted of course to be accomplished, like all GCI students, in academics and sports. But they also wanted to spout their ideas for the redemption of black people, especially in apartheid South Africa. The words of Bob Marley’s ‘Revolution’ spoke to them. They wanted to be free. And they wanted to set free those they thought were in bondage.

> It takes a revolution
> To make a solution…
> Like the bird in the tree
> The prisoner must be free.

They also had the irrepressible Fela Anikulapo-Kuti nearby spouting forth his own ideas for social change from his Shrine in Lagos. The Afrobeat king was a personal hero and model for many of Tewe’s classmates. They looked at their society riven by corruption, injustice and economic inequality. And like their Afrobeat hero, they thought they had the answers to these problems. Until much later, when they discovered they didn’t.

One of the most interesting Griersons to be selected as Head of Grier House in that era was Edobor Aloba. When his ’72 set became fifth formers, for one reason or the other, higher school classes (A levels) were cancelled in GCI. Thus, in the absence of more senior boys in the sixth form when these boys were in Form 5, they were pressed into duty as Head of school, Heads of Houses and school prefects. Aloba, who had always impressed everyone including his classmates with his character, intellect and grace under pressure, was selected as the Head of Grier House for the 1975/76 session. Prior to this, he was never known to have lost his temper or to have ever punished a junior boy. But what made him stand out in the annals of Grier House was that as Head of House he had a pet. This was a dog which the boys named ‘Mascot.’ This canine became the favorite of every boy in the House. They loved the way ‘Mascot’ barked loudly and wagged his tail vigorously as he bounded up and down the sidelines to cheer the Grier team on during interhouse games.

The ’70 and ’71 sets who came just before Aloba and Ifaturoti’s classmates of 1972 were unfortunately passed over for important leadership positions when their time came. This situation resulted from the cancellation of the 6th form (Higher school) after the ‘70 set reached the fifth form. They never had the chance of going into the Sixth Form. They therefore missed the opportunity of having any of their classmates selected as Head of House, school prefects, captains of sports and Head of School. Gboyega Akin-Deko ’70, son of the first old boy to be made Grier Housemaster after the legendary V. B. V., had cause later in life  to ask the proverbial ‘what ifs.’  Of this ’70 set, Victor Jones (football) and Akin-Deko (cricket and hockey) were two of the few who had the chance of playing sports for house and school at a high level. But they never had the chance of being made captains of their respective sports, for these were positions usually occupied by 6th form boys. Still, they were able to represent GCI and Western State in their individual sports when they were in Form 5 during the 1973/74 school year. In the ’71 set, though they too could not become Prefects, Head of School or Head of House, many of the boys made up for this by etching their deeply names in the annals of Grier House sports. Akin Alade ’71 and Wale Ajomale ’71 were on the House and school hockey teams. Segun Yerokun ’71, an outstanding sportsman, played cricket for Grier House, GCI and Western State from 1973 to 1975. He was also the hockey goalkeeper for the school. The loss of the ‘70 and ‘71 sets in being unable to hold top leadership positions when their turn came became a gain for the 1972 set which was subsequently gifted with 3 sets of house and school prefects. This was when they were in Form 5, then in Lower and Upper Six.

Another fascinating Head of House of that era was Jide Jegede. His well-known nickname was ‘Penay.’ However, no one has been able to explain the origin of this cognomen which followed him throughout his life. He came to GCI from Comprehensive School, Aiyetoro as an HSC student and was assigned to Grier House. People who knew him talked of his pleasing and commanding presence. He was tall, handsome and likeable. One friend recalled that he had a ‘killer’ smile which wrinkled the corners of his mouth. And then he would break into a grin, which was often. He had a kind word for everybody, especially his juniors. For his leadership qualities and contributions in sports to the House, for he played cricket and hockey at a high level, he was made the Head of House for the 1977/1978 session. But he had to step down from this position before he completed his term because of complaints that he had entertained a member of the opposite sex overnight in his room as Head of house.  He was replaced by the outstanding athlete and sprinter, Bode Winsala, who became a very able acting Head of House. This was not the first time in the history of the House that a Head of Grier House was replaced in the middle of his term. But Jegede escaped further scrutiny by passing the JAMB exam that year and going off to the University of Lagos.

Winsala went on to occupy the substantive post of Head of House the next academic year 1978/79 on his own merits. One of our Grier House success story, he was born in Ibadan to parents who considered themselves to be indigenes of Ibadan though his mother’s ancestors came from Ilesha. His family background was typical of that era. His dad worked at the University of Ibadan as a conference administrator, while his mother was a schoolteacher throughout her working life. Throughout his childhood, Winsala heard stories about GCI. And this was the secondary school he always wanted to attend. But being a bright student, he left his primary school, I.C.C. in Mokola a year early in Primary 5, but was admitted to Ibadan Boys High School. But throughout his stay in that school, he remained undeterred in his quest to eventually go back to his first love. Thus, when the opportunity presented itself, he joined GCI in Form 5 at the beginning of the school year in September 1976.

As a Grierson, Winsala immediately became known as a star on the athletic field. He was a devilishly fast sprinter. Among his many laurels were winning the interhouse long jump, 110 meters hurdles and the 4 x 100 meters relay for Grier House during the 1978/79 session. He also played football for the Grier House team in 1976/77. And he was a member of the Oyo State athletic team in 1977/78. The Grier Cup competition was no longer in contention in his time. So Winsala did not have the chance to square off against those famous schools from Lagos - King’s College, St Gregory’s or Igbobi College - like Ojutalayo and Adeyemi-Wilson a decade earlier. He would later recall that his proudest moment as a Grierson was hoisting the Athletic Shield in 1978/79, the same year he was Head of House. This was a victory attributed by the devout Winsala to the fervent prayers he directed to the Almighty after he had acquired a Gideon’s Bible a year earlier.

A more placid and typical example of a Grierson of that generation was Yemi Adegoke who was in the House from 1975 to 1980. Years later, he would declare that, despite many challenges, he had a good time in Grier House in those waning years of its greatness. But he did not fail to notice the deteriorating state of the amenities provided to students in his own time compared to what he heard was the case in previous years. For things had become decidedly worse than at the time of Tewe who had entered school 3 years before him. Adegoke and his classmates hung their heads when they heard the senior boys talk with nostalgia of  the better times they had when they first came to Grier House. Adegoke did not participate in sports at the high level usually associated with many Griersons profiled in this narrative. According to him, he was not alone in this lack of distinction in the sports arena. Grier House did not win any major interhouse competition during his time. Still, Adegoke loved his House and his famous school. And when he found himself a senior in Forms 4 and 5, he did his best to keep the old traditions alive by personal action and example. He was confident he was able to keep a few junior boys in line without resorting to any harsh punishments.

Adegoke’s classmates of the 1975 set are important in this narrative because of one  distinction. They were the last class set of Griersons to enjoy the full complement of activities  and amenities of living as boarders in Grier House throughout their time in GCI. It is fitting that we talk about them and what they did with their lives after leaving GCI. Probably the best representative of that class was Gbenga Jegede. The last of 5 children, his father, Emmanuel Jegede, was a senior radiographer at the University College Hospital Ibadan who later read Law. His mother, Theresa, was a staff at the Family Planning Clinic in the same hospital. Jegede would later recall with fondness his childhood years in the secluded tree-dotted UCH compound off Orita-mefa, where he lived with his parents and siblings. For his dad was given privileged and much sought after staff quarters among resident doctors, hospital matrons and high administration officials employed by the university teaching hospital. It was in that middle class milieu that Jegede met his lifelong friends, Segun Cole, Jide Ogunro, and Bola Akioye, all of whom later attended GCI.

Jegede had his primary education at the Alafia Institute, Mokola from 1967 to 1975. When the time came to apply to secondary schools, he took the entrance examinations for GCI, Loyola College, Lagelu Grammar School and Comprehensive High School, Aiyetoro. But there was never any doubt in his mind which school he was going to attend. It was a decision made easier by the fact that his 2 older brothers had attended GCI.  These two - Adetokunbo (Grier House) and Abiodun (Carr House) – filled his ears with tales of their privileged status as members of that prestigious school.

On his entry to Grier House in September 1975, Jegede had his transition from primary to secondary school considerably smoothed by the presence of his older brother who was then in Carr house and the mentorship of a kind and brilliant ‘teur,’ Yinka Gbotosho, who was a classmate of his brother. Jegede found that he loved all the school and house traditions. And he thrived on the daily rituals of student life. He took an early interest in the GCI marching unit which he joined in his first year. He came to love the parades and the March Pasts at the Liberty Stadium during important national festivals and anniversaries. Then in Form 2, he joined the Army Cadet Unit. With his keen ear for music, he also joined the school band, ‘Sounds Incorporated,’ for which he played the keyboard. When he became the leader of the GCI Marching Unit, he helped to win for GCI the first prize trophy on several occasions at annual ‘march pasts’ at the Liberty Stadium. In his sixth form, to no one’s surprise, Jegede was selected as Head of School. By then, he was also the Head of the Army Cadet Unit as well as co-prefect for Hockey.

From 1976, the number of boarding house students steadily dwindled. Thus just a few boys of the 1977 set joined the boarding house when their set was in Form 2 with a few joining the group in the next 3 to 4 years. These Griersons included Femi Sofowora, Kunle Bammeke, Dipo Amao, Gbenga Olunloyo, Leye Oni, Sokunbi, and Sina Alade.

Tunji Taiwo of the 76 set later recalled his experience living in the midst of that dying breed of Grier House boarders. ‘I personally spent only three months in the boarding house. But it felt like six years. Those few months gave me the opportunity to experience virtually every aspect of boarding school life. All the house traditions were still around. I thoroughly enjoyed the treasure hunt, mixed socials and house suppers. I even passed the house test with flying colours, although, true to tradition, a Form One boy, Bola Akioye, was declared the winner.’

According to Taiwo’s recollection, the last full set of boys in the Grier House dormitory came in in September 1976. Only 27 new GCI students were boarding students assigned to Grier House for their first year. This group included Femi Sofowora, Kunle Bammeke, Dipo Amao, Gbenga Olunloyo, Leye Oni, Sokunbi, and Sina Alade. They all took the house test and were fully integrated into the dormitory system. This was the year the cricketer, Yinka Gbotosho, was Head of House though he was only in the fifth form. For that was the year A level classes were temporarily cancelled in GCI.

The following year in 1977, initially only 2 boys joined the boarding House in September. They were Awosan and Frederick Ladapo. Others, including Seyi Osibodu, came in later during the school year. Over the next two years, about half a dozen additional boys joined that ’77 set. They were Umo Antia, Emmanuel Akpan, Gbenro Onibokun, Morufu and Jelili. But by this time, house traditions were being jettisoned, and new boys who came into Grier House did not take the House test.

Meanwhile, by government fiat, the school’s census swelled. There were 240 students in Class 1 in that 1977 set which had 6 arms in Form 1. Over ninety percent of them were day students. Seyi Osibodu of that 1977 set remained a true Grierson and GCI boy in the old mold. His older brother Osibodu had been a stalwart football full back for Carr House and the school in the mid to late sixties. Seyi knew the drill. ‘I will be a real GCI boy,’ he told himself.

So, he made sure he enjoyed the few House and school traditions that remained. He joined the school cadet unit and served as the sword-bearing officer during their colorful parades. After one such occasion at the Liberty Stadium in 1982, he and the rest of the GCI contingent were invited to luncheon at the State House by Governor Bola Ige. That, he said later, was one of his most treasured moments in his years in Grier House and GCI.

The problem of the dwindling intellectual quality of GCI students began to be an issue in this era. All students into GCI before 1977 were admitted through the National Common Entrance Examination. The Oyo State Common Entrance was introduced in 1977. And from then on, apart from the absence of a full boarding system for all students to inculcate the age-old GCI culture of ethics and discipline, academic quality also dropped. There were more arms in each class, far too many overcrowded classrooms, a higher level of indiscipline and lower standards.
