api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
> ‘The heroes have come home
> Home to a new country.’

The end of World War II and the return to the old abode in Apata Ganga was a renaissance for Grier House. But this period also marked the exit of V. B. V. Powell, its seemingly immovable leader, from the scene. V. B. V. was now a balding and stodgy, but still athletic middle-aged white man. He left Grier House when he was made the school Principal in 1944. Before that, he was the Acting Principal from 1941 following the retirement of W. T. C. Field. Then, in 1948, all of a sudden, he was gone from Ibadan for good. He had been dispatched to Ughelli as the first Principal of the new Government College in that town on the outskirts of Warri.

Of course, the students in Grier House never thought they would get over the departure of their beloved tutor, sports coach, House Master and Principal . They remembered how when they returned to Apata Ganga in September 1945, in his irrepressible fashion, V. B. V. had brought around a great rock from the rocky terrain surrounding the school. He had this placed in front of the Grier House building. He told the students that this stone was to be known as ‘the Cairn.’ It would be a symbol of their return home after their forced sojourn in Lagos and Oke-Ado. Some of these students knew, from their vociferous reading, that this was an old Scottish custom. And they asked themselves, ‘Is V. B. V. also a Scotsman?’

***

The new set of Griersons who turned up on the house grounds in Grier House in January 1946 could be described as a hopeful and confident generation. The timidity and fear of white tutors which had characterized the behavior and attitude of the earlier sets were gone. These young men were witnesses to the recent world war. Back home in their towns and villages, they had heard stories from their fellow Nigerians who had fought alongside white soldiers and officers in Burma, Cameroons and Tangayika. These men had captured white men – German and Italian -  and had herded them into prison camps as prisoners of war. Some of them had been decorated for their efforts. Now they wore shiny medals of tin and bronze pinned to their breasts especially on the day of celebration known as V Day – Victory Day.

Thus, the new set of students assigned to Grier House after the war possessed the quite new notion that there was no reason for black men to serve the white skinned ‘oyinbos’ forever. With proper education and the right opportunities at their disposal, they were convinced that anything was possible for their generation. Surely, they had the same brains and intellectual potential as young men of other races who were born in Europe and America. They only wanted to prove that they were equal to any white man. They could and would become scientists and physicians who would discover new viruses and devise new ways to treat old diseases. They would be activists and policy makers who would find the solution for many social ills. And they would be engineers and architects who would design and build bridges, factories and tall buildings all over the country. There was no reason why one of them could not one day lead a world body like the United Nations, or even win the Noble Prize. They could rule not just their country Nigeria, but the world.

One of those young men who came in the set of 1946 was an 11-year-old boy from Abeokuta. Ever since he could crawl and ask questions, everyone knew he was precocious. And his parents indulged his whim of reading every book he lay his eyes on. Before he enrolled in GCI, he had spent almost a year at Abeokuta Grammar School, one of the famous grammar schools founded by the CMS in 1913. This school had produced a steady stream of schoolteachers, clergymen and lawyers for Yorubaland over the previous three decades since it was founded. Its principal was the already famous Reverend Israel Ransome Kuti, one of Nigerian’s foremost educationists. But this boy’s parents thought his talents would blossom even more in the favored environment of the new government school in Ibadan. This was why they made him take the entrance exam to Government College Ibadan, even though he was already enrolled in another secondary school which most families in their town thought was quite excellent.

This young man’s name was Wole Soyinka.  Once installed in GCI, his gift for assimilating words and language into highly imaginative prose and poetry became manifest. Soon, with the tutelage of his ‘oyinbo’ tutors, he was able to speak and write English almost to perfection. His essays in class invariably received the highest mark possible. And they were read out in class by the white English master as an example to the other students. But then, Soyinka was always in trouble. For he was a rebel, forever fighting for many causes. This meant he was against many entrenched attitudes and ways of behavior of his time.  Like the unnamed hero in the poem by Marechera, the celebrated poet from Southern Rhodesia, Soyinka always seemed to be saying:

> I am against everything.
> I am against war,
> And I am against those
> that oppose war.

Some said he was born that way. But was this really so? Didn’t his education and experience in GCI have something to do with the development of his vibrant character and irrepressible attitude? For, even as he read all the books that he could find in the school library and learned to read and speak English almost as well as his English born teachers, Wole felt a discontent in his soul. It was a reaction against what he sensed was the colonization of his mind and soul by his colonial education. He felt that his African nature was being stripped from him. He was being asked to foreswear the orishas, iwins and anjonus of the Yoruba folk tales he had loved so well as a child.  He knew that these beings from the other world populated his dreams and were real to most of his people. But they were described by his ‘oyinbo’ tutors as pagan -  the uninformed and superstitious fancies of a primitive people. It is fair to say that Soyinka already possessed at that time the wide cultural perspective and poetry-infused imagination that would eventually lead to his Nobel Prize four decades later.

As a student in GCI, Soyinka resisted any attempt by the tutors and even his fellow students to curb his imaginative ways and free spirit. Soon, he began to realize that he longer felt any affinity with the orthodox Christian doctrine with which he had been brought up in Abeokuta in his parents’ household and in his church and school. Rather, his refuge and succor now lay in the secular books and poems he read, and the music he listened to, which, in his own words, gave him ‘an intensity of faith that was different from the narrow religious kind.’ This new way of faith embraced the entire human universe, yet it contained a personal message for every human being.

Young Soyinka’s world in GCI revolved around his self-nurturing of his naturally rich imagination and an ease in manipulating the white man’s language into vivid streams of consciousness. These inspired his early attempts at poetry, prose and drama. His own private world, even in a school that was set up for science and technology, placed little emphasis on Mathematics or Science. He left these subjects to his other schoolmates who wanted to be physicians and engineers. He did not lean towards sports either, even though he knew that the very fabric of GCI was woven from the thread of hearty competition on track, field and swimming pool. Soyinka was so ill-suited for sports and physical exertion of any kind that he was the last boy in his class in his House to swim the required 3 lengths of the swimming pool to get his ‘standard points.’

When the hour for sports came in the afternoon after siesta, while other boys headed off to the Main Field, Soyinka would sneak off to the orchard between Grier House and Swanston House. It was a place the boys called Unter den Linden, a name first given to it by the German internees who had occupied the GCI compound during the war years. Those German teachers, engineers and clergymen and their wives, overcome with homesickness for their faterland while the war raged in Europe, had named this grove after a famous boulevard in Berlin. Ensconced in his lair and safe from prying eyes, Soyinka would climb into the lower branch of a tree. There he would daydream, read from a novel of boyish adventure or try to memorize a volume of poetry by William Blake which he had been given as a present by a tutor.

Despite his love of Romantic English poetry, his penchant for daydreaming and his whimsical flights of fancy, Soyinka had a highly political mind for his age. He may have spoken for many in his generation when he explained to his classmates about their need to resist the new man they were all becoming. He saw their British-influenced education, despite the many advantages it would give them, as a subtle colonization of the mind of bright young black people all over Africa by their white masters. Soyinka made up his mind that this was a species of oppression and dehumanization against which he must fight. And fight he did against what he perceived as oppression anywhere he could find it, while he was in GCI. He questioned the need for prayers on too many occasions at too many school activities. He resisted the incessant rules which ran against his need to be different and free. He therefore broke rules, skipped chapel on Sundays although he sang in the choir, and disagreed on many topics with his seniors, prefects and tutors.

Soyinka knew that his views were controversial. Sometimes, they were heartily unpopular. For instance, he abandoned his faith in the Christian religion while still relatively junior in school. And he had no qualms about arguing the logic of his apostacy before his friends and even his tutors. He was always logical and persuasive in doing this – so much so that he won an essay competition with an article which he brazenly titled ‘Ideals of an Atheist.’ For once, as he admitted later, it was a prize he did not care to tell his parents about. At that time, his dad, S. A. Soyinka nicknamed ‘Essay’ and his mother, who Soyinka christened ‘Wild Christian’ in his books, could not countenance the reality of their adored first-born son being a ‘pagan.’  Until their dying day, Soyinka’s parents were stout in their Christian belief.

Soyinka also quarreled with some of his classmates. And on occasions, he was known to have engaged in physical fights. Akinkugbe ’46, who was in Swanston House with Soyinka, described one of the clashes he had with the impetuous and unruly young poet.

‘I had become so fed up with being nettled constantly by Soyinka, that one day we decided to fight it out physically. This came to the attention of the senior boys in the house, and they decided it had to be done officially with rules, like a regular boxing match. Somebody produced gloves. Soyinka and I strapped them on, and we had a go at it. I must have gone into a fog, for I cannot remember how it went. All I know is that at the end of this bout, my hands were raised in victory, and I was told I had won. Soyinka later said I bloodied his nose.’

On another occasion, he was bodily thrown out of the school library through a glass door by a much bigger classmate who he had insulted. He sustained a horrible gash that almost cut off his foot. This injury required stitches performed without anesthesia by the school nurse. But the whole week he had off while he recuperated in the dormitory while he was excused from classes.

allowed Soyinka to indulge his love of reading. More than once, he was punished for breaking bounds late at night to trek to town to watch a movie at the Odeon Cinema in Oke-Bola. And on another occasion, he inadvertently came upon one of the senior boys, a well-known cricketer from Grier House, in a compromising position with the teenage daughter of the gardener in one of the old, abandoned buildings with which the vast GCI compound abounded. After this, that particular senior boy did not dare punish Soyinka for even the direst infraction. But he never forgave Soyinka for his shame and embarrassment. For his troubles, Soyinka was shifted from one House to the other. Placed initially in Swanston House, he spent time in Field House, and then Carr House. He ultimately landed in Grier House which would be his last home before he left GCI in 1950.

These questions have often been asked. ‘Could Soyinka be called a Grierson when he only spent his last year in school in Grier House? And with his known aversion to sports, could he have had any affinity with a House that prided itself on the ethos created by the sports-obsessed V. B. V. Powell?’

The answer is “Yes, Soyinka was indeed a Grierson.”

In his later years, Soyinka looked back with fondness at his time in GCI and Grier House. And perhaps, we should understand that even though he appeared to be so different from everyone else, like many Griersons and GCI boys of his generation, Soyinka acquired the discipline, hard work and the constant aspiration for excellence and perfection that would be the wellspring of his tumultuous life. He learned these lessons from GCI and took them to heart. In his own words, his youthful philosophy was: ‘Be what you are despite what people may want you to be. Be original. Question everything. Be a leader, not a follower!’

In this summation of his ideals, we can say that Soyinka was the prototypical GCI boy and Grierson of his post-war generation. We know that many of his classmates went on to become intellectuals, pacesetters and rule breakers. Two of Soyinka’s classmates in that 1946 set, who were also assigned to Swanston House, were Muyiwa Awe and Ladipo Akinkugbe. Akinkugbe stayed throughout his years in GCI in Swanston, while Awe left Swanston to go to the new Field House when it was created in 1948. All three, later in life, made a name for themselves as world-renowned academicians and university professors.

Still, we have to admit that Soyinka was unique. He had special qualities that were not possessed by any of his contemporaries, brilliant though they all were. Even at that time, when he was a student in GCI and Grier House, he was an inveterate idealist and dreamer. And he was brave and completely fearless. He cared little for his own safety or comfort when fighting on behalf of others. He would often put his own life on the line in defense of a good cause. Soyinka saw himself as Peter Pan up in arms against Captain Hook. Or was it Jim Hawkins pitting his wits against the pirates on Treasure Island? He became one of the heroes in the adventure books he loved to read. But even when he grew older and left GCI, when he should have been comfortable and settled into a good job that his education and connections should have brought him, Soyinka constantly placed himself in harm’s way in a life-long crusade fighting for the rights and freedom of others.

Another intellectual of that post 2nd World War generation, who was a Grierson and who was also somewhat of an outsider and rebel like Soyinka, was Omololu Olunloyo. He came into Grier House two years later in the 1948 set. Unlike Soyinka, Olunloyo loved sports. He played cricket at a high level, thereby establishing his bona fide as a Grierson. He was an accomplished opening bowler for the House and the school. But the singular gift Olunloyo bequeathed to Grier House was similar to what Soyinka left behind. This was the reverberating echo of the brilliant mind of a loner and iconoclast who went on to become a world-renowned mathematician and maverick politician.

Yet another Grierson of that post-war generation, but with a different set of personal attributes, was Davis Olatunji Ogunseinde. He entered Grier House with the 1950 set. He was not brash, intellectually domineering or argumentative like Soyinka and Olunloyo. Even as a teenager, he carefully steered his thoughts and actions around the proverbial golden mean of the Greek philosophers. ‘Nothing in excess,’ he always told himself. Even as a boy, he knew he came from the newly-minted Yoruba middle-class stock. And he wanted to remain so when he grew up. His dad, Daniel Olufuwa Ogunseinde, was a businessman. He was a Westernized African gentleman of the new educated class who hailed from Abeokuta. By 1950, the senior Ogunseinde had settled in Ibadan. He had become reasonably well off. He owned a 2-storey building in the Agbokojo area of Ibadan. His various business concerns brought in sufficient income for him to be able to send his first son to Government College Ibadan without the need for a government scholarship.

While he was in Grier House between 1950 and 1955, young Ogunseinde did not resent the discipline, bullying, or the overbearing attitude of seniors and prefects. Nor was he bothered by the British manners of speech and behavior that were drilled into him and other boys. Early in life, watching an ‘oyinbo’ doctor at Adeoyo Hospital, he had resolved to be a physician. So, in GCI, he paid attention to science subjects. In the laboratory, he dissected all kinds of frogs and insects presented to him with gusto. He also did reasonably well in sports, which made him a true Grierson in the old tradition. And while he never became a celebrated champion, he represented Grier House creditably in football and cricket.

***

In 1946, the application process and entrance exam into GCI had not changed since 1930. The rigorous paper examination and daunting 2-day interview were continued from pre-war years. Only the best students from primary schools all over the Western Region and Lagos continued to be selected to enter GCI, which had now become a truly elite school. Its students competed against King’s College, Igbobi College, St Gregory’s College, Government College Zaria and Government College Umuahia. GCI boys were proud to be grouped among these ‘colleges,’ which were considered the best and most competitive in the land - not the ‘grammar’ schools or ‘boys high’ schools. In particular, GCI boys looked down with disdain at students from the IONIAN group of secondary schools in the Western Region who they began to refer to as ‘ayo’ schools.

After the war years, Grier House continued to consider itself superior and more innovative compared to its only rival and nominal senior, Swanston House. And for Griersons, the daily routine of the lives of the students still followed the ‘Cambridge blue’ standard imposed by V. B. V. Powell in 1930. This routine was enforced and followed quite gladly by students like Ogunseinde, from the time they woke up at 6.15 in the morning till ‘lights out’ at 9.45pm. Senior boys still lorded it over junior ones, especially the newcomers in Form I. And house prefects, now called Powellites in honor of V. B. V., continued to rule the roost. The most accomplished senior boy in Form VI was invariably made the Head of school, a position that had by this time in the early 1950s accumulated an aura of great honor, power and prestige.

School life changed drastically for students allocated to Grier House when a new building was completed and opened for Grier House in 1952. Built of solid cement brick, it was constructed around a grass covered quadrangle with 4 blocks of buildings. The walls of sold brick, unlike the earlier Grier structure blocks made from red clay, were designed to last for decades. In structure and design, the Grier House set of buildings was identical to the building that had just been built for their new neighbor, Field House in 1948.

When they took stock of their new crisp group of bungalows, the students and their Housemaster remembered the exploits of Odiase and Arubayi, those now legendary first prefects in Grier House who had been chosen by V. B. V. Powell from the pioneering 1930 set. Two blocks in the new building continued to be named after them. These two old Griersons were the never-to-be-forgotten folk heroes of Grier House. From now onwards, they would be celebrated in the rendition of the history of the House told to fresh students and on house tests. A third block between these 2 blocks was named after Mr. Herrington, the Biology and Agriculture teacher who had played a great part in assisting V. B. V. Powell in setting up the machinery for running Grier House in those early years after 1930. But when the time came for this ceremonial naming, this gentleman was not around. For he had left the school, having retired and gone back to England. The last block in the new Grier House building, which alone would remain unnamed, was simply called the Day block.

At that time, this Day block did not house any dormitories and was used only during the day – hence its name. But later, the Head of House was assigned his bedroom there and the House Master was also given an office there. A large room in the Day block was then assigned to House Prefects who were now rather ceremoniously called Powellites in homage to the first Housemaster, V. B. V. Powell. It was at this time that the Reading room, a space created next to the prep room, was stocked with books. For the students in Grier House, this room became a subsidiary library to the main school library. The books on its shelves were obtained from England. For in the early 1950s, there were very few books written by native born Nigerians or published locally. The Reading Room also had a shelf for newspapers, magazines and journals from England. The Tatler, News of the World and the Daily Mirror all had honorable mention. This Reading room was also filled with memorabilia that honored the exploits of the House in sports. One of its most treasured features was the Honors Board, which was carved each year out of iroko wood by the boys themselves. This wooden board was etched and inscribed with the names of the House Master, Head of House, Powellites and those Griersons deemed to have brough honor and glory to the House in the previous year. Mainly though, it honored the sports heroes of Grier House from year to year. Trophies and other awards won by Griersons were displayed on shelves in the Reading Room. Over the years, this reading room became a place for students to sit around in their few leisure hours in the evenings and on weekends. There, they played card games and listened to music and news on a small “Rediffusion” radio. Needless to say, most of the music they heard was either European or American, all following the popular tastes in England in the early 50s.

The enclosed bare ground within this ranch-style grouping of 4 bungalows that constituted Grier House was planted with ‘Port Harcourt’ grass. This was the same native-grown grass that had been used for the turf on the school cricket field. The grass and walk paths were bordered with low shrubs of boxwood. This inner courtyard was divided into four rectangles. It was now called the quadrangle, or ‘quad,’ as in Cambridge or Oxford University fashion. All Grier House boys were taught that it was their sacred duty to trim these hedges and keep the grass clean and mowed with their sharpened thin cutlasses known as ‘oja’gba.’ Students were forbidden from ever crossing any lawn, especially this special quadrangle in the very heart of Grier House, unless they were keeping it well-mown and tidy.

It is fair to say that generations of boys kept this rule religiously for decades afterwards. It was a rule set in stone by those Griersons of the post-2nd World War generation.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: How Grier House was Founded

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
> The housemaster led his boys by example;
> And because he himself was highly disciplined,
> he had no difficulty enforcing discipline.
> — Gabriel Akin Deko ‘30

> With its harsh discipline,
> Grier House was like the Sparta of ancient Greece;
> Swanston was more like Athens in those early days.
> — Sabiru Biobaku (Bisiriyu) ‘32

Grier House came into being in January 1930. This was the year in which the school of which it was a part, Government College Ibadan, began a new life as a secondary school. For a year before that, this school was a teacher training college. The students who had already spent a year in the teacher training college were now merged with a fresh new intake of bright young lads into the new school. All of them had been given their admission letter on merit, based on worthy recommendations by their primary school principal and a personal interview in which the prospective student was asked about himself and his family. His intellectual bona fides were then tested with probing questions on English grammar, vocabulary and arithmetic.  In January 1930, when this school opened its doors for the first time, it was to be  a boarding secondary school for boys in the British public-school model. All the students, old and new, were assigned to 2 residential dormitories. At the beginning, these 2 dormitories were simply named after the respective housemasters appointed to take care of the students in each house. Later that year, the first house was renamed Swanston, the other became Grier.

Now, let us start this account, like all great stories, from the beginning. The story of Grier House started with a decision by the British colonial authorities in the Education Department of the Western Region of Nigeria at the end of the 1920s. The gentlemen in charge of policy at this government office decided to establish a middle school owned and run by the government in 1929. It would be a step above the primary schools which had sprouted all over the southern provinces of Nigeria since the latter half of the previous century. The school was established in the capital city of the Western Region which was Ibadan. It was initially meant to be a Teacher Training college. But a year later it became the first ‘model’ boarding secondary school run by the government for boys in this part of the country.

The idea for the formation of the school came from a white man called S. M. Grier, the Director of Education for the Southern Provinces of colonial Nigeria, and E .R. J. Hussey, (1885-1958) the man who replaced him in that position. The first boarding House of the school, which would later emerge as GCI, came with the establishment of the Teacher Training College in 1929. This was Swanston House. It was named after another expatriate Englishman who was the Deputy Director of Education under Grier.

Grier House was named after Selwyn Macgregor Grier who was born in England half a century earlier on April 1, 1878. He was the eldest child of Richard Macgregor Grier (born1835, died 1894), a scholar and clergyman of the Church of England who was the dean of a town called Rugeley and prebendary of Lichfield. His mother was Grace Allen, the daughter of well to do upper middle-class parents. Grier’s parents had only one other child, his sister, Lynda, who later in life became a noted champion for the education of girls and was Principal of Lady Margaret Hall at Oxford University.

Grier was educated by his parents at a prestigious public school in England, Marlborough College. He did well in school. He received accolades in the mandatory studies of Latin, Classics and Mathematics. He also featured prominently in sports. Thus, on leaving school, he had no difficulty in securing a place at Cambridge University where he enrolled in  Pembroke College in 1897. On coming down from Cambridge, he did not want to be a clergyman like his father. And the Army was out of the question, for he had no stomach for military drill. He thought he would try his hand at tutoring. He therefore taught for five years at two public schools similar in  prestige to the one he had attended. He was a master at Berkhamsted School, Hertfordshire (founded in 1541) from 1901 to 1902. Then he taught at Cheam School (founded in1645, and famous as the preparatory school attended by King Charles III of Great Britain and his father, Phillip, Duke of Edinburgh) from 1902 to 1905.

But Grier soon became bored with life in post-Victorian England. He decided he wanted to see the world. His application was accepted at the Colonial Office in London, and he was sent overseas to the new Colony and Protectorates in Nigeria, where he was made the Assistant Resident for Zaria Province in 1906. He was a bright and diligent worker, and he made a good impression on his superiors. He was also liked by the ‘natives.’  He soon became a full Resident in his own rights and was sent to Bauchi in 1912. It was soon after this that he was transferred to the South, to serve in the Western regional capital of Ibadan in 1913, a year before Nigeria was united as a country under the British flag, with Alfred Lugard as Governor-General.

From there, it was all promotions and honors for the rising young colonial officer. From 1921 to 1925, Grier served as Secretary for Native Affairs. And in 1925, he was appointed Director of Education of the Southern Provinces. Indeed, it was in that position that Grier suggested and pushed the idea of a school for boys that would be established and run by the Western Regional Government. His first idea was for this to be a Teacher Training College, but the plan was later changed to that of a boys-only secondary school. This was how Grier became the ‘founding father’ of Government College, Ibadan.

But before these new plans bore fruit, Grier was on the move. While he was on a short leave back home in England, he was promoted and transferred to the West Indies. He was now the Colonial Secretary for Trinidad and Tobago. To go with his new position, he was made a Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George (C.M.G.) in the same year, 1929. More honors followed. In 1934, this decoration was upgraded to that of Knight Bachelor of St Michael and St George. Then, as the crowning glory to his service to his monarch and country, in 1935, Grier was appointed Governor of the Windward Islands of the West Indies, an event that was relayed to Ibadan and Grier House by telegram. This is the origin of the’ red letter day’ tradition in Grier House. And in 1936, Grier was finally created a knight (K.C.M.G.) by King George VI.

Sadly, Grier did not stay for any length of time in his position of privilege as Governor. He had to resign his post the next year 1937 due to  worsening eyesight which had now rendered him functionally blind.  After Grier returned to England later that year, he lived peacefully in his home in Surrey. He surrounded himself with memorabilia of his time in Ibadan and the West Indies. And he communicated frequently with V. B. V. Powell, his protégé at the Education Department who was now the House Master of Grier House and later Principal of GCI.

Grier never married and had no children. He died peacefully in his sleep on November 8, 1946. This news was brought to Grier House. But it was not tagged as a ‘red letter day,’ and for obvious reasons, was not celebrated.

***

From its auspicious beginning, Grier House was destined to be up and running in no time at all. This singular achievement was mainly due to the herculean efforts of another British gentleman who was appointed the first Housemaster. This was Villiers Barcham Vaughan Powell, a relative of the famous Robert Baden Powell (1857-1941) who had founded the Boys Scouts movement in 1910. Like Baden-Bowell, V. B. V.  was a man of action who felt very comfortable in the company of young people. He was a well-read man who loved sports, and he was devoted to the outdoors. Like Grier, he had attended Cambridge University, where he distinguished himself as a noted athlete, and competed for his college, his university and England.

Born in 1904 in New Zealand to upper middle-class parents, V. B. V. Powell was educated at some of the best public schools and colleges the British Empire had to offer during and after the First World War. What is of note is that at every school or college he found himself, V. B. V. shone like a star. He started at Christ’s College, Christchurch, one of the most prestigious preparatory boarding schools for boys in New Zealand. From there, he went to England where he attended Clifton College, one of the original 8 public schools in the United Kingdom, before being admitted to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge University. From his youth, his three given names were so singular and unusual, even in aristocratic circles in England, that his friends and tutors called him by his initials. He was also called ‘Pip’ by his more intimate friends

Soon after leaving Cambridge, V. B. V. joined the Colonial Office with the intention of being an educator and administrator in the Colonies. He was immediately dispatched to Nigeria. And in 1927, aged only 23, he was appointed Superintendent of Education in Western Nigeria. It was from there that he was selected as a pioneer member of staff to teach Mathematics and History, when the forerunner teacher training school that later became GCI came into being in 1929. When Grier House was founded as the second residential dormitory of the newly established GCI in 1930, it was not surprising that this young man, still in his mid-twenties, was chosen to be the first Housemaster. For despite his young age, he was already known for his intelligence, talent for organization and boisterous energy.

That year 1930 was a difficult time back home in England, The post Great World War financial slump made life difficult for rich and poor. And following the Great Crash of the previous year 1929, many formerly comfortable and well to do families that Powell knew in England, Australia and New Zealand  had lost their fortune. V. B. V. therefore knew he was lucky to have a job in a field he loved. Working as an educator in one of the better-known outposts of the Empire was his opportunity to make a man of himself. V. B. V. felt this job as the Housemaster of Grier House was worth devoting all his brain and efforts to.

The first thing V. B. V. knew he had to do was to appoint ‘prefects’ from among the students. Some of these boys would be new. But some had already been a year in the school, having been seconded from Swanston house which was the dormitory of the earlier Teacher Training College. He wanted the more mature students who would supervise the other students and be responsible to him. They would help him maintain discipline and orderliness on the house grounds. And they would preserve and represent at all times the dignity and prestige of the brand-new House. He had to choose them carefully. For he was looking for attributes which he knew were uncommon – intelligence, emotional maturity and that hard-to-define trait that he called ‘leadership qualities.’ He wanted them to be leaders, not bullies. He also wanted them to be decently good in sports. This was how early in that year 1930, V. B. V. chose Johnson Odiase, Eduweye Arubayi, Andrew Sagay, Henry Fadayiro, S. O. Temietan, A. E. Adeniran, David Edgal and Samuel Omenai as the first prefects for Grier House.

What we know is that when he was appointed Housemaster of Grier House in January 1930, V. B. V. was determined, despite his youth and inexperience in teaching at any secondary school up to that moment, to instill his British upper-class values into his Nigerian students. This included his ideal of the gentleman.  In a first-year class with the youngest boy being about 16 years old, some of his older students were only 5 years younger than their ‘oyinbo’ housemaster.  In fact, they could have been his younger siblings. V. B. V. may therefore be forgiven if he treated his students with something akin to sibling affection. He knew they had come a long way from home. Indeed, for many of these students, it was their first time away from their village or small town in the Yoruba hinterland or their fishing community hidden among the creeks of the Niger Delta.

V. B. V. thought he understood these young men. They had left their rural homes to be part of this experiment in education devised by the white man. And was he not himself an exile from his own homeland? His childhood friends and family were thousands of miles away across the sea. He may therefore have treated his boys with what some of the other white tutors thought was indulgence. But he combined this easy familiarity with a firm hand and an insistence on obedience and discipline. In return, he received the intense loyalty and affection of these boys. By setting a personal example and by constant exhortation, V. B. V. was determined to drive home into his students his love for books, personal integrity, discipline and sports.

It is an historical fact that V. B. V. succeeded beyond his own fanciful dreams. He became so successful in molding the character of these first Griersons that they stood out in those early months in comparison to their colleagues in Swanston House, the only other house in the school. As one of these old Swans said decades later, “It was as if the light that shown out of V. B. V. Powell’s eyes bore into those Grier House boys and ignited in them something bright and magnificent.”  Two of those Grier boys who fell under the influence of V. B. V.’s ‘shining’ light were the young Akin Deko from Lagos and Andrew Sagay from Warri. They were in that special first set of pupils that came into Grier House in 1930.

On weekends, V. B. V. would invite sone of the boys to his house. These were his prefects and a few other boys from Grier House who were his favorites – Odiase, Arubayi, Edgal, Deko, Temietan and others. Most of them were, like him, very active in sports. He would serve them tea with cubes of sugar and buns. He would talk about England, his years in Cambridge, and his other ‘oyinbo’  friends and mentors in the Education Department who had put in the hard work that made Government College Ibadan and Grier House come to being.

One day, one of the boys said, ‘You have told us all about Grier. How he went to the West Indies and became a Governor, and all that. But what happened to Swanston? What about him?’

V. B. V.’s face took on a sad look. He looked intently at the boy. Then he said, ‘Swanston was sent home to England on leave later in that year 1929. The idea was that he would get a promotion and maybe move to a plush position somewhere else in the colonies. But he fell ill on the boat on the way home and died on the trip. He never got back to England.’

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: Sports in Grier House, Part 2
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: Our chronicles record that the years between 1958 to 1966 were bumper years for sports in Grier House. So many great sportsmen populated that era especially in athletics and cricket that we may sometimes lose count. Most notable among…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
Our chronicles record that the years between 1958 to 1966 were bumper years for sports in Grier House. So many great sportsmen populated that era especially in athletics and cricket that we may sometimes lose count. Most notable among these were Abimbola Onajin, ’58 (cricket), Famuyiwa ’58 (football) Adeyemi-Wilson (athletics) Akanji ’58 (football) and Ogunmoyela I ’63 (multiple sports). Of this group, special mention must be made of Oluyomi Adeyemi-Wilson.

Yomi Adeyemi-Wilson was born in the Campos area of Lagos Island to a family of Lagosian who trace their roots to the Kenta district of Abeokuta. He owed his family name to his grandfather, Gabriel Wilson, who was one of the first in Egbaland to learn the white man’s language and become a Christian. As far as it is known, this nineteenth century patriarch was the first to adopt the Wilson surname after being baptized as an onigbagbo. Young Adeyemi-Wilson spent 5 years at Igbobi College before he came to GCI for his Higher School certificate. Although he had already made up his mind to be an engineer and focused on Mathematics and Physics, he obtained a Distinction (A1) in History at the School Certificate exam and was regarded as an allrounder. When he arrived in GCI, he started off as a day student living inside the school compound with one of the tutors, Mr. Sofenwa. However soon after Adeyemi-Wilson came to stay with this tutor, his host and guardian was promoted and transferred to Comprehensive High School, Aiyetoro. Adeyemi-Wilson therefore packed his belongings and was taking them to the boys’ quarters of another tutor, when the Principal, D. J. Bullock saw him and personally took him to Grier House and asked the housemaster to give him a room in the newly built HSC block there.

The rest is history. Adeyemi-Wilson, who specialized in the high jump, triple jump and long jump, became as celebrated an athlete as Ojutalayo had been 2 years earlier. He captained the Grier House and GCI athletics teams, broke the school records in all his 3 events and won the Victor Ludorum in 1964. To cap it all, he set a Grier Cup record in the long jump and became forever a GCI and Grier House legend. For his achievements in GCI, he was made a school prefect in Upper Six even though he had only been in school for a year for his Higher school. He was also the recipient of the Headmaster’s Prize which was given to him by the principal, Mr D. J. Bullock as the best student graduating from the school that year

***

Our chronicles from that era spanning the first half of the new decade of the 1960s - those giddy years after Independence - tell us that Grier House continued to do very well in most sports. This was especially true in athletics, football and cricket. Why was this? It is possible that Griersons of that era wanted to reassert their claim as the one House - the home of Ekperigin - whose sports legacy ran deepest in the whole of GCI. This was reflected in the honor roll for the winner of the Victor Ludorim trophy given to the best athlete in GCI. In 1962, it was Ojutalayo, whose exploits are already noted in this narrative, who became the cynosure of all eyes after winning this prestigious trophy. In the process, he became the new hero to all junior boys in Grier House. And in 1964, as we have seen, it was another Grierson, Adeyemi-Wilson, who not only won the Victor Ludorum, but topped the medals table in the high jump, long jump and triple jump at the Grier Cup finals.

With regard to football, there is unanimity that Grier House was very good in the first half of the decade. In one momentous year 1965, the two top positions in the pecking order in the school’s leadership hierarchy were admirably combined in the single person of one Grierson and athlete. This was Olaniyi Akanji. He was the captain of the senior football teams for both Grier House and the school that year. He was also the Head of Grier House. When as a junior boys, he began to captivate audiences on the small Grier House field behind the prep room and on the larger  GCI Main Field, he was nicknamed ‘Gento.’  This was due to the similarity of his playing style to that of a star European footballer of that era. This was Francisco ‘Paco’ Gento Lopez (1933-2022), the speedy Real Madrid left winger who was capped 43 times for Spain, played in the 1962 and 1966 World Cups, and was named the greatest Spanish footballer to ever play el deporte rey, the beautiful game.

As the center forward and captain of the Grier House and school team, Akanji was assisted by  Faseiku ‘62, nicknamed Amasco, at the inside left position. These two stars were surrounded by a singular cast of Griersons in the skill positions. These included Ogunshona, Shittu and Ohiomoba in Upper Six; Aiyegbayo (Jazzy Aiye) Lower Six, Taiwo Cole in Form 5, and Oyekan and Faseiku in Form 4. The goalkeeper was the unflappable Leke Diana who was in Form 5. This indomitable team did Grier House proud and won the senior football trophy in 1965.  Not to be outdone, the boys on the Grier House junior football squad easily cruised past Field House in the semifinals to face the heavily favored Carr House in the final. This Grier House team was captained by Sofeso, and included names like Oyelese, Lamidi, Arubayi and Aladegboye in Form 3; Olubajo (nicknamed ‘Bazuaye’), Efuwape and Aribisala in Form 2, and Aderemi in Form 1. The goalkeeper was Osita Anerobi who was repeating Form 1, but etched his name into Grier House lore for his heroics that day. The boys practiced and executed to perfection the new 4-2-4 system which had been developed by the Brazilian national team and espoused by the Stationery Football Club in Nigeria. And they delivered. Grier House won the junior interhouse trophy in football that year, in 1965 with the winning goal scored by the captain Sofeso who hit a ball from midfield that caught an idling Babayale by surprise. But when the boys brought the trophy back to the House, it was a small, much-dented tin cup that fitted inside the palm of one hand.

Grier House was no slouch in athletics either in that decade of accomplishment. In 1965, Grier House won the junior and senior 4 x 100 yards relays. The members of that historic senior relay team that year were Adegbite ’61 (nicknamed Jeff Silla) as first leg, Awosoji ’61 as second leg, and Badejoko ’59 in the third leg position. Ernest Odigie ‘60, who would be the Head of House the next year, was the anchor. Eyewitnesses record that he ran away from all contenders to breast the tape. But later, boys from Swanston House would claim that Odigie was almost caught at the finish line by Popoola ’60 of the ‘blue’ House. The next year, 1966, Grier House won the Athletic Shield outright, highlighted by a first-place finish in the long jump by Oredein (Ore Defta) ’61.

It was in this era that Ogunmoyela ’63 made his mark. He was the eldest of the Ogunmoyela brothers, which included Gbenga ’65 and Tosin ’68. All three Ogunmoyelas were stand-up sportsmen and champions in Grier House. The senior Ogunmoyela (known as Ogunmoyela I in school parlance) who entered the school in 1963, shone in academics and multiple sports at a high level. When he was in Form 4 in 1966, he won a tightly contested interhouse table tennis championship that was celebrated not only in Grier House but all over the school. His opponent that year was Thomas of Carr House, a flashy player with a cocksure personality who reveled in his undefeated status up till that moment. Ogunmoyela I also played football, hockey and cricket for the house and school. He was captain of the house table tennis team which won several interhouse trophies on behalf of Grier House. He also captained the GCI Football and Table Tennis teams. A confident leader who combined strictness with a permissive disposition towards his juniors, he was made Head of House in his final year in Sixth Form in 1969.

Despite such outstanding athletes and uplifting victories, by the end of that decade, Grier House’s days of glory appeared to be coming to an end. Its few victories were confined to football and athletics. But even there, some said its victory in junior football in 1965 was due to the spectacular performance of one Form 1 boy. This was the goalkeeper, Osita Anerobi ’64, whose moment of glory on the football field on behalf of Grier House could not save him from dropping out of GCI at the end of that year due to poor academic grades. After this, Grier House barely clung to its football dominance which now became a fading glory. The 1967 junior football team could not escape the semifinal stage when it faced Carr House. The bright spot in that match was a miraculous goal scored from midfield by the Grier house outside left, Babalola 67. The other members of that team were Towo Aderemi ’65 (captain), Jobi Ososanya ’65, Gbenga Ogunmoyela ’65, Ogunsola ’65, Babalola ’65, Apata ’65, Ogunyemi ’65, Macauley ’66, Okuboyejo ’66, and Oluwole ’67 (goalkeeper). The next year 1968, Grier House redeemed its honor. It brought back the junior interhouse football trophy.

***

Outside football, in the last few years of the 1960s, Grier House completely ceded mastery in the sports of hockey and cricket to Swanston House and to a lesser degree, Field House. Swimming was no longer a sport contested for in GCI. So, Grier House was not called upon to defend its honor in a category in which it had, in former years, won so much fame. And even though lawn tennis was now being reintroduced, it was no longer a hotly contested interhouse sport in the school. Grier House did win the Table Tennis inter-house trophies for both the Junior and Senior categories in 1966 with the help of boys like Jaiyesimi ’63, Efuwape ‘62, Ogunsanwo ’63, Balogun ’63, Ogunmoyela ’63, Famuyiwa ‘63. and Taiwo (nicknamed T-Mod) who came to GCI for his Higher School in 1965 and 1966.  Other Grier House sports heroes in that era at the tail end of the 1960s included Ogunmoyela I, Ogunmoyela II and Bambo Oyekan ‘62.  Ogunsanwo ’63 and Osho ’64 were members of the school and State Table Tennis teams after winning the interhouse championship in that sport for the house.  In 1969, Jones ’63 was the captain of the house and school basketball team which also included Kehinde Adegbesan ’63 and Thompson Olumoko (HSC 69-70). Yinka Lawal ’63 played hockey for the school team up to Form 4. He was also a member of the Grier House team that won the interhouse trophy in Table Tennis in 1967.

Thus as the 1960s came to a close, Griersons could say that the decade had been one of unprecedented enthusiasm and high performance in sports.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: Sports in Grier House, Part 3
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: In the latter half of the 1960s, Grier House began a new era of enthusiasm and high performance in sports. The heroes who emerged in our narrative of sports in Grier House between 1966 and 1975 start with Gbenga Ogunmoyela (Ogunmoyela II)…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
In the latter half of the 1960s, Grier House began a new era of enthusiasm and high performance in sports. The heroes who emerged in our narrative of sports in Grier House between 1966 and 1975 start with Gbenga Ogunmoyela (Ogunmoyela II) of the ‘65 set. He was Head of House as well as captain of Hockey in 1971. He played cricket, football and hockey for Grier House, becoming the captain of hockey in his last year in school. Coming into Grier House a year later was Tokunbo Olusile ‘66, another multi-sport athlete who was in the Grier House junior team in football in 1968 that won the interhouse championship. He played cricket for the school from the time he was in Form 3. And he was made the school cricket captain and school prefect in his final year in 1972. Standing shoulder to shoulder with these two was the third Ogunmoyela brother, Tosin (Ogunmoyela III) of the 1968 set.

Like his two famous brothers, Tosin was an all-rounder who represented the house and school in lawn tennis, cricket, hockey and football. In cricket, as a senior, he was the wicket-keeper for the school team, But his ‘forte’ lay in football and hockey. Among the many trophies he brought to Grier House was  the junior football cup in 1970,  and also the junior hockey laurels the same year. He captained both teams. By the time he left school in June 1974, Ogunmoyela III also had the honor of being the leader of the school Army Cadet unit. For his skills in army drills, apart from his academic standing, he was admitted to the Nigerian Defense Academy in Zaria after he finished from GCI. But his parents opposed his pursuing a career in the military. Tosin Ogunmoyela, like his brother Gbenga, was one of the few GCI students to make both the State and National Hockey teams in the same year.  The only other GCI boys of that era who could claim that distinction were Jide Ogunnaike ’65 from Swanston House, Kole Wellington ‘65 also of Swanston, and Biodun Alli ’67 of Field House.

Another Grierson deserving accolades in sports in that era that spanned the late 60s into the early 70s was Oyekan ‘66 who captained the Grier House football team in 1972. A year later, all eyes turned to one Grierson - Muyiwa Osundolire of the ’67 set. He was one of those spectacular allrounders who emerge once in a generation from Grier House. He dazzled in every sport that was his pleasure to play for Grier House and GCI. For this young man, the experience of sports was a pleasure. For he truly loved sports. Talking about him years later, his teammates  marveled at Osundolire’s ball handling skills in hockey.

‘Believe me, he always hugged the ball like a lover,’ remarked a classmate from another House who had the misfortune of playing opposite Osundolire in a key interhouse senior hockey final.

Indeed, when Osundolire had possession of the ball during a hockey match, no opposing player could take it from him. He held on to the ball, keeping it close to his feet as he made his deft back-and-forth moves. He would dribble around the outstretched hockey stick of any opposing player who tried to tackle him until he saw an opening to pass the ball or hit a shot at the goal. To all who watched him, or played with him or against him, he was a phenomenon - like a being from outer space. As a true all-rounder, Osundolire was the nearest that Grier House ever came to naming an athlete ‘captain of all games’ since that title was bestowed on Harding Ekperigin in 1937.

As good fortune would have it, it was also at this time that another transformative sportsman, this time in athletics, appeared in Grier House. But he did not start with his set from Form 1. He had completed the first five years of his secondary schooling at another school. His name was Taiwo Orungbemi, but the popular nickname by which he was generally known was ‘Masai.’ After completing his Form V at Aquinas College, Akure, he came to GCI and Grier House in January 1971 to join the 1966 set in the lower sixth form. His athletic career had already been noticed at his former school where he had established himself as a dominant quarter-miler who dominated every regional athletic competition that he took part in. This included the Grier Cup,

Orungbemi’s transfer to GCI in 1971 placed him in the premier development pipeline for Nigerian athletics. He blossomed in Grier House and GCI. And his specialty remained the 400-meter race. His performance in this event at the Grier-Powell Cup in 1971 and 1972 earned him attention on the national level. This led to his selection as a Nigerian International for the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich, West Germany. He was part of the elite 4×400 meters relay team that included other iconic Nigerian quarter-milers such as Bruce Ijirighwo, Musa Dogon Yaro, Mamman Makama, and Robert Ojo. Orungbemi also went on to represent Nigeria at the 1974 Commonwealth Games in Christchurch, New Zealand. His talent secured him an athletic scholarship to Mississippi State University in the United States, where he recorded a blazing 400 meters time of 45.0 seconds.

But it was an era of sports decline for Grier House even though Orungbemi and other stars added brief spectacular sparks of athletic brilliance to the fortunes of Grier House in the early 70s. But the decline had set in nevertheless and nought could retrieve this  Thus, by the end of that decade, Grier House was no longer viewed as a force in sports to be feared by other Houses in GCI as was the case in former times.

***

Grier House basked in the bright light of cricket as another era of dominance in that sport was ushered in the mid to late 60s. Worthy Griersons like Bambo Oyekan ’62, Gbekeloluwa Oguntimehin ’63, Yemi Famuyiwa ’63 and Eddie Jone ’63 set the pace.  Later in the decade, it was Adetokunbo Olusile ’66 and Bayo Wiliams ’68 who stepped in. Others in that era who shone in interhouse cricket on behalf of Grier House were Adebayo Amole ’65, Abayomi Olasimbo ’65, Fola Oyekan ’66, as well as Gbenga Jaiyesimi, Bolanle Ayodele and Adeyemi Oluwole all from the 1967 set. And when the 1960s ended, capable young cricketers emerged to take their place. These were boys who were encouraged by the examples of past Grier House cricket legends like Leslie Harriman ’49, Adebowale Tade ‘51, Jide Bademosi ‘53, and Bimbo Onajin ‘58. The list is too long for every hero in that era to be included here. But the standouts who played at a high level for Grier House in the early to mid-1970s were Deji Otegbeye ’69, Olusegun Yerokun ’71, Tokunbo Adesida ’72 and Yinka Gbotosho ’73. They were followed later in that decade by younger Griersons who also played cricket with credit for house and school. These were boys like Jide Adedeji ’72, Ibidapo Akande ’73, Fela Ifaturoti ‘73, Jide Otegbeye ’74, Ladi Seriki ’74 and Leke Otegbeye ‘78.

Year after year during the 1970s, these young cricketers from Grier House wrought havoc on the carefully laid plans of their opponents. The supremacy at the wicket that they conferred on successive Grier House teams brought tears to the eyes of boys from other Houses including Powell, which joined the GCI community in 1973. For instance, paced by a relentless bowling attack led by Deji Otegbeye ‘69, Grier House won the interhouse cricket trophy in 1974. And this feat was repeated several times before that decade was over

Two names in particular deserve a place of honor in that era - Adetokunbo Adesida ’72 and Yinka Gbotosho ’73. In their time, their names were roll calls of excellence. Tokunbo Adesida was born in Cricklewood, London to highly educated middle-class Nigerian parents. His father had an MBA from Harvard. His equally accomplished mother became the Chief Nursing Officer for Ondo State. His family returned to Nigeria when Tokunbo was still a toddler. They then lived in the Ago Taylor area of Ibadan which was not far from the GCI compound in Apata Ganga. Tokunbo often visited Apata Ganga to hang around the GCI house grounds and playing fields with his cousin, Seyi Adesida (Field House, ’69 set).

This was how Tokunbo fell in love with the sport of cricket which was often played by the younger boys in GCI by throwing a tennis ball at an empty barrel behind one of the Houses. The ‘batsmen’ defended this ‘wicket’ with crudely manufactured wooden bats. Thus, by the time he was admitted to GCI and came to Grier Huse as a student in 1972, Tokunbo already fancied himself to be a bowler in the making. He would pitch the ball with such ferocity that he was called a ‘demon bowler.’ Indeed, he became very speedy in getting many a good batsman out. This was how Tokunbo Adesida gained fame as a bowler not just in Grier House but throughout the school. He was a rare specimen – a left-handed bowler who was as comfortable with the inswing as the outswing. It was no surprise that when he was in Form 3, he was invited to join the Men’s team of the Western State Cricket team to play and tour with team members who were much older than him.  It was also lucky for him that the captain of this Western State team was Jide Bademosi, Grierson ’53, who mentored him and taught him the finer aspects of bowling and batting.

With this exemplary tutelage from a master, Tokunbo became captain of the Grier House and school cricket team when he was in Form 5. He became captain though he was not in the Sixth Form  because in that year, the higher school (A Levels) course was cancelled in GCI, although it was restored the next year. What this meant was that Tokunbo was captain of the GCI team for 3 years from 1976 to 1979 - not only when he was in Form 5, but in the 2 years he was in Higher School. Under his leadership, Grier House won 2 interhouse cricket trophies 2 years in a row. He also captained the Western Regional team that won the Morrocco-Clark trophy the last year it was contested in 1977. With this victory, Grier House cricket had come full circle. Tade ‘51 of Grier House captained the Western Region team that won the maiden Morocco- Clarke cup in 1954. Here was another Grierson captaining another Western Regional team that would take home this iconic trophy the last time it was played for.

Tokunbo Adesida did not limit himself to one sport when he was in Grier House. He played hockey, tennis and soccer with equal zeal and excellence. In football, he was the penalty taker for the school team. It was said that he could loft the ball inside the net from anywhere on the field. He was that good. After leaving GCI in June 1979, with the state of the country portending poor prospects for a young man with his brains and talents, he left for greener pastures outside Nigeria. He found a new home in the United States, where the next year, 1980 he gained admission to Rutgers University, New Brunswick, New Jersey. He obtained his degree in Geology and began to work professionally in that field in many parts of United States. But his undoubted talents did not leave him. Tokunbo continued to play cricket throughout the United States especially in the states of Maryland, New Jersey and New York. He led many cricket clubs whose members invariably appreciated his talent and marveled at those special skills which should have taken him to higher grounds.

Ranking shoulder to shoulder with Adesida, Yinka Gbotosho made his entry into Grier House in 1973. Like Adesida, he was another generational talent who seemed to have imbibed cricketing skills with the water he drank from the taps in Grier House. He was good from the start, and his excellence never left him. When he was in Form 2, he was invited by Jide Bademosi ‘53, who had now become the ubiquitous mentor to generations of cricket players from Grier and GCI to play for teams outside GCI. Following Bademosi as his mentor and guardian, Gbotosho attended various camps for young players and played in cricket matches all over Western Nigeria and Lagos. Thus, he attended the Oyo State youth camp that prepared young sportsmen all over the state for the National Sport Festival in 1977.  The story was confirmed by Gbotosho himself that Bademosi, who Gbotosho and other proteges always called ‘Uncle Ajyde,’ had to visit Gbotosho’s parents at home in Ibadan to convince them to allow their young son to go these camps and tournaments far away from home. Many times, this meant staying in hotels with adults. Bademosi promised to be his chaperone. Gbotosho was only thirteen years old.

Foremost in his generation, Gbotosho was a trailblazer for cricket in Grier House, GCI and the nation. However, Gbotosho was not the only young Grier House cricketer who benefited from the patronage and mentorship of Jide Bademosi. One such Grierson was Olusegun Yerokun ’71. Born in Ibadan, his dad, Simeon Alabi Yerokun was a civil servant who became a politician in the First Republic representing Oyo North in the Federal House of Representatives under the platform of the NCNC after the 1959 elections. He also served as a Commissioner for Western State after the military took over. His mother was a teacher, nurse and businesswoman. Because of his dad’s travels, Yerokun grew up in Lagos, but came back to Ibadan to attend GCI. In sports, he started with hockey. But as a left-hander, his handling of the hockey stick was a bit awkward. The coach Mr Singh, a Sikk from India who was seconded to the Western State Sports Council, turned him into a hockey goalkeeper. It was that position that secured Yerokun a place in the GCI and Western State hockey teams.

In cricket, Yerokun was a left-handed leg spin bowler. He played for the Grier House and GCI junior cricket team in Forms 2 and 3. And from Form 4, he not only played for the school, he was a member of the Western State cricket team. This was when Jide Bademosi became his mentor. Thus it was that Bademosi, a Grier House sports icon from the mid to late 1950s became the inspiration and impetus for the sports ascendancy of generations of younger Griersons,

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: The End of an Era
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: It is true that 1980 has become a year of infamy in the eyes of many GCI old boys. This is not only because that year marked the implementation of a new government policy that abolished the boarding school system that had been the heart…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
> ‘Ichabod, Ichabod,
> The glory has departed.’
> — Jóhann Ludwig Uhland (1787-1862)

It is true that 1980 has become a year of infamy in the eyes of many GCI old boys. This is not only because that year marked the implementation of a new government policy that abolished the boarding school system that had been the heart and soul of GCI since its founding 50 years earlier. The government also moved swiftly to implement its “catchment area” policy. This meant GCI would now only admit primary school pupils who lived in and around Apata Ganga. In addition, the admission process was no longer the carefully planned and competitive process it had been for half a century. Now, admission to GCI became shoddy and unplanned, shrouded in the suffocating blanket of Nigerian bureaucracy.

Thus, the last full set of boarders in Grier House was the 1976 September set which had 27 students in the first Form. All indications are that the seniors and prefects left to manage Grier House in those challenging and uncertain times did a good job. They kept up the spirit of the boarding students as they toiled in the prep room, keeping up with house chores and competing on the playing fields against Field, Swanston, Carr and Powell. They did their best to keep up the old House traditions, rules and discipline. ‘Teurs’ were assigned to the new boys as in the old days. Yinka Gbotosho, who was in Form 5 that year, was the Head of House. He saw to it that all the new students took the house test and that they were fully integrated into the dormitory system.

The following year, 1977, only 2 boys joined the boarding House in September. They were Awosan and Frederick Ladapo. Through the course of the next two years, 5 additional boys joined: Umo Antia, Emmanuel Akpan, Gbenro Onibokun, Morufu and Jelili. By this time, due to the paucity of senior boys who had actually experienced the full dormitory tradition that normally served to inculcate the younger students into the ways of the House, many Grier House rules and traditions fell by the wayside. Thus, not all new boys were able to take the House test. This famous rite of passage had become more or less voluntary.

Each class in the school in 1977  had 6 arms (streams) with a census of about 240 per class for each year. At this time, over 50% of the GCI student population were day students. But by the beginning of the 1979/80 session, 80% of new intakes into GCI were day students. It was true at this time that new students admitted to GCI were still assigned to Grier House as well as the other Houses for the purpose of classification and inter-house competitions. But big cracks in adherence to and compliance with the old traditions, rules and culture of Grier House and the rest of GCI became noticeable from the beginning.

The job of prefects and seniors, who were supposed to maintain discipline and keep junior boys in line, became more difficult. Senior students in that era who were school prefects like Griersons Ope-Ewe Olumide ’73 and Adegbemisola Oladunjoye ’76 bore the brunt and frustration of this. They complained bitterly to the principal, who could do little to ameliorate the situation. All the prefects could do was to try their best while they rued the general indiscipline among their fellow students, especially the juniors. They noted the high rate of lateness and even non-attendance for the morning Assembly, but there was little they could do.

These overworked prefects could not even count the number of students who now broke those small rules that made GCI what it was. Junior boys now routinely kept their shirts untucked out of their shorts, wore dirty or incomplete uniforms, and wore incorrect footwear to school. In this latter category, there were boys who were actually seen wearing bathroom slippers to class. Enforcing the wearing of socks was out of the question. The problem of enforcing discipline was compounded by the fact that an erring student could not be held back after school hours since he was a day student who had to go home to eat lunch. And he could not be brought back to the school compound on the weekend to serve his punishment as in the old days. The prefects also knew that were they to try and enforce any of the time-honored disciplinary methods, the parents of these students would be outraged. They had not experienced anything akin to this overbearing attitude of GCI senior boys and prefects with their other children attending other schools.

Most of the boarding students remaining in Grier House when school resumed in September 1980 after the government announced its decision to ban boarding schools across the state, became day students or left the school. The only boys remaining in the Grier House dormitories were mainly those admitted in or before 1976. Rumors were rife among the students and even the tutors that a plan was afoot to rid Grier House of all its boarding students and use its buildings for another purpose. Most of the remaining boarding students in Grier House were therefore moved to Field House. A year later, they were again moved to Carr House. Out of the 220 students admitted into Form 1 in GCI in 1978, 40% were boarders. In 1981, Tunji Taiwo of the ’76 set, who was now in Form 5, and 11 other boys were all that remained of the boarding students holding out in four rooms of the Grier House building. These boys were Adepoju, Adejobi, Aikhoje,  Ayodeji, Ajayi, Odutola, Adenekan, Bello, Akinyede, Elegbede and Adelakun..

The next year 1982 would be the final nail in the coffin for dormitory life in Grier House. That year, Gbenga Jegede, a Grierson of the ’75 set was Head of School. This was his seventh year in Grier House, and he was now in the Upper Sixth form. But as the Head of School, he did not have to live inside the Grier House building. He had his own private apartment with bedroom, private shower and toilet close to the Central Dining Room. Of course, this arrangement had been the case for Heads of schools in GCI since 1964. Thus, one could say that at least in one respect, the old days had not completely departed. The head of Grier House that year was Babalola Thompson, Jegede’s close friend who had taken over after Jegede was selected as the Head of school.

Despite all the changes around him, Jegede saw himself as a product of the old GCI – a school built on honor, academic excellence and ascendancy in sports. That year, he was eighteen years old. He had already proven himself as belonging in the ranks of those leaders that GCI and Grier House had produced for more than half a century. He believed that Grier House and GCI had combined to give him a good education and had taught him discipline, leadership, the usefulness of participating in sports, and most importantly how to live in a close community of many individuals with different attitudes on life.

A photograph, taken that year 1982 of Jegede and other school prefects, has survived. Looking at it now, we can see seven confident looking young men with Jegede at the center. They stand with heads-up stances in a well posed group on a grass lawn in front of the Assembly Hall. They are all wearing dark grey trousers, long sleeved white shirts and blue-and-maroon striped school tie - the outfit in their time for GCI seniors on formal occasions. In the center of the group, Jegede looks confidentially into the camera. He is tall, slim and good-looking, with keen bright eyes and an enigmatic smile that seems to linger around the corners of his mouth. We should not be surprised at his poise and confidence. For in his final year in school, Jegede could look back at his 7 years in GCI with pleasure and satisfaction. From Form 2, he had been a member of the school’s select Army Cadet Unit. Now in his final year, he was the leader of that unit. He must have been aware of how dashing and commanding he looked in his ceremonial military uniform whenever he reviewed his platoon at a parade for visiting dignitaries. He was also the leader of the school marching team which held the GCI banner high when it came first in the March Past ceremony at the Independence Day celebrations at the Liberty Stadium. And of course, he excelled in sports, as all good Griersons did, and played hockey for his house and school.  Indeed, he captained both teams. Now as the outgoing Head of School of the best school in his part of the country, can we be surprised that this young man would be confident of his accomplishments and be very hopeful of the ambitions he entertained for himself in the future?

When he posed with his fellow prefects for that picture in June 1982, Jegede knew with some sadness that he belonged to a special set of Griersons. He and his classmates entered the House in 1975. And they would be the last to spend the entirety of their school years in the formal well organized boarding house system that had characterized Grier House since 1930. In future years after they had had departed, future generations who wanted to be boarders would have to live in quasi private hostels cramped into a single house – Carr House. This of course was a picture for the future that did not much bother these happy buoyant final years students. So, on his last day in school in July that year, Jegede went to Grier House to say farewell to his classmates and juniors still living in the house. They walked around the familiar rooms, the HSC block, and the quadrangle one last time before they packed their bags to leave the school for good. They looked intently at each other and sighed. They were not sure if Grier House would be there when they came back for a reunion in another year. They were like characters in ‘The last of the Mohicans.’

Our narrative from that year tells us that three months later in September 1982 at the beginning of the 1982-83 academic year, all the boarders who should have resumed in Grier House, along with the remaining boarding students in Field House, were moved to Powell House. For some of the students, the shock of this forced relocation was almost as bad as if they were moving to a totally different school. They had to move at very short notice all their possessions and gear, both personal to each student and those that belonged to the House as a whole – trophies, documents, beds, lockers and so on that had accumulated in that House for 30 years after the current building was put in place in 1952. No single boy was allowed to remain behind in Grier House. And the place could have become a ghost town except that its buildings were rapidly taken over by a completely new school created by the government – the Apata Ganga Grammar School.

The result of this non-boarding policy was disastrous not just for Grier House but for the whole school. From that academic year beginning in September 1982, the quality of GCI students in academics, sports and leadership potential dropped steadily. And Grier House, that place of traditions, which had established itself for half a century as the doyen of Houses in a nationally-recognized school, now existed in name only. Its students, along with the school of which they were a part, descended a long, painful downhill slope. This became a four-decade long decline, that would later be known as the ‘lost years.’

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: The Head of Grier House as a Sports Paragon: the Onajin Example
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: Our narrative tells us that in the decade after Independence in 1960, sports continued to play a larger-than-life role in the affairs of Grier House. This went into the selection of its student leaders. Most of the Heads of House in that…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
Our narrative tells us that in the decade after Independence in 1960, sports continued to play a larger-than-life role in the affairs of Grier House. This went into the selection of its student leaders. Most of the Heads of House in that era were expected to have an unimpeachable sports record. And many were school captains in their sport. These were the big men on campus who wore their school colors – caps, blazers and maroon-and-blue ties - with pride. In this group, we had Griersons like Maito, the football captain who was the Head of House in 1960. Then it was Eboreime, a champion athlete who received the nod in 1963. Onajin, a much-admired cricket icon, was selected as Head of House in 1964. In 1965, it was Niyi Akanji, a football maestro in the mold of Maito, who occupied the top seat in the Grier House leadership hierarchy. He was followed by the noted athlete, Ernest Odigie in 1966. Two years later in 1968, the Head of House was Bambo Oyekan, a sturdy cricketer, although he later moved to the position of Head of school the same year.  In similar vein, the Ogunmoyela brothers, Kayode in 1969 and Gbenga in 1971, were multi-sport athletes and captains of the school team in their sport, who everyone knew, when their turns came, to be virtual locks for the Head of House position. Two words described all these Griersons who were chosen as heads of Grier House throughout the 1960s - natural-born leaders and paragons of sports.

A representative Grierson of that era who was universally admired as a natural leader and sports icon was Abimbola Onajin. Like two of his famous classmates, Funso Famuyiwa and Niyi Akanji, Onajin entered GCI in the 1958 set. His father, Samuel Olaniyi Onajin, hailed from Ondo but settled in Ibadan after securing employment with the Western Region Agriculture Department in Moor Plantation. Thus, his residence and place of work - in the same sprawling tree-dotted compound -  were located right next to the GCI compound. Thus, as a boy growing up in the mid-1950s, Onajin lived next door to GCI. The primary school he attended was the N.A. school which abutted the east end of the GCI playing field with no fence between the two. Thus, young schoolboys from this primary school could often be seen in the afternoon after school watching a relay race or a cricket match on the GCI Main Field. It could be said that young Onajin grew up with GCI on his mind. There was never any doubt which secondary school he was going to attend when his turn came.

It also helped that Bimbo Onajin’s 2 older brothers had attended GCI and were Griersons. His eldest brother, Michael Olubunmi Onajin of the set of ’49, set the bar high for his younger siblings. During his time, he was Head of House and captain of cricket for Grier House and the school. A second brother, Olufemi Kehinde Onajin followed in 1955.  He too had a great career in academics but did not participate in sports at a high level.  So, when Bimbo Onajin entered Grier House in January 1958, according to the accepted terminology, he was referred to during roll calls as Onajin III. Onajin III was no slouch in the classroom or on the sports field. He wanted to be an engineer. So, he stuck to science subjects, especially Physics and Mathematics. Every GCI boy in those days was either going to a physician or else an engineer. GCI students did not go for Arts subjects or Social Studies. And as a rule, they did not become lawyers, accountants or personnel managers. They were not good as politicians either – maybe because GCI products were too honest and morally rigid as a result of the ethical upbringing instilled in them in their ‘colonial’ British school.

Onajin was a bright lad, the kind of student Grier House and GCI were built for. He achieved all his objectives in coming to GCI.
