He played several sports and he became captain of cricket not only for Grier House but the school. And in his final year in the Upper Sixth form, he was made a school prefect and Head of Grier House. But this position ended with an asterisk, for Onajin transferred to Swanston House in the middle of his tenure as Head of Grier House. This was the result of a fallout he had with his Housemaster over the discipline of erring junior boys. He remained a dutiful and morally upright Grierson and GCI boy even at his own peril. He would rather defend truth and honor than bow to pressure to do what he thought was not right.

Incidentally, Bimbo Onajin had yet another brother Olakunle (Onajin IV) who was admitted to GCI in 1968. But this Onajin declined to come to Grier House. Due perhaps to what had transpired between his brother and the Housemaster in Grier House, Onajin IV opted instead for Field House where, true to his family tradition, he too had a stellar career and became Head of House.

What stands out to the chronicler of Griersons in that golden area between the late 50s and early 60s was the surfeit of extraordinary characters that were in Grier House in that period. These were students with singular gifts who were equally good in the classroom, the science laboratory, and the sports field. We just have to look at some of the classmates who came in with Bimbo Onajin in the class of 1958 - boys like Funso Famuyiwa and Niyi Akande who were ace footballers and became school prefects. But it needs to be said that not all Bimbo Onajin’s classmates in Grier House in that exceptional set made their name as sportsmen. For instance, there was Ahmed Abdulai, whose claim to fame was not athletics. He was an albino, and his poor eyesight in the glare of the afternoon sun precluded a career in football or cricket. But he was very good academically and shone in Literature and Creative Writing. He went on to become a very successful lawyer.

As we can see from the example of Onajin, Grier Heads of House in the 1960s were chosen based on a simple formula. They had to be paragons of sports. They were reasonably good in academics. And they were leaders who knew how to make other students idolize them and follow them. But by the early 1970s until the end of the decade, this system for the selection of Heads of House in Grier House was briefly altered. No longer were Grier Heads of House to be rigidly chosen from a roll call of its acclaimed sports heroes. Rather, student leaders were selected for their character, academic ability and leadership qualities. This change was epitomized by Olurotimi Jaiyesimi in 1972, Olubolanle Ayodele in 1973 and Yomi Shobowale from September 1973.

From that time onwards over the course of that decade, this change in custom in the selection of Grier Heads of house presaged the calamity of 1980. That was the year that the state government  announced the abolition of  the boarding system in secondary schools all over the state. The result was the total disappearance of student dormitories in Grier House by September 1982. And after this, the position of Head of Grier House lost its power and allure.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: The Legend of Victor Ojutalayo
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: After Harding Ekperigin and Jide Bademosi, the third great Grier House sportsman was Victor Ojutalayo. It was he who received the intergeneration sports baton from Bademosi. Ojutalayo met Bademosi in school, having arrived in Grier House…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
After Harding Ekperigin and Jide Bademosi, the third great Grier House sportsman was Victor Ojutalayo. It was he who received the intergeneration sports baton from Bademosi. Ojutalayo met Bademosi in school, having arrived in Grier House in 1955, two years after Bademosi entered.  Victor Ojutalayo’s father, Gabriel Elusoji Ojutalayo, was himself a GCI old boy. But he was in Swanston House and belonged to the 1931 set with school number 94. In those pioneer days, when GCI athletes ran on their bare feet, the elder Ojutalayo earned fame as a notable long-distance runner who was given the nickname “Sukuru Boy” – schoolboy - by the older athletes from the Nigerian Army and Police who he competed against.

On entering GCI and being assigned to Grier House, young Ojutalayo was determined to tread in his father’s footsteps. And not only that, he set out to improve on his father’s legacy. And in doing so, he was undeterred by the fact that his two brothers who were admitted to GCI the same year as him were in different Houses. One of his brothers, Kole, was in Carr House. The other brother, Johnson, had been assigned to Swanston House. Despite every other attachment of filial love and affection, Victor would go on to prove the superiority of maroon over blue and orange. In the years that followed, as a Grier House stand-out, Ojutalayo emphatically stamped his mark as a generational talent on the athletic field. And in doing so, he brought tears to the eyes of his brothers whenever he faced their Carr and Swanton teams.

Like his dad before him, the tall and lanky Ojutalayo became a star in mid and long-distance track events. Over the years, he won so many laurels for Grier House and GCI that his friends stopped counting. He capped his stellar school career by winning the Victor Ludorum trophy in 1962, his last year in school. By this time, he was in Upper Six and was a much admired and beloved Head of School under the famous D. J. Bullock, the last expatriate principal of GCI.  By this time, Ojutalayo had already shown that he was marked out for leadership and greatness. In the classroom, on the House grounds, and on the sports field, he came to the notice of everyone who met and interacted with him. The words used to describe him were ‘natural-born leader,’ ‘achiever,’ and ‘best of the best.’ He was admired, by teachers and fellow students alike, for his discipline, focus and commitment to excellence in everything he put his mind to.

Victor Ojutalayo became a Grier House legend not because he won many trophies during his time. It was because he was a champion who broke records. Thus, between 1958 and 1962, he held the National Senior Record and the Commonwealth Secondary School Record in the 880 yards and the mile. And on one memorable day in 1957, he broke the GCI record in the mile previously held two decades earlier by his father, Gabriel. While still in school, Ojutalayo was already making a name for himself as an international athlete. He competed for the Nigerian national team while still in Grier House. And his exploits were faithfully recorded and celebrated by the national newspapers and sports journals of the day.

Many more stories have come to us of Victor Ojutalyo and his high achieving contemporaries, including some who did not attend GCI.  One of these was his dear friend and fellow national athlete. This young man was Sydney Asiodu, who served as Head Boy of Igbobi College in the same year that Ojutalayo was Head of House in GCI. Both were brilliant on the sports field as well as in the classroom and other arenas of striving and endeavor. They were popular heroes who were admired not just in their respective schools, but all over Nigeria. Those who observed them closely declared they were the bright young hopes of their newly independent country. In fact, Asiodu and Ojutalayo were the first recipients of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Scholarship for Excellence in Sports.

But Asiodu was an Ibo from the eastern part of Nigeria which seceded from the rest of the country at the start of the Nigerian Civil War to form the shortlived, ill-fated enclave of Biafra in 1967. The story that Ojutalayo later told his family was that at the beginning of that national crisis, he pleaded with his friend Asiodu to stay behind in Lagos. But when his friend was unrelenting, saying he had to be with his family who had all gone back to the East, it was Ojutalayo who took Asiodu to the motor park to begin that fateful journey into Biafra. A few months later, Asiodu, one of the most promising sports men and academicians of his generation, was dead – a casualty of the deadly Biafran-Nigerian war. That scene at the motor park, which was the last time the two friends would ever see each other, was a farewell that Victor Ojutalayo would never forget.

Our narrative says that Victor Ojutalayo became celebrated as a Grierson because of his vision, brilliance and undisputed talent in and outside the sports arena. His legacy is clear and disputed. He cemented for his generation in the late 50s and early 60s the sports dominance of Grier House that had been established by those who came before him – heroes in their time like Ekperigin and Bademosi.

api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.title: The Story of Famuyiwa and ‘Mighty’
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.excerpt: When the new year dawned on January 1, 1955, the lives of most Griersons continued to follow the old pattern. As with previous generations since 1930, the boarding students were allowed no time for idleness between the wake-up bell at 6 am…
api::dare-to-learn-excerpt.dare-to-learn.body:
> ‘When all the world is young
> And all the trees are green,
> Young blood must have its course
> And every dog his day.’
> William Thackeray (1811-1163)
> ‘These are the days of our youth,
> Our days of glory and honour.’
> Wilfred Scawen Blunt (1840-1922)

When the new year dawned on January 1, 1955, the lives of most Griersons continued to follow the old pattern. As with previous generations since 1930, the boarding students were allowed no time for idleness between the wake-up bell at 6 am and lights out at 9.45pm. The rhythm of their lives flowed calmly like the surface of a placid lake in a quiet valley protected from powerful storms by high mountains on all sides.  But within this calm water, there was a new element bubbling below the surface. This was the murmuring of a new political awakening up and down the colonized country of Nigeria. For in that year 1955, hopes for independence from Great Britain were on everyone’s mind. The parents of these happy students and even their neighbors talked of nothing else. The students heard all about it when they went home for vacation. Their tutors mentioned it in class. And in the newspapers, they read that their politicians, especially their own very progressive premier in the Western Region, shouted out loudly that something would be done in this regard in a very short time. Indeed, many people speculated that Independence for Nigeria from Britain would occur very soon indeed – at most before the end of the decade.

Perhaps because of these hopeful rumblings and rumors of Independence for their nation, many Griersons who were in school during this era sensed that they had entered GCI at a happy and propitious time indeed. This surely was the dawn of a new golden age of freedom and possibilities in the history of their beloved House and school. For never in the history of the school had the students had it so good. As the 1950s went on its delightfully hopeful way before giving way to the turbulent 1960s, our chroniclers tell us that it was a happy time for most Griersons.  Food in the school had improved. The students lived in better dormitories, newly built in 1952. Sports facilities and equipment were better and more readily available. And the quality of the teachers left nothing more to be asked for. These boys in Grier House had come of age at a time when their country was getting richer and more assured of its status as an emerging nation on the world stage. Their country Nigeria was beginning to be referred to as the giant of Africa – a sleeping giant that is. The parents of these students were more educated and more financially viable than was the case with students a generation ago. Gone were the days when the average GCI student or Grierson was the son of a subsistence farmer from a rural backwater in Yorubaland or a struggling fishermen casting his net in the creeks of the Niger Delta. These boys were younger, better clothed and in better health than students of the previous generation.

Many of these Griersons who came in the late 1950s and the early 1960s were the sons of civil servants, politicians and well to do businessmen. Some of them were second generation Griersons. Their fathers had attended GCI in those earlier years in the 1930s. Their names, when called out during the morning assembly, rang like a roll call of Grier House history – Ojutalayo, Arubayi, Deko, Beckley, Ajomale, Ifaturoti, and Otegbeye. And some families – not just those with old boys as patriarchs, sent their children, sometime two or more siblings at the same time, to Grier House and GCI in droves. These siblings with the same last name were referred to as Famuyiwa I and II, Enobakhare I and II,  Osemekhian I, II and III, and on and on. Grier House and GCI had become legacy institutions.

A typical member of this generation was Olufunso (Funso) Famuyiwa. He came into Grier House with the 1958 set, but he had a younger brother, Oluyemi, who came in 5 years later in 1963. According to accepted Grier House usage, Yemi was called Famuyiwa II. In true Grier House fashion, both became great sportsmen. The older brother, Funso, played football for the house and school, the younger, Yemi excelled in cricket at the house and school level.

The Famuyiwa family history was typical of that era. Both their parents were well-educated middle-class professionals and civil servants. Their mother was a nurse at Adeoyo Hospital Ibadan, while their father was a civil servant and teacher who had been educated at Wesley College Ibadan. This was one of the first educational institutions for the training of teachers in the nation. It was the same school that was the alma mater of such notables as Obafemi Awolowo, the first premier of the Western region and Samuel Ighodaro who at that time was serving as the Minister of Justice under Awo. Ighodaro was a famous jurist and politician who sent several of his sons to GCI including Wilfred Ighodaro, a Grierson of the 1961.

The Famuyiwa family hailed from Ilesha. But their father, John Oladapo Famuyiwa, led a peripatetic existence when his children were growing up in the 1940s and 1950s. This was due to his job as a teacher and civil servant which took him to several towns and cities in Lagos and the Western Region. His occupation included stints as a teacher at his old school, Wesley College, Ibadan and at Ansarudeen College Lagos. At one time, he was also First Secretary in the Western Region Ministry of Education. By the late 1950s, when his first son Funso was preparing to enter GCI, the elder Famuyiwa had settled in the Oke Ado area of Ibadan, where he had built a comfortable residence.

Funso Famuyiwa attended the N.A. Practicing School Ibadan. At that time, this was one of the best primary schools in Ibadan which specialized in preparing students for entry into prestigious secondary schools like GCI. His parents were determined that Funso should go to the best secondary school in the Western Region, and this is exactly what he did. After passing the tough entrance examination and interview, Famuyiwa was admitted to GCI. His resumption date in Grier House, where he was assigned to, was supposed to be in September 1957. But it was at this time that the government of the Western Region decided to change the school year for all secondary schools in the Region to the calendar year system starting in January and ending in December. Previously, some schools like GCI had their fresh intakes every September echoing the British system. Thus, instead of coming in in September 1957, Famuyiwa and his set started school in January 1958.

In Grier House over the next seven years, Famuyiwa enjoyed the life of a typical GCI boarding student of that era. He played sports at a high level, representing Grier House and the school in football and specializing in the long jump in athletics. He also did very well in his schoolwork. He paid particular attention to science subjects, and was always at the top of his class in Zoology. Very early in life, he had decided he wanted to be a physician.

When Famuyiwa arrived in Grier House on that January day in 1958, he met two other young boys with whom he formed a tight circle which included other boys who shared their interests especially for sports.  All three were bonded by a lasting love for Grier House and a natural comfort with the rigors of the athletic field. These two boys were Bimbo Onajin, who would later become captain of cricket for Grier House and the school, and Niyi Akanji who became captain of football. Both became Heads of Grier House in their time, but with separate ironic twists to their stories. Akanji did not come back early to join his other classmates of the ’58 set for Higher School. So, he finished higher school a year later and was Head of House in 1965. Onajin, a brilliant student, generational sportsman and leader of men, was Head of House in 1964. But he had to transfer in the middle of that year to Swanston House after a fallout with his Housemaster, Mr. Oyetunji.

But there was more than athletic supremacy to the story of why Funso had such a great time in Grier House. On the social side of school life, Funso found that there were more opportunities now than in the past for GCI boys to meet and chat up girls who attended plays staged in the school assembly hall by students of the GCI Dramatic Society. The school plays he remembered watching during his days in GCI included Galileo, Sweeney Todd and A Man for all Seasons. As usual, the girls’ schools that GCI boys wanted to be associated with were St. Annes, St Theresa’s, Yejide and St. Louise. Famuyiwa, for his part, found himself favoring St. Theresa’s. Something about their school uniform and beret stole his heart.

And as was the case with Grier House boys in the previous generation, music from the gramophone playing loudly at the Saturday social nights was the glue that bound together their social life. At this time in the late 1950s, a new local music genre had recently been added to the repertoire of imported popular music from England and America. This new music was called  ‘highlife.’ A mixture of American jazz, West Indian calypso, Cuban rhythms and a heavy dose of African drums, this music was the reincarnation of the old palm wine music of Julius Araba and Fatai Rolling Dollar from the 1940s and early 1950s. Its main champions of the new era were Ambrose Campbell who would soon decamp to England and Bobby Benson who was based in Lagos.

Sports however remained the universal milieu through which status was gained in Grier House. Like all Griersons since the beginning of the House, Famuyiwa and his classmates had to participate in all the sports that had been introduced to GCI since the time of V. B. V. Powell. These of course included swimming. Famuyiwa noticed that the best swimmers among the students were boys from the Ijaw area of the Western Region. He too learnt to swim and rather enjoyed it. But sadly, by the time Famuyiwa was in the fifth form in 1962, the school swimming pool, which was still in its old location next to the principal’s house, was in a deteriorating state. This became so bad - along with the high cost of maintenance and filling the pool up with water -  that this swimming pool, long a staple of life in GCI since the 1930s, was abandoned a couple of years later in 1964. The cost of building and maintaining a new swimming pool proved to be too prohibitive for the Western Region government. A few years later, an arrangement was made for our boys to learn their swimming at the nearby privately owned Lafia Hotel. Alas, the days of every Grierson having to swim 3 lengths of the 50 feet pool to attain his standard points in swimming, and not disgrace himself and his House, became a relic of the past.

The Grier House that Famuyiwa came into in 1958 was still a credible power in GCI interhouse sports, especially in cricket. After all, the exploits of Tade in cricket were still recounted in the house legends, and Bademosi ’53, the formidable batsman and bowler would not leave Grier House until 1960 and by the time Famuyiwa came to know him more intimately, had already hoisted several trophies won by his team on behalf of Grier House. Sports-loving Griersons of that era who were proud to call themselves proteges of this Bademosi included not just Famuyiwa and Onajin, but Ojutalayo who came in 1956 and the aforesaid Akanji.

But it must be said that the adoration with which these younger boys held Bademosi had as much to with his talent on the sports field as his general swagger and panache. Thus, these boys tried to copy Bademosi’s mannerisms. One was his special walk which required the shoulders to be held slightly sideways while moving forward. They also  ‘flew’ the collar of their shirts the way Bademosi did, even though they had to do this without getting caught and punished. Famuyiwa and his friends also loved Bademosi because he went easy on them and was never known to have punished a junior boy throughout his time in Grier House. Famuyiwa was more inspired now more than before to choose Medicine as his future career when it became known to everyone in Grier House that Bademosi was going to attend the University College Ibadan to become a doctor. It is certainly no accident that Famuyiwa too went on to study Medicine at the University of Ibadan.

But while his hero Bademosi made his mark in cricket, Famuyiwa devoted his skills to the football field. He started representing the school team right from his first year in school in Form 1 as a member of the ‘mosquito’ team. By Form 2, he had graduated to the junior team. He led Grier House to win the junior football trophy in Form 3. And by Form 4, he was on the first eleven of the Senior school team. Famuyiwa remembered that the school football captain was his Grier Head of house. This was Moito, a great defender and stalwart of the backfield. Famuyiwa would always remember vividly the day GCI played against Loyola College and the match took place on the Loyola field. His parents came to watch him play. But the GCI team lost to Loyola by a lone goal.

What happened was this. Playing in his customary outside left position, Famuyiwa had to go up against an impenetrable Loyola College full back, a giant of a man nicknamed ‘Mighty.’ Famuyiwa dribbled past this ‘Mighty’ character once, trying to score a goal. But after this, Mighty’s philosophy of ‘if you miss the ball, don’t miss the leg’ carried the day. Famuyiwa’s usual modus operandus was to rely on his speed while he made his shifty moves in the wings to display the defenders before crossing the ball to his center forward waiting just outside the opponent’s goal post. But on that day, ‘Mighty’ repeatedly struck at Famuyiwa’s shin, studiously ignoring the ball. This illegal tactic paid off. ‘Mighty’ did not allow Famuyiwa to move anywhere. It was not a day of glory for GCI. The boys sneaked back into their ‘Black Maria’ with cries of “Up Loyo!” ringing in their ears from jeering Loyola College boys who had gathered around the GCI school lorry. But next year, 1964, which was Famuyiwa’s final year, he had his revenge. That year, GCI beat Loyola College and reached the semifinal round of the Thermogene Cup for secondary schools in the Western Region.

Famuyiwa also remembered that anytime the King’s College team came to play in GCI, the boys from Lagos would be camped in their dormitory in Grier House. Segun Bucknor of King’s College, though he did not play football, always managed to make the trip to Ibadan with the team. In the late evening after the match, on the Grier House grounds, Bucknor would take out his guitar. He would then regale boys from both teams with highlife and ‘pop’ tunes.  According to Famuyiwa, Bucknor was a great character even in those days. Not surprisingly, he became a noted soul musician in Lagos in the 1960s and 1970s with the nickname ‘adorin sogba sogba’ on account of having shaved his head which reputedly was going bald.

api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.title: About Extracurricular Activities
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.summary: The wider mission of the Grier History and Traditions Committee beyond the Museum and Library.
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.body: The responsibilities of the Grier History and Traditions Committee go beyond establishing and maintaining the Grier Museum and Library. The wider mission of this Committee is to organize students living in the Grier House dormitory so they can engage in various activities (outside sports) outside the classroom. Therefore, the Museum and Library also oversees the following activities for the students:

api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.title: Grier Museum & Library Student Coordinators
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.summary: Student Librarian, Deputy Librarian, custodian and janitor of the Museum and Library.
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.body:
Extra-curricular Student Leadership: Apart from the Head of House and other house prefects chosen formally each year by the house and school authorities, capable leaders among the students will be chosen for the extracurricular activities initiated or reintroduced from old traditions by the Grier House History and Traditions Committee. These student positions and tasks include:

- The maintenance of the physical space of the Museum and Library in the positions of Librarian, Deputy Librarian, custodian and janitor.

These students assigned to the above positions and tasks will be excused from some of the chores required of students in the House.

api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.title: Grier House Marching Band
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.summary: Parade drums, trumpets and flutes to galvanize Grier House teams at interhouse sports.
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.body:
Grier House Marching Band for which parade drums, trumpets, flutes and other musical instruments have been made available. This group will perform at all interhouse sports events to galvanize our Grier House teams to the highest level of performance. Their role will be similar those of ‘cheerleading’ teams in school sports in the United States. This Grier House Marching will be at the forefront of the efforts to teach other Griersons in the proper rendition of our House Song, our Grier House pep song and other lively tunes they have composed or have been taught. Beyond Grier House, they will also entertain at other school events both on the field and in the Assembly Hall.

- Officers of the Grier House Marching Band which now include the Band Major, 5 drummers (on bass, tenor, snare drums, and cymbals), and 4 singers.

api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.summary: Students restarting the Mustard Seed House magazine as an online publication.
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.body:
An Editorial team has set to work to restart the “Mustard Seed” House magazine as an online publication on our website. This magazine which will be solely created, edited, published and managed by Grier House students, is planned to be published twice a year, December and June.

api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.title: Others
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.summary: Saturday Night Socials, board games, music and the audiovisual learning system.
api::extracurricular-activity.extracurri.body:
**Saturday Night Socials**

An occasion for students to come together for a fun-filled evening in the prep room with debates, recitations, drama sketches, song competitions and even physical sports like boxing with gloves and pillow fights. The highlight of the evening is always music (played in the old days on the gramophone) and dancing.

**Also supported by the Museum and Library**

- Audiovisual learning system based in the library and museum, with computers, monitors, speakers and printers with WiFi connectivity
- Radio and digital music to be blared out from wall mounted speakers for Saturday night social nights and other social events in the Museum/Library and adjoining reading room (prep room)
- Board games for our students including Monopoly, Ludo, Draughts, Scrabble and our traditional ‘ayo.’

api::archive-item.archive-item.description:
Interview of Wole Soyinka, following his release from detention on October 8, 1969, for his unsanctioned talks with the secessionist Biafran rebel leader Col. Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu.

Arrest date: August 17, 1967. Release date: October 8, 1969.

Charges: He was not formally charged or tried; he was detained without trial by the federal military government under General Yakubu Gowon after meeting with Biafran leaders and calling for a cease-fire during the Nigerian Civil War, leading to accusations of being a Biafran sympathizer, spy, or conspiring with rebels.

api::home-page.home-page.welcomeText:
Grier House, founded in 1930, is one of the 2 foundational boarding Houses of Government College Ibadan, one of the most renowned historically elite boarding secondary schools in Africa. Boys who have passed through Grier House call themselves Griersons. Through the generations, Griersons have played leading roles in the cultural, academic and political development of Nigeria and the African continent.

The Grier Museum and Library, established in October 2026, is a legacy project that encapsulates the narratives and aspirations of generations of Griersons.

Welcome to the online platform of the Grier House Museum and Library, a living repository of the history, achievements and legacy of generations of Griersons. Here are the stories, photographs, experiences and contributions of past and current students who have passed through the walls of Grier House, ensuring that future generations know what Grier House has stood for since it was founded in 1930.

> “Through this initiative, the story of Grier House has been given a permanent place in the historical records of Government College Ibadan.”
> — Wilfred Ighodaro ‘61

> “If you know anything, share it. If you don’t know something, search for it.”
> — motto of the Grier Museum and Library

This platform is not just about the past. Click on the menu contents to learn what is going on currently in Grier House, what the  House Governor has to say, and what current students have to say through their narratives published in the iconic Grier House magazine, The Mustard Seed.
api::home-page.home-page.supportTitle: Please Support the Grier Museum & Library
api::home-page.home-page.supportIntro: To maintain the Grier Museum and Library we need both books and cash donations:
api::home-page.home-page.supportBooks:
We need BOOKS at all times to keep the Library well stocked. The books we have are of the highest quality and we want to maintain this standard. It is fair to say that there is no major or important book published in Western literature in the past 400 years that is not represented in our collection - from Shakespeare (3 different volumes of his Complete Works) and Chaucer (The Canterbury Tales) to Milton (Paradise Lost & Paradise Regained), Dickens (Tale of Two Cities, Great Expectations) and Thomas Hardy (The Mayor of Casterbridge). We have such rare original books as ‘The Origin of Species’ by Charles Darwin, Dante’s ‘Inferno’, ‘Das Kapital’ by Karl Marx (English translation ‘Capital’) and Leo Tolstoy’s ‘War and Peace.’ All major Nigerian writers are represented - Wole Soyinka, Chinua Achebe, Cyprian Ekwensi, Elechi Amadi and others. Also the historical classics like Wole Ademoyega’s ‘Why we struck’ and other Civil War epics like ‘Reluctant Rebel.’ We want our future fiction and historical book donations to approach this high standard.

This is a reference library for rare books not just for our students but for our old boys and other visitors. We also want to appeal to reputable bookshops in Nigeria to donate books that our children can use in the classroom and for test review and preparations for the Senior and Junior Secondary School certificate exams.
api::home-page.home-page.supportMoney:
And we always need cash donations because we are not just setting up a Museum and Library. Grier House is expanding the spectrum of extracurricular activities for its students in the following areas:

- Audiovisual learning system based in the library and museum, with computers, monitors, speakers and printers with WiFi connectivity
- Grier House Marching Band with trumpet, drums and other instruments to galvanize our boys and players during interhouse competitions - a first in GCI
- Mustard Seed editorial team
- Chess club
- Radio and digital music to be blared out from wall mounted speakers for Saturday night social nights and other social events in the Museum/Library and adjoining reading room (prep room)
- Board games for our students including Monopoly, Ludo, Draughts, Scrabble and our traditional ‘ayo.’
- Money for the upkeep, maintenance and replacement of Museum and Library equipment, books and supplies

api::museum-library-page.museum-library-.history:
## Why a Library for Students in Grier House?

What are the advantages to our young Griersons in having all these books at their disposal in the library section of the GRIER MUSEUM AND LIBRARY. These books range from story books on adventure to textbooks, exam reviews books, atlases, dictionaries and encyclopedias.

There are indeed many. For instance, from the hardcover book “Encyclopedia of Africa”, our students will learn that the country in Southern Africa now called Zambia was named after its largest river, the Zambezi. And that Lake Victoria, the famous source of the Nile River has nothing to do with Victoria Falls, which is on the Zambezi River. Zambia was the former Northern Rhodesia. River Zambezi forms the border between this country and its neighbor Southern Rhodesia which is now known as Zimbabwe after the ancient civilization and ruins of that name.

Indeed, many older Griersons now in their 70s and 80s are going back to the Grier Museum and Library anytime they are in Ibadan for the pleasure of poring over these books to refresh their learning in the ambience of framed iconic photos on the walls, original oil paintings, and trophies in glassed cabinets reminding us of all of our Grier House legacy.

As Akin Tewe. ‘72 said, “We can never stop learning new things.” For our students, the motto of this Library, quoting Diderot’s famous Encyclopedia (completed in France in 1772) is “if you know something, share it; And if you don’t know search for it.”

We want our students to know that no knowledge is useless. Knowledge indeed is power. It brings light into our personal lives and understanding into the wider world. It leads to a more progressive, cooperative and understanding society. It is the first thing a man acquires that leads to wisdom and understanding!

— Oladele Olusanya ‘65
